0.name: Kimsuky
0.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Kimsuky, also known as APT43, Springtail, Thallium, Velvet Chollima, Emerald Sleet, Black Banshee, and G0086, is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group. Its key malware and tools include the AppleSeed backdoor, the BabyShark malware (with its ReconShark component), Endoor, and XenoRAT. Its TTPs involve credential and input capture, screen capture, data exfiltration over HTTP, and the use of phishing lures disguised as official documents. The group primarily targets entities in South Korea, Japan, and the United States, with a focus on government, think tanks, and organizations involved in foreign policy and nuclear security, to conduct espionage in support of North Korean strategic interests.[/profile]

1.name: T1503
1.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1503, known as "Credentials from Web Browsers," is a technique within the Credential Access tactic. It operates on multiple platforms, including Windows, by extracting stored credentials from web browsers like Chrome, Firefox, Safari, and Edge. Adversaries achieve this by reading specific browser files, such as Chrome's 'Login Data' database, and executing SQL queries to retrieve encrypted credentials. These can then be decrypted using system functions like `CryptUnprotectData` on Windows, leveraging the victim's cached logon credentials. The technique is also associated with exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2019-2215 and CVE-2019-16098 to facilitate access.[/profile]

2.name: XenoRAT
2.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]XenoRAT is a remote access tool (RAT) written in C# and compatible with Windows 10 and 11. Its key technical behaviors include using command and script interpreters (T1059), capturing keystrokes (T1056.001), performing screen capture (T1113), and leveraging remote services (T1021) for lateral movement, often delivered via phishing (T1566). Associated infrastructure indicators include domains such as siloamclinic.com, kyungdaek.com, gbionet.com, meatalk.com, and vwellpain.com.[/profile]

4.name: TutRAT
4.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TutRAT is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT). It uses phishing (T1566) for initial access and leverages remote services (T1021) for lateral movement. Its key technical behaviors include keylogging (T1056.001) for credential access, screen capture (T1113) for data collection, and the abuse of command and scripting interpreters (T1059) for execution. It has been associated with infrastructure domains such as meatalk.com, vwellpain.com, gbionet.com, kyungdaek.com, and siloamclinic.com.[/profile]

5.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter
5.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) is an Execution tactic technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, IaaS, ESXi, Office Suite, and Identity Provider platforms. It involves adversaries abusing built-in or cross-platform interpreters like Unix Shell, Windows Command Shell, PowerShell, Python, JavaScript, and Visual Basic to execute arbitrary commands, scripts, or binaries. Commands can be delivered via initial access payloads, executed through interactive shells, or run remotely via services, and are often obfuscated to evade detection.[/profile]

6.name: Keylogging
6.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Keylogging, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1056.001, is a credential access and collection tactic used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and network devices. It works by intercepting user keystrokes to capture credentials, employing methods such as hooking API callbacks for keystroke processing, reading raw data from the hardware buffer, modifying the Windows Registry, or installing custom drivers. Adversaries may also clear browser cookies to force re-authentication and increase capture speed. This technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT28, Lazarus Group, and Kimsuky.

23.name: HappyDoor
23.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]HappyDoor is a malware entity. Its known aliases include DOORME and SiestaGraph. It has been associated with groups such as APT23, APT41, APT17, Dagger Panda, Earth Lusca, Tonto Team, and Wet Panda. Its key technical behaviors involve establishing persistence by creating accounts (T1136), using encrypted channels for command and control (T1573), and performing impact activities like stopping services (T1489) and encrypting data (T1486). It also gathers victim host information (T1592). Its infrastructure includes domains like syrsd.p-e.kr, users.nya.pub, ai.hyyeo.p-e.kr, and jp.hyyeo.p-e.kr, with a C2 endpoint at http://jp.hyyeo.pe.kr/index.php.[/profile]

32.name: T1136
32.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1136, known as "Create Account," is a persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud environments. Adversaries create local, domain, or cloud tenant accounts to establish secondary credentialed access, reducing reliance on persistent malware. In cloud environments, accounts may be created with limited service-specific permissions to evade detection. This activity is often followed by modifying account roles for privilege escalation, as seen in operations by groups like Scattered Spider and Indrik Spider.[/profile]

37.name: T1124
37.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1124, System Time Discovery, is a Discovery tactic technique applicable to Windows, macOS, Linux, Network Devices, and ESXi platforms. It involves gathering system time, time zone, or uptime to aid in scheduling malicious tasks, inferring victim location, or triggering time-based payloads. Specific methods include using commands like `net time \\hostname` or `w32tm /tz` on Windows, `systemsetup -gettimezone` on macOS, `show clock detail` on network devices, `esxcli system clock get` on ESXi, and system calls like `time()` on Linux. It has been associated with groups including Lazarus Group, FIN7, and Volt Typhoon.

39.name: T1564
39.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1564, known as Hide Artifacts, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Office Suite platforms. This can also include creating isolated computing regions, such as through virtualization, to hide malicious artifacts from security tools.

40.name: T1105
40.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) is a Command and Control tactic used on Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. Adversaries use native utilities such as `copy`, `certutil`, PowerShell's `Invoke-WebRequest` on Windows, and `curl`, `scp`, `wget` on Linux/macOS/ESXi. The technique is distinct from internal Lateral Tool Transfer (T1570) and adversaries may subsequently delete transferred files (T1070.004). It is widely used by numerous threat groups including APT29, Lazarus, and Volt Typhoon.

41.name: T1027

Adversaries may also split payloads into benign-seeming parts, encode portions of files to hide strings, or use obfuscated scripts. This behavior is commonly employed by groups like APT41, Sandworm Team, and Kimsuky to evade signature-based detection during initial access or execution.

42.name: T1573
42.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1573, Encrypted Channel, is a Command and Control tactic used across Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves using encryption algorithms to conceal C2 traffic, moving beyond standard protocol protections. Implementations may use asymmetric cryptography (T1573.002), like RSA or ElGamal, where data is encrypted with a public key and decrypted with a private key. This technique is vulnerable if secret keys are embedded within malware, enabling reverse engineering. Associated vulnerabilities include CVE-2021-21551 and CVE-2022-31199, and it has been used by groups like APT29, OilRig, and FIN6.[/profile]

43.name: T1486

70.name: T1218

Examples include using Microsoft-signed tools like odbcconf.exe with its REGSVR flag to load malicious DLLs or abusing Linux binaries like split. This technique has been associated with groups including Lazarus Group, Volt Typhoon, and Cobalt Group.[/profile]

Since these autostart programs often run with higher privileges, adversaries can use them to elevate access. Related methods for achieving this persistence on macOS include modifying plist files to influence launch behaviors or inserting applications into startup locations.

99.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Software Discovery is technique T1518 within the Discovery tactic, targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, and ESXi. It involves adversaries enumerating installed software and versions to assess the environment, identify security measures, and discover potential vulnerabilities for privilege escalation. This information shapes follow-on actions, such as lateral movement or targeted exploitation, and is commonly used by groups like MuddyWater, Volt Typhoon, and Mustang Panda.

100.name: Software Discovery
100.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Software Discovery is a Discovery tactic technique (ID: T1518) applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating installed software and versions on a system or in a cloud environment to inform follow-on actions, such as identifying security measures or finding vulnerable software for privilege escalation. This reconnaissance can be performed using commands like `dir`, `reg query`, `netsh`, and `Tasklist`. Associated threat groups include SideWinder, MuddyWater, and Volt Typhoon.

101.name: T1090
101.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1090, known as Proxy, is a command and control technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. Adversaries use connection proxies to direct traffic between systems or to act as an intermediary for C2 communications, avoiding direct connections to their infrastructure. Tools like HTRAN, ZXProxy, and ZXPortMap enable this traffic redirection. Proxies manage C2, reduce simultaneous outbound connections, provide resiliency, and help avoid suspicion, with adversaries often chaining multiple proxies to disguise traffic sources. This method is associated with groups including APT41, Volt Typhoon, and Sandworm Team.[/profile]

102.name: T1071
102.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1071, Application Layer Protocol, is a command-and-control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and network devices. It involves adversaries embedding commands and exfiltrated data within the traffic of legitimate OSI application layer protocols—such as HTTP(S), DNS, SMTP, or SMB—to blend with normal network activity and avoid detection. This method is distinct from using custom C2 protocols (T1094) and can be supported by adversary-controlled DNS servers (T1583.002).[profile]

103.name: Hijack Execution Flow
103.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Hijack Execution Flow, identified as T1574, is a defense evasion, persistence, and privilege escalation technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries executing malicious payloads by subverting how the operating system locates and runs programs or libraries. Specific methods include poisoning file directories or the Windows Registry, manipulating the KernelCallbackTable in a process's PEB to redirect function calls, and hijacking the virtual dynamic shared object (vdso) to inject code. These mechanisms allow execution to be masked under legitimate processes, often exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2021-44228.

104.name: T1112
104.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1112, "Modify Registry", is a Windows-specific technique used for Defense Evasion and Persistence. Adversaries interact with the Windows Registry using tools like the built-in `reg` utility or remote APIs to hide configuration data, malicious payloads, or impair defenses. Modifications can include altering system settings to store plaintext credentials, enabling macros, or creating pseudo-hidden keys by prepending names with null characters to conceal persistence mechanisms. It is commonly used by groups like APT41, Wizard Spider, and Volt Typhoon.

105.name: T1059.001
105.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1059.001, known as PowerShell, is an execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries abusing the PowerShell scripting environment to run commands and scripts, often for discovery and code execution. This can be achieved through cmdlets like `Start-Process` and `Invoke-Command`, or by downloading and executing payloads from the internet directly in memory. Execution can also occur without the `powershell.exe` binary by leveraging the underlying `System.Management.Automation` assembly. The technique is widely used by numerous threat groups, including APT29, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater.[/profile]

106.name: PowerShell
106.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PowerShell is a Windows-specific execution technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1059.001) within the Execution tactic. It is a native command-line and scripting environment abused by adversaries to run code, often without invoking powershell.exe directly by leveraging the System.Management.Automation DLL. It can execute commands locally or remotely (e.g., via Invoke-Command), download and run payloads from the internet, and is a core component of frameworks like Empire and PowerSploit. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups and can exploit vulnerabilities like CVE-2017-0144 (EternalBlue).[/profile]

107.name: Modify Registry
107.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Modify Registry is a Windows-specific technique (T1112) used for Defense Evasion and Persistence. Adversaries interact with the Windows Registry using tools like Reg.exe or remote access tools to hide configuration data, impair defenses (e.g., enabling macros), store malicious payloads, and maintain persistence. This can involve modifying service keys for privilege escalation, altering file associations for execution, or using pseudo-hidden keys to conceal activity. It is commonly used by groups like APT41, Wizard Spider, and Volt Typhoon.

108.name: Windows Command Shell
108.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Windows Command Shell, identified as T1059.003 in the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an Execution technique for the Windows platform. It involves adversaries abusing the native command-line interpreter (cmd.exe) to execute commands and payloads, either as a single command, interactively via a command and control channel, or through batch files (.bat, .cmd) for scripting operations like loops and conditionals. The shell can also be invoked remotely via services like SSH. Numerous threat groups, including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7, are known to employ this technique.

109.name: Input Capture
109.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Input Capture is a MITRE ATT&CK technique with ID T1056, used for Credential Access and Collection on Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices. It involves capturing user input to steal credentials, employing methods like transparent Credential API Hooking or deceptive Web Portal Capture to log credentials from login pages. Adversary groups such as APT39 and APT42 have been associated with this technique.

110.name: Application Layer Protocol
110.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Application Layer Protocol, designated as T1071 under the Command and Control tactic, operates on platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. Adversaries use standard OSI application layer protocols like HTTP/S, DNS, SMB, SSH, or RDP to blend command-and-control traffic with normal network activity, embedding their communications within the protocol's client-server exchanges to avoid detection and network filtering.

112.name: Endoor
112.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Endoor is a malware entity. Its key technical behaviors include Input Capture for credential theft, using Application Layer Protocol (T1071) like HTTP for command and control, Screen Capture for data collection, Process Injection for defense evasion, and OS Credential Dumping. It has been associated with infrastructure indicators such as the domains and IPs 'minish.wiki.gd' and '210.16.120.210'. Retrieved information suggests potential relations to other malware like Doorme, Siestagraph, and ShadowPad, with ShadowPad being linked to groups including APT41 and Earth Lusca.[/profile]

113.name: Nikidoor
113.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Nikidoor is a malware that uses the Application Layer Protocol (T1071) for command and control, specifically communicating with domains like minish.wiki.gd and IP addresses such as 210.16.120.210. It employs techniques including Process Injection (T1055), OS Credential Dumping (T1003), Input Capture (T1056), and Screen Capture (T1113) to steal credentials and data from compromised Windows, Linux, and macOS systems.[profile]

128.name: T1056
128.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1056, Input Capture, is a technique within the Credential Access and Collection tactics targeting Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices. It involves capturing user input to obtain credentials, using methods that can be transparent to the user, such as Credential API Hooking, or deceptive, like Web Portal Capture. Associated threat groups include APT39, APT42, and Storm-1811, and it has been linked to vulnerabilities including CVE-2017-8291, CVE-2020-1380, CVE-2022-30190, and CVE-2024-21410.[profile]

132.name: T1055
132.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Process Injection, designated as MITRE ATT&CK T1055, is a defense evasion and privilege escalation technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves executing arbitrary code within the address space of a separate, legitimate live process to evade process-based defenses, potentially access system resources or elevated privileges, and mask malicious activity. Specific implementations include abusing utilities like `mavinject.exe` for DLL injection or manipulating Thread Local Storage (TLS) callbacks to redirect process execution before its legitimate entry point.

133.name: T1003
133.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is OS Credential Dumping, identified as T1003 under the Credential Access tactic, targeting macOS, Linux, and Windows platforms. This technique involves adversaries dumping account credentials, often in hash or plaintext form, from operating system components like caches and memory. The obtained credentials are then used for lateral movement and to access restricted information. Associated vulnerabilities include CVE-2023-36025 and CVE-2024-20399, and the technique is linked to groups such as APT28 and APT29.

134.name: Process Injection
134.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Process Injection is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1055, primarily used for Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves executing arbitrary code within the address space of a separate live process to evade detection and potentially gain elevated privileges. Common sub-techniques include DLL injection using APIs like `VirtualAllocEx` and `CreateRemoteThread`, Portable Executable (PE) injection, and proc memory injection via the `/proc` filesystem on Linux to overwrite process memory. This method is widely used by threat actors such as APT41, Wizard Spider, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]

135.name: OS Credential Dumping
135.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]OS Credential Dumping is technique T1003 under the Credential Access tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves extracting account login material like hashes or plaintext passwords from operating system components such as security account manager (SAM) files, process memory (e.g., LSASS), or cached domain credentials. This stolen data enables lateral movement and is a precursor for password cracking. The technique is linked to vulnerabilities like CVE-2023-32231 and is used by numerous threat groups including APT28 and Mustang Panda.[/profile]

137.name: TRANSLATEXT
137.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TRANSLATEXT is a malware family, also known as translatext, attributed to the Kimsuky group. It primarily functions as a malicious Google Chrome browser extension, masquerading as Google Translate to evade detection. Its key behaviors include defense evasion, information collection, and data exfiltration, implemented via four malicious JavaScript files. The malware targets web browsers, specifically Google Chrome, and has used infrastructure such as the domains ney.r-e.kr and webman.w3school.cloudns.nz for command and control.[/profile]

157.name: T1176
157.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1176, Browser Extensions, is a persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries abusing software extensions for applications like web browsers or IDEs to maintain access. Malicious extensions can be installed via social engineering, compromised marketplaces, or direct system access, often masquerading as legitimate tools. They inherit the host application's permissions, enabling data exfiltration or command tunneling while blending into normal workflows, making detection challenging. This method can be linked to other techniques, such as modifying LNK files to trigger malicious extensions.

158.name: Software Extensions
158.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Software Extensions is a MITRE ATT&CK technique (T1176) under the Persistence tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves abusing modular components of software applications like browsers and IDEs to maintain access. Malicious extensions are installed via official marketplaces, social engineering, or direct loading, often inheriting the host application's permissions to blend into normal workflows, execute arbitrary code, and establish backdoors.

159.name: T1555.003
159.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1555.003, also known as Credentials from Web Browsers, is a credential-access technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves extracting saved credentials from browser storage files, such as Chrome's 'Login Data' database, and decrypting them using system functions like `CryptUnprotectData` on Windows. Adversaries may also scrape browser process memory for credential patterns. This technique is employed by numerous threat actors, including APT41, MuddyWater, and Volt Typhoon, to harvest credentials for potential reuse across systems.

160.name: T1071.001

Adversaries use common application layer protocols like HTTP/S and WebSocket to blend malicious communications with normal web traffic, embedding commands and data within standard protocol fields and headers to evade detection and network filtering.

162.name: reconshark
162.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ReconShark is a component of the BabyShark malware attributed to the Kimsuky group. It employs T1497 for Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, T1567 for Exfiltration Over Web Service, T1071 for command-and-control via Application Layer Protocols like HTTP, T1219 using Remote Access Tools, and T1112 to Modify the Windows Registry. It targets Windows systems and uses infrastructure including domains like joongang.site, mitmail.tech, makeoversalon.net.in, and worldinfocontact.club.[/profile]

239.name: T1041
239.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1041, known as Exfiltration Over C2 Channel, is an Exfiltration tactic technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves stealing data by encoding and transmitting it over an adversary's existing command and control communication channel, using the same protocol established for C2 to blend exfiltration with normal traffic. This technique is commonly associated with groups like Lazarus Group, APT39, and Wizard Spider, and is often used in conjunction with other methods like Automated Exfiltration or Scheduled Transfer.

242.name: T1497
242.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1497, Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, is a Defense Evasion and Discovery technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves malware detecting analysis environments by checking for artifacts like security tools (e.g., Sysinternals, Wireshark), virtual machine indicators, or a lack of legitimate user activity. Upon detection, it may alter its behavior, disengage, or use sleep timers to evade temporary sandboxes. Groups like DarkHotel and Contagious Interview have used this technique, which is also associated with vulnerabilities such as CVE-2021-34527.[/profile]

244.name: T1567
244.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1567, Exfiltration Over Web Service, is an exfiltration technique used on platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries leverage legitimate external web services, like pastebin.com, to transfer stolen data, often using SSL/TLS encryption for protection. This method provides cover by blending with normal network traffic to services that firewall rules may already permit. Related threat groups include APT28, BlackByte, and Magic Hound.[/profile]

245.name: T1064
245.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1064, known as Scripting, is a deprecated MITRE ATT&CK technique. It was categorized under the Defense Evasion and Execution tactics and was applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technique involved adversaries using scripts like VBScript, PowerShell, or batch files to speed up operations and bypass process monitoring by interacting directly with the OS API. Scripts were often embedded as macros in Office documents delivered via spearphishing to achieve execution.

246.name: T1059
246.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1059, Command and Scripting Interpreter, is an Execution tactic technique applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and other platforms. This execution can occur through embedded scripts in initial access payloads, interactive terminals, or by leveraging remote services, providing a foundational method for system interaction and control.

247.name: T1219
247.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1219, also known as Remote Access Tools, is a command-and-control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries abuse legitimate remote access or desktop support software (e.g., graphical or CLI tools, Chrome Remote Desktop) to establish interactive C2 channels, often inheriting user permissions for troubleshooting or management. These tools can be installed post-compromise for redundant access, to create reverse connections, or as malware components, and their installation routines may establish persistence. The technique is associated with groups like Carbanak, MuddyWater, and FIN7, and can be facilitated through user execution via social engineering.[/profile]

248.name: T1543
248.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1543, Create or Modify System Process, is a MITRE ATT&CK technique for Persistence and Privilege Escalation on Windows, Linux, macOS, and Containers. It involves creating or modifying system-level processes like Windows services, Linux daemons, or macOS launchd agents (Launch Daemons or Launch Agents) to execute malicious payloads at system startup or on a scheduled interval, thereby maintaining access and potentially elevating privileges. Adversaries may install new or tamper with existing services, which can run with high-level SYSTEM or root permissions.[/profile]

249.name: Exfiltration Over Web Service
249.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exfiltration Over Web Service, identified as T1567 within the Exfiltration tactic, is a technique used across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries leverage legitimate external web services like cloud storage or social media platforms to covertly transfer stolen data, often using SSL/TLS encryption for protection and blending in with normal, permitted network traffic to avoid detection by firewalls. Groups such as APT28 and BlackByte have been associated with this method.[/profile]

250.name: Scripting
250.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This entity, Scripting, is the deprecated MITRE ATT&CK technique T1064, which has been consolidated into Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059). It falls under the Defense Evasion and Execution tactics and is applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. The technique involves using scripts like VBScript, PowerShell, or batch files to automate malicious operations, bypass process monitoring by interacting directly with OS APIs, and embed malicious macros within documents (e.g., via spearphishing attachments) as an alternative to software exploitation. It is associated with offensive frameworks such as Metasploit, Veil, and PowerSploit.

251.name: Remote Access Tools
251.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Remote Access Tools is a Command and Control technique, identified as T1219, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries using legitimate remote desktop or management software (e.g., graphical desktop support or command-line tools) to establish an interactive C2 channel, often creating a session that inherits local user permissions. These tools can be installed post-compromise for redundant access, may include persistence mechanisms like Windows Services, and are abused by groups including Carbanak, MuddyWater, and FIN7.[/profile]

254.name: Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion
254.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1497, used for Defense Evasion and Discovery on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves detecting analysis environments by checking for artifacts like security tools (e.g., Sysinternals, Wireshark), virtual machine hardware/processes, or limited user activity, and then altering malware behavior—such as using sleep timers, disengaging, or withholding payloads—to evade detection. Sub-techniques include System Checks (T1497.001) and User Activity Based Checks (T1497.002). It is associated with groups like DarkHotel and OilRig.[/profile]

255.name: AppleSeed - S0622

276.name: Exfiltration Over C2 Channel

This technique involves adversaries stealing data by encoding and transmitting it over the same, existing command and control (C2) communication channel and protocol, blending stolen data with normal C2 traffic to avoid detection. This technique is often preceded by phishing and is associated with groups like Scattered Spider and LAPSUS$.

389.name: Linux.Gomir

It is associated with the Gold Dupont group. Its technical behaviors include performing System Checks to detect and avoid virtualization and analysis environments, conducting Application Window Discovery to list open windows and identify security software, and employing Indicator Removal to delete or modify logs and files to erase evidence. It communicates with command-and-control infrastructure, such as http://216.189.159.34/mir/index.php.

390.name: GoBear
390.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GoBear, also known as gobear, is a Go-based backdoor malware family exclusively linked to the Kimsuky group. It abuses legitimate, stolen certificates for defense evasion. Key technical behaviors include performing system checks to detect virtualization, discovering application windows, and removing indicators. It operates on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms and has been observed using infrastructure such as http://216.189.159.34/mir/index.php.

391.name: Troll Stealer
391.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Troll Stealer is an information stealer written in Go, associated with the Kimsuky group. It has been delivered via a dropper disguised as a legitimate security program installer and features code similar to the Kimsuky-associated AppleSeed malware. Its key behaviors include gathering victim network topology (T1590.004), discovering application windows (T1010), performing system checks for virtual environments (T1497.001), and removing indicators (T1070). It targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms and has used infrastructure such as the C2 server http://216.189.159.34/mir/index.php.[/profile]

420.name: T1010
420.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1010, Application Window Discovery, is a Discovery technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS to gather a listing of open application windows. Adversaries abuse native system features like Command and Scripting Interpreter commands and Native API functions to perform this enumeration. The gathered information can identify how the system is used, pinpoint potential data for collection, and discover security software to evade. This technique has been used by groups including Lazarus Group, Hexane, and Volt Typhoon, and it can support other techniques like credential phishing by monitoring user activity.

681.name: Automated Collection
681.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Automated Collection is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1119 under the Collection tactic, targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, SaaS, and Office Suite. It involves using automated techniques like command and scripting interpreters to search for and copy data based on criteria such as file type, location, or name at scheduled intervals. In cloud environments, adversaries leverage cloud APIs, CLIs, or ETL services for automated data collection, and the technique often incorporates File and Directory Discovery, Lateral Tool Transfer, and cloud discovery methods to identify and gather resources.

762.name: T1221
762.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1221, known as Template Injection, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves adversaries inserting malicious references into user document templates, such as those in Office Open XML (OOXX) or RTF files, to conceal and fetch payloads when the document is opened. This method can evade static detection by lacking typical indicators until execution and can also be abused for Forced Authentication by injecting SMB/HTTPS URLs to capture credential hashes. It has been used by groups like Gamaredon Group and APT28.

764.name: T1480
764.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1480, Execution Guardrails, is a Defense Evasion technique for macOS, Linux, Windows, and ESXi. It constrains payload execution to specific intended targets by checking for adversary-supplied environmental conditions, such as specific network share names, attached devices, files, domain names, or IP addresses. This ensures the payload only runs in the correct environment, preventing collateral damage and exposure in unintended systems like sandboxes. A sub-technique, Environmental Keying (T1480.001), uses cryptographic methods to derive decryption keys from these target-specific values.

765.name: T1559
765.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1559, Inter-Process Communication, is an Execution tactic technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves abusing OS-specific IPC mechanisms like Windows COM and DDE or Linux sockets and pipes to execute arbitrary code or commands locally. This can facilitate privilege escalation or lateral movement and is sometimes exploited via vulnerabilities like CVE-2021-28310.

766.name: T1047
766.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1047, known as Windows Management Instrumentation, is an Execution tactic technique for Windows. It abuses the WMI infrastructure to execute commands locally or remotely, often via tools like wmic.exe or PowerShell. Adversaries use it to run payloads, perform discovery, or inhibit system recovery, as seen in commands like `wmic.exe Shadowcopy Delete`. It can be accessed remotely via services like DCOM or WinRM and is also used in script-based execution methods, such as invoking scripts embedded in XSL files via the `/FORMAT` switch.[/profile]

780.name: T1203
780.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Exploitation for Client Execution, identified as T1203 under the Execution tactic and applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries exploiting software vulnerabilities in client applications, such as web browsers, Microsoft Office, or common third-party software like Adobe Reader, to achieve arbitrary code execution. Exploitation can occur through user interaction, like opening a malicious document from a spearphishing email, or without direct action via drive-by compromises. It is associated with numerous threat groups and specific CVEs, including CVE-2017-10271 and CVE-2024-21888.

822.name: OwlProxy
822.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]OwlProxy is a malware used in targeted attacks, notably against Taiwan government agencies in 2020 and the semiconductor industry in 2019, attributed to the APT Chimera group. It employs techniques for persistence like Boot or Logon Autostart Execution, credential theft via Input Capture, and command and control through Web Services. Its delivery is linked to Phishing and it conducts System Network Connections Discovery. Targets have been primarily in Taiwan, with infrastructure connections noted in the Lao People's Democratic Republic, Viet Nam, and the Russian Federation.[/profile]

823.name: T1049
823.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1049, System Network Connections Discovery, is a Discovery technique for Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves querying the system for active network connections and sessions using utilities like netstat, `net use`, `net session`, `lsof`, `who -a`, `w`, or device-specific commands such as `show ip sockets` or `esxi network ip connection list`. This can reveal connected systems and services within local or cloud environments to inform subsequent adversary actions.[/profile]

824.name: T1102
824.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1102, known as Web Service, is a Command and Control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries abuse legitimate external web services, such as those from Google, Microsoft, or Twitter, to relay data to and from compromised systems, hiding C2 traffic within expected, often SSL/TLS-encrypted, communications with these popular sites. This method can protect backend infrastructure from discovery and provides operational resiliency, as evidenced by use from groups like Gamaredon Group, FIN6, and Turla. It is also referenced in the context of lateral movement for tool transfer via services like Dropbox.[/profile]

825.name: Ninja
825.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Ninja, also known as S1100, is a C++-based malware family used by the APT group ToddyCat (G1022) since at least 2020 for network penetration and remote control, allowing multiple simultaneous operators. Its key behaviors include Boot or Logon Autostart Execution for persistence, Input Capture for credential access, and using Web Services for command and control. It has targeted government and military entities in Europe and Asia, with observed deployment via the Samurai malware, and utilizes infrastructure and phishing for initial access.[/profile]

826.name: System Network Connections Discovery
826.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Network Connections Discovery is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1049 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries querying for active network connections to map communication pathways and connected services. Technical execution uses commands like netstat, net use, and net session on Windows; netstat and lsof on Mac/Linux; show ip sockets or show tcp brief on network devices; and esxi network ip connection list on ESXi servers. This activity is commonly associated with groups like APT41, Lazarus, and MuddyWater.

827.name: SessionManager
827.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SessionManager is a malware with no known aliases. It is attributed to the Electrum group. Its key TTPs include Boot or Logon Autostart Execution for persistence, Input Capture for credential access, and the use of Web Services for C2 communication, often leveraging phishing for initial access and CVE-2022-30190 for exploitation. It performs System Network Connections Discovery. It has targeted infrastructure in the Lao People's Democratic Republic, Viet Nam, and the Russian Federation.[/profile]

828.name: Gelsemium
828.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Gelsemium (also known as 狼毒草) is a cyberespionage group active since at least 2014, targeting governmental institutions, electronics manufacturers, universities, and religious organizations in East Asia and the Middle East. Its key malware includes OwlProxy, Ninja, and SessionManager, and it employs TTPs such as Boot or Logon Autostart Execution for persistence, Input Capture for credential access, and exploitation of vulnerabilities like CVE-2022-30190. The group's operations show infrastructure connections to the Lao People's Democratic Republic, Viet Nam, and the Russian Federation, and it is motivated by intelligence gathering.[/profile]

829.name: Web Service
829.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Web Service is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1102 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi. It involves using legitimate external web services like Google, Microsoft, or Twitter for C2 relay, blending with normal network traffic to avoid detection. The technique leverages SSL/TLS encryption for protection and can dynamically change infrastructure for resilience, with groups like Gamaredon and APT32 known to use it.[/profile]

868.name: TA0033
868.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA0033 is a placeholder identifier for a collection of command and control techniques. The retrieved information describes specific methods adversaries use to obscure C2 traffic, including adding junk data to protocols to hinder analysis and using custom C2 protocols instead of standard application layer protocols. These techniques aim to evade detection by blending malicious communications with normal network activity or making them difficult to decode.

871.name: T1210
871.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exploitation of Remote Services, designated T1210, is a Lateral Movement technique targeting Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries exploiting software vulnerabilities in remote services, such as SMB, RDP, MySQL, or web servers, to execute adversary-controlled code and gain unauthorized access to internal systems. This often follows network discovery to identify vulnerable targets, with servers being high-value objectives, and can lead to privilege escalation. Known associated vulnerabilities include CVE-2022-29464, CVE-2022-31199, and CVE-2020-1472.[/profile]

873.name: TA0043
873.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA0043 is the Reconnaissance tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It encompasses the initial phase where adversaries gather information to plan future operations. This includes techniques such as searching public code repositories (T1593.003) to find sensitive data like source code or credentials, which can aid in developing exploits or gaining initial access. Adversaries may also conduct discovery activities, like identifying security software and file path exclusions (T1564.012), to understand the target environment and identify locations to hide malicious artifacts.

876.name: TA422
876.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA422 is a malware entity attributed to the Sofacy/APT28 group, which is an established Russian threat actor. It employs spearphishing with malicious links, such as those mimicking Google spreadsheets, for initial access. For persistence, it uses Boot or Logon Autostart Execution via Windows Registry keys. For credential access, it utilizes Forced Authentication to capture NetNTLM hashes and OS Credential Dumping. Its command and control infrastructure has leveraged domains like downloadfile.infinityfreeapp.com and opendoc.infinityfreeapp.com, and it can use Web Services for C2. It is associated with vulnerabilities including CVE-2023-32231 and CVE-2023-23397.[/profile]

878.name: APT28
878.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]APT28, also known as Fancy Bear, Sofacy, Sednit, Pawn Storm, Forest Blizzard, and STRONTIUM, is a Russian state-sponsored cyber espionage group attributed to the GRU. Its key custom malware includes OCEANMAP, MASEPIE, and STEELHOOK backdoors, which employ Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA) and Dynamic Resolution for command and control evasion. The group's TTPs include Forced Authentication to steal credentials and the use of spearphishing documents. It primarily targets government, defense, and political organizations in Europe and North America, with recent campaigns observed against entities in Montenegro, Lithuania, Romania, Bulgaria, and Luxembourg, motivated by geopolitical intelligence gathering and influence operations.[/profile]

915.name: T1187
915.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1187 (Forced Authentication) is a Credential Access technique for Windows platforms. It works by tricking a system into automatically sending authentication credentials (like NetNTLM hashes) to an adversary-controlled server. This is commonly achieved by embedding a resource link (e.g., `file[:]//[remote address]/Normal.dotm` or `\\[remote address]\pic.png`) in a spearphishing document, .SCF file, or via the `EfsRpcOpenFileRaw` function, forcing an SMB or WebDAV authentication attempt when the file is opened or its icon is rendered. The captured hash can then be used in relay or brute-force attacks.

917.name: Forced Authentication
917.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Forced Authentication, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1187 under the Credential Access tactic for Windows platforms, is an attack where adversaries trick a system into automatically sending authentication material, such as NetNTLM hashes, to a controlled server. This is commonly achieved by embedding a link to a remote SMB or WebDAV share in a spearphishing document (via Template Injection) or a crafted file like .SCF or .LNK placed where a user will access it. The technique can also exploit the EfsRpcOpenFileRaw function to force SMB authentication via the MS-EFSRPC interface. The captured hashes can be used in relay or offline brute-force attacks. It has been associated with groups like Dragonfly and DarkHydrus and is linked to vulnerabilities including CVE-2023-23397.[/profile]

925.name: XAgentOSX
925.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]XAgentOSX, also known as XAgent, is a trojan attributed to the APT28 threat group and is a port of their CHOPSTICK/XAgent malware for the macOS (OS X) platform. Its key behaviors include capturing user input for credential access (T1056), querying the system registry for discovery (T1012), collecting data from the local system (T1005), and archiving collected data prior to exfiltration (T1560), with command and control conducted via standard application layer protocols (T1071).[/profile]

926.name: XAgentOSX - S0161
926.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]XAgentOSX is a trojan, also known as XAgent, used by APT28 and is a port of their CHOPSTICK malware. It targets the macOS (OS X) platform and employs techniques including Input Capture (T1056) for credential theft, Application Layer Protocol (T1071) for command and control, and Screen Capture (T1113) for information collection. It also uses Archive Collected Data (T1560) to compress data prior to exfiltration.[/profile]

928.name: T1012
928.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Query Registry is technique T1012 within the Discovery tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries interacting with the Windows Registry to gather system, configuration, and software information, often using utilities like Reg.exe. This data is used during automated discovery to inform subsequent actions, such as whether to fully infect a target. For example, adversaries may query specific registry keys like HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Nls\Language to infer the system language and geographical location.

929.name: T1560
929.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1560, "Archive Collected Data", which falls under the Collection tactic and is applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries compressing and/or encrypting collected data prior to exfiltration, using utilities, third-party libraries, or custom methods to obfuscate the data and minimize network footprint. It is often used in conjunction with data staging (T1074.001) and has been associated with numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN6.[/profile]

930.name: T1005
930.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1005, known as Data from Local System, is a Collection tactic technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries searching local file systems, configuration files, local databases, virtual machine files, or process memory for sensitive data prior to exfiltration. This is commonly executed using command-line interpreters or automated scripts. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT29 and Volt Typhoon, and can be facilitated in cloud environments by creating new, less-restricted instances to mount volume snapshots for data access.

931.name: Archive Collected Data
931.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Archive Collected Data, identified as T1560 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is a Collection tactic technique used across Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves compressing or encrypting collected data prior to exfiltration to obfuscate content and minimize network footprint. This can be executed using built-in utilities like `tar`, `zip`, `makecab`, or `certutil` for encoding, third-party libraries such as Python's rarfile or zlib, or through custom implementations like XOR encryption. The technique is commonly associated with data staging procedures (T1074) and is leveraged by numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN6.[/profile]

932.name: Query Registry
932.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Query Registry is a Discovery technique (T1012) used on Windows platforms to gather system intelligence. Adversaries interact with the Windows Registry to collect information about the OS, configuration, and installed software, often using the built-in Reg utility. This data aids in automated discovery to inform subsequent attack decisions. The technique is associated with groups like APT41, Lazarus Group, and Volt Typhoon.

933.name: Data from Local System
933.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Data from Local System, identified as T1005, is a Collection tactic technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. Adversaries search local file systems, configuration files, databases, virtual machine files, and process memory for sensitive data prior to exfiltration. This is commonly executed using Command and Scripting Interpreters like cmd or a Network Device CLI, which interact with the file system, and may involve Automated Collection. Numerous threat groups, including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7, have employed this technique.[/profile]

935.name: NanoCore
935.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]NanoCore, also known as NanoCore RAT, is a modular remote access tool developed in .NET that has been used since 2013. It has been associated with threat groups including APT33, the Gorgon Group, and Silverterrier. Its key technical behaviors involve using web services for command and control and exfiltration, often leveraging protocols like HTTP/S to blend with normal traffic, and it is commonly delivered via phishing or exploitation of vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-38831. It primarily targets the Windows platform, with infrastructure indicators including specific webhook URLs.[/profile]

936.name: Crimson
936.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Crimson, also known as Crimson RAT, is a remote access Trojan used by the Transparent Tribe APT group since at least 2016. It employs Application Layer Protocols like HTTP/S for command and control, using specific C2 servers such as newsbizupdates.net and 64.188.25.206, and can propagate via USB worms. The malware has been used in phishing campaigns and exploits vulnerabilities like CVE-2023-38831, primarily targeting Windows systems in locations including Ukraine.[/profile]

938.name: SmokeLoader
938.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SmokeLoader, also known as smokeloader, is a complex, multi-functional malware attributed to groups like Smoky Spider and UAC-0006. It uses techniques such as Phishing and Exploitation for Client Execution (e.g., via CVE-2023-38831) for initial access and employs Application Layer Protocols like HTTP/S for command and control, including exfiltration over web services to blend with normal traffic. It primarily targets Windows systems, with recent campaigns focusing on Ukrainian financial and government institutions, and uses infrastructure like webhook.site for communication.[/profile]

943.name: Exploitation for Client Execution
943.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exploitation for Client Execution, designated as T1203, is an execution tactic targeting macOS, Linux, and Windows platforms. It involves adversaries exploiting vulnerabilities in client applications like web browsers (e.g., via drive-by compromises or spearphishing links), office suites (e.g., Microsoft Office via malicious documents), and common third-party software (e.g., Adobe Reader or Flash) to achieve arbitrary code execution, often without requiring user interaction in browser-based attacks. Specific vulnerabilities such as CVE-2024-21893 and CVE-2023-46805 are linked to this technique, which is utilized by numerous threat groups including APT28, APT29, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]

946.name: MASEPIE
946.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MASEPIE, also known as masepie, is attributed to the APT28 intrusion set and is a backdoor deployed on systems belonging to targeted individuals and organizations. It uses Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA) and Dynamic Resolution for command and control (C2) evasion, establishes Multi-Stage Channels for C2 obfuscation, and employs Boot or Logon Autostart Execution for persistence. Its C2 infrastructure includes domains like czyrqdnvpujmmjkfhhvseabz1q5olrum5.oast.fun, and it has targeted entities in locations including Argentina, Poland, and Kazakhstan.[/profile]

947.name: STEELHOOK
947.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]STEELHOOK, also known as masepie, is attributed to APT28. Its key technical behaviors include using PowerShell scripts to steal credentials from Google Chrome's Local State and Login Data files, and employing techniques like Domain Generation Algorithms and Dynamic Resolution for command and control. It targets Windows platforms and has been observed using infrastructure like e-wody.firstcloudit.com and various .oast.fun domains.[/profile]

949.name: OCEANMAP
949.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]OCEANMAP, also known as the OCEANMAP Backdoor, is a malware attributed to the APT28 intrusion set. Its key technical behaviors include using Dynamic Resolution and Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA) for command and control to evade detection, and employing User Execution for initial compromise, often via malicious documents. The malware has targeted entities in locations including Argentina, Poland, and Azerbaijan. Its infrastructure involves domains like e-wody.firstcloudit.com and utilizes DGA domains such as those under the .oast.fun subdomain pattern.[/profile]

1028.name: Email Collection
1028.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Email Collection is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1114 under the Collection tactic. It targets email systems to gather sensitive data, such as trade secrets or incident response details, from mail servers or clients. Adversaries may use tools like MailSniper to automate keyword searches on platforms including Exchange, Office 365, or Google Workspace. This technique is associated with groups like Silent Librarian, Scattered Spider, and Hafnium.[/profile]

1029.name: T1189
1029.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1189, Drive-by Compromise, is an Initial Access technique targeting Windows, Linux, macOS, and Identity Provider platforms. It involves compromising a user's system when they visit a website, often through injected malicious scripts, malvertising, or exploiting vulnerable browser plugins without requiring direct user interaction beyond browsing. This method is distinct from server-side exploits and is frequently used in targeted watering hole attacks. A related preparatory activity is Drive-by Target (T1608.004), which involves staging malicious content on controlled or compromised infrastructure.

1030.name: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution
1030.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution, known as T1127, is a Defense Evasion technique targeting Windows platforms. It involves abusing legitimate, often digitally signed, software development utilities (like debuggers or compilers) to proxy the execution of malicious payloads. This method exploits the inherent trust in these signed applications to bypass application control solutions, including Windows Smart App Control, by hijacking their reputation to run arbitrary code.

1031.name: Drive-by Compromise
1031.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Drive-by Compromise (T1189) is an Initial Access technique targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, and Identity Provider platforms. It involves gaining system access when a user visits a compromised or adversary-controlled website. The process typically includes automatic script execution to profile the browser and plugins for vulnerabilities, followed by the delivery of exploit code, which may leverage injected malicious scripts, malvertising, or compromised cloud storage. This technique is distinct from server exploitation and is often used in targeted watering hole attacks against specific communities.

1032.name: Multi-Stage Channels
1032.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Multi-Stage Channels is a command and control technique (T1104) within the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves creating separate C2 stages to obfuscate detection, where an initial tool calls back to a first-stage server for instructions and may upload a second, more capable RAT to redirect to a distinct second-stage server, with stages typically hosted on non-overlapping infrastructure and potentially using fallback channels.

1033.name: T1114
1033.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1114 (Email Collection) is a Collection technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, and Office Suite platforms. Adversaries target user email to gather sensitive data, including trade secrets or incident response details, by collecting or forwarding emails from mail servers or clients. This activity is associated with groups like Silent Librarian and Scattered Spider. The technique is referenced in the context of adversaries using tools like the ExchangePowerShell module to clear mailbox data and remove evidence of their collection operations.[/profile]

1034.name: T1127
1034.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1127, known as Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves adversaries abusing signed developer utilities, such as msxsl.exe or WinDbg, to proxy and execute malicious code. This leverages the trusted reputation of these legitimate tools to bypass application control solutions like Smart App Control, effectively hiding malicious activity within a trusted process.

1035.name: T1104
1035.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Multi-Stage Channels, designated as T1104, is a command and control technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves creating multiple, distinct stages for C2 to obfuscate detection. The first stage typically calls back to an initial server for basic instructions, host information collection, and tool updates, and may upload a second, more fully-featured remote access tool (RAT) to redirect to a second-stage server. These stages often use separate, non-overlapping infrastructure, and the initial loader may incorporate backup callbacks or fallback channels. This technique has been associated with groups including APT3, APT41, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]

1036.name: T1021
1036.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1021, also known as Remote Services, is a Lateral Movement technique in the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries using valid accounts to log into services that accept remote connections, such as SSH, RDP, VNC, and telnet, to perform actions as the logged-on user and move laterally across a network. This can include accessing domain-joined machines, SaaS/IaaS services, or management platforms like VMware vCenter. The technique can be abused through legitimate remote management tools, such as Apple Remote Desktop on macOS, which leverages VNC and SSH protocols, and it can be used in conjunction with privilege escalation methods like SID-History Injection to gain access to otherwise inaccessible domains.

1048.name: Remote Services
1048.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Remote Services, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1021 within the Lateral Movement tactic, operates across Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries use valid accounts to log into services accepting remote connections like SSH, RDP, VNC, and telnet to perform actions as the authenticated user. This includes leveraging domain credentials to access multiple machines or services such as VMware vCenter, and abusing legitimate administrative tools like Apple Remote Desktop (ARD), which combines VNC and SSH protocols, to gain remote code execution and move laterally within a network.[/profile]

1111.name: information stealer
1111.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Information Stealer is a malware type, not a specific family, that employs techniques like OS Credential Dumping (T1003) and Process Injection (T1055) to steal credentials and data. It is delivered via Phishing (T1566) and has been used in campaigns by groups like TA530, which have leveraged fileless loading methods such as Word macros and PowerShell. Associated infrastructure includes domains like settings-panel.frge.io and downloading.infinityfreeapp.com, and it has been observed targeting organizations in locations including the United States, South Africa, and the Central African Republic.[/profile]

1171.name: T1078
1171.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1078, Valid Accounts, is a technique used across the Defense Evasion, Initial Access, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation tactics on platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud services. It involves adversaries obtaining and abusing credentials of existing accounts to bypass access controls, gain persistent access to remote systems like VPNs or network devices, and pivot across the network. Attackers may use inactive accounts to evade detection and often leverage these credentials without malware to blend in with legitimate activity. This technique is foundational and is used by numerous threat groups to support other actions like accessing admin shares via SMB or modifying authentication processes.

1175.name: T1110
1175.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1110, known as Brute Force, is a Credential Access technique applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and network platforms. It involves systematically guessing account passwords through repetitive interaction with an authentication service or by cracking offline password hashes. This technique is often combined with other behaviors like OS Credential Dumping for initial access or lateral movement, and specific sub-techniques like Password Cracking are used in related attacks such as AS-REP Roasting to compromise Kerberos authentication.[/profile]

1176.name: Valid Accounts
1176.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Valid Accounts is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1078, used for Defense Evasion, Initial Access, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation across platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud services. It involves adversaries obtaining and abusing credentials of existing user, domain, local, or cloud accounts to bypass access controls, gain persistent remote access to services like VPNs, and pivot across systems. This technique often leverages compromised, default, or inactive accounts to evade detection, and is associated with numerous threat groups including APT29 and Scattered Spider.

1177.name: Brute Force
1177.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Brute Force is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1110 under the Credential Access tactic. It operates across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. The technique involves systematically guessing passwords using a repetitive mechanism, either through online interaction with an authentication service or offline against acquired password hashes. It is commonly used to gain initial access via services like SSH, RDP, or SMB, and can be combined with other techniques such as OS Credential Dumping. Threat actors like APT28, APT29, and OilRig have employed this method.[/profile]

1178.name: T1557
1178.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1557, known as Adversary-in-the-Middle, is a technique used in the Collection and Credential Access tactics, applicable across macOS, Linux, Windows, and Network Devices. It involves positioning between networked devices by abusing protocols like ARP, DNS, or LLMNR to redirect traffic through an adversary-controlled system. This enables follow-on actions such as network sniffing, credential interception, and transmitted data manipulation. Adversaries may also use this position to perform downgrade attacks on communication protocols like TLS. The technique is associated with groups like Kimsuky and Sea Turtle and can be facilitated by hardware additions for network tapping.

1179.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
1179.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Adversary-in-the-Middle, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1557, falls under the Collection and Credential Access tactics and targets macOS, Linux, Windows, and Network Devices platforms. This technique involves positioning a controlled system between networked devices by abusing protocols like ARP, DNS, or LLMNR to redirect traffic, enabling activities such as network sniffing, credential interception (including tokens and cookies), and transmitted data manipulation. Adversaries may also use this position to execute downgrade attacks on communication protocols like SSL/TLS. The technique is associated with threat groups like Kimsuky, Sea Turtle, and Mustang Panda and can be facilitated by vulnerabilities or the installation of rogue digital certificates.

1240.name: Web Protocols
1240.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Web Protocols is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071.001 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries using common web protocols like HTTP/S and WebSocket to conceal command and control traffic by embedding data within standard packet fields and headers, thereby blending with normal network activity to avoid detection.

1243.name: T1027.002
1243.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1027.002, known as Software Packing, is a Defense Evasion technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows. It involves compressing or encrypting an executable to change its file signature and evade signature-based detection, with decompression typically occurring in memory. Packers like MPRESS and UPX are common tools, though adversaries may use custom packers. The technique is associated with groups including APT41, APT29, and Volt Typhoon, and has been linked to vulnerabilities such as CVE-2024-21410 and CVE-2023-3467.

1245.name: Software Packing
1245.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Software Packing is a defense-evasion technique (ID: T1027.002) used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves compressing or encrypting an executable to alter its file signature and evade signature-based detection, with common packers including UPX and MPRESS. The packed code is typically decompressed in memory during execution, and adversaries may also employ custom or virtual machine-based packing to avoid artifacts associated with known tools.

1246.name: Encrypted Channel
1246.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Encrypted Channel is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1573 under the Command and Control tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and ESXi. It involves adversaries using encryption algorithms to conceal C2 traffic, separate from any inherent protocol encryption. Implementations are vulnerable to reverse engineering if secret keys are hardcoded within malware or configuration files. The technique is associated with groups like APT29, Bitter, Tropic Trooper, and Magic Hound, and is linked to several CVEs including CVE-2025-27920 and CVE-2024-21410.[/profile]

1247.name: T1568
1247.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1568, known as Dynamic Resolution, is a Command and Control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves malware using a shared algorithm with adversary infrastructure to dynamically adjust C2 parameters like domain names, IP addresses, or port numbers, enabling evasion and facilitating Fallback Channels. This technique is associated with groups including APT29, Gamaredon Group, and Transparent Tribe. A specific sub-technique, T1568.003 DNS Calculation, uses calculations on DNS response data to determine the C2 port and IP address.

1248.name: Dynamic Resolution
1248.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Dynamic Resolution is a command and control technique, identified as T1568, used to evade detection by dynamically establishing C2 connections. It operates across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Malware uses a shared algorithm with adversary infrastructure to dynamically adjust connection parameters like domain names, IP addresses, or port numbers, often serving as a fallback channel when primary C2 is lost. Associated threat groups include APT29, Gamaredon Group, and Bitter.[/profile]

1249.name: T1003.001
1249.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]LSASS Memory, designated T1003.001 under the Credential Access tactic for Windows, involves accessing credential material from the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service process memory. Adversaries can harvest credentials directly from memory or dump the LSASS process to a file for offline analysis using tools like procdump (e.g., `procdump -ma lsass.exe lsass_dump`) or built-in Windows utilities such as `comsvcs.dll` via `rundll32.exe`. The dumped file can then be parsed with tools like Mimikatz using commands `sekurlsa::Minidump` and `sekurlsa::logonPasswords` to extract plaintext passwords, hashes, and Kerberos tickets. This technique is associated with vulnerabilities like CVE-2020-1472 and numerous threat groups including APT28 and Volt Typhoon.

1250.name: LSASS Memory
1250.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]LSASS Memory, identified as OS Credential Dumping: LSASS Memory (T1003.001), is a Credential Access technique targeting Windows platforms. It involves accessing or dumping the memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (lsass.exe) to harvest stored credentials like hashes and plaintext passwords. Common execution methods include using tools like Procdump (e.g., `procdump -ma lsass.exe`), Mimikatz with commands like `sekurlsa::logonPasswords`, or built-in Windows utilities such as `rundll32.exe comsvcs.dll MiniDump`. Adversaries may also abuse the silent process exit mechanism via WerFault.exe or manipulate Security Support Provider (SSP) DLLs loaded into LSASS to capture authentication data.[/profile]

1251.name: T1566.001
1251.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Spearphishing Attachment (T1566.001) is an Initial Access technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves sending targeted emails with malicious attachments like Office documents, executables, or PDFs to gain execution, often relying on User Execution (T1204). Adversaries manipulate file extensions and use social engineering to trick users into opening the attachment, which may exploit vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-35636 or CVE-2024-36401. This technique is widely used by numerous threat groups including APT29, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.

1252.name: Spearphishing Attachment
1252.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Spearphishing Attachment is a technique identified as T1566.001 within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, primarily under the Initial Access tactic and applicable to multiple platforms. It involves sending targeted emails with malicious attachments, such as Microsoft Office documents, executables, PDFs, or archived files, to gain access to victim systems. Execution typically relies on user interaction to open the attachment, which may exploit vulnerabilities (like associated CVEs including CVE-2023-23397 and CVE-2024-21413) or directly run a payload. Adversaries often use social engineering lures, provide instructions to bypass protections, and manipulate file extensions or icons to disguise malicious files as legitimate documents.

1253.name: T1071.004
1253.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1071.004 (DNS) is a command and control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries abusing the Domain Name System (DNS) protocol to blend malicious communications with legitimate network traffic, often for beaconing or tunneling. This can be achieved by embedding commands and data within various DNS record types like TXT or A records. The technique is used by numerous threat groups including APT41, OilRig, and Fin7, and can be complemented by related sub-techniques like adding junk data (T1001.001) or using standard encoding (T1132.001) to further obscure C2 traffic.[/profile]

1254.name: DNS
1254.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DNS is the standard MITRE ATT&CK technique T1071.004 for Command and Control on Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries using the DNS application layer protocol to blend malicious traffic with normal network activity, often by tunneling commands and data within DNS queries and responses. This method, known as DNS tunneling or beaconing, can embed data in fields like TXT or A records and is difficult to detect due to its resemblance to legitimate administrative traffic.[/profile]

1255.name: T1568.002
1255.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1568.002, also known as Domain Generation Algorithms (DGAs), is a Command and Control technique for macOS, Linux, Windows, and ESXi. It dynamically generates destination domains for C2 traffic to evade blocking and tracking, moving beyond static lists. DGAs produce domains as random strings (e.g., istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru) or concatenated words (e.g., cityjulydish.net), often using time-based seeds to create thousands of potential domains per period (hourly, daily). This method is also used for establishing Fallback Channels when primary C2 is lost and has been employed by groups like APT41 and TA551.[/profile]

1256.name: Domain Generation Algorithms
1256.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Domain Generation Algorithms (DGA) is a command and control technique with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1568.002, operating within the Command and Control tactic on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It dynamically generates a large number of potential command and control domains algorithmically, often using time-based seeds or concatenating random letters or words (e.g., istgmxdejdnxuyla.ru), to evade blocklists and tracking. This method is frequently used by groups like APT41 and TA551 and can serve as a fallback channel to reestablish lost C2 connections.

1264.name: SilentGh0st
1264.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SilentGh0st, also known as silentgh0st, is the oldest variant of a Gh0stRAT malware family, offering extensive functionality through a rich set of commands and modules. It is associated with the Chinese-aligned threat actor "Unfading Sea Haze". Its key technical behaviors include keylogging for credential access and exfiltrating stolen data over its command and control (C2) channel. Its infrastructure includes domains such as dns-log.d-n-s.org.uk, payroll.mywire.org, provider.giize.com, mail.bomloginset.com, and employee.mywire.org. It has evolved into newer variants like InsidiousGh0st, TranslucentGh0st, EtherealGh0st, and FluffyGh0st.

1265.name: Stubbedoor
1265.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Stubbedoor is a malware entity. Its key behaviors include keylogging for credential access and exfiltration of stolen data over its command and control (C2) channel. It is associated with infrastructure indicators such as airst.giize.com, linklab.blinklab.com, dns.g8z.net, sopho.kozow.com, and provider.giize.com.

1266.name: FluffyGh0st
1266.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]FluffyGh0st, also known as a variant of SilentGh0st, is a malware featuring dynamic plugin loading and a lighter footprint for evasive operation. It is associated with keylogging (T1056.001) and exfiltration over its C2 channel (T1041) as part of the Collection (TA0009) and Initial Access (TA0001) tactics. Its infrastructure includes domains such as mail.bomloginset.com, news.nevuer.com, api.bitdefenderupdate.org, mail.simpletra.com, and fc.adswt.com.

1267.name: InsidiousGh0st
1267.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]InsidiousGh0st, also known as an evolution of SilentGh0st, is a Go-based malware. It is attributed to unknown groups.
