Its infrastructure involves domains such as cdn.g8z.net, images.emldn.com, bit.kozow.com, linklab.blinklab.com, and mail.simpletra.com.

1268.name: gh0st RAT
1268.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Gh0st RAT is a public-source remote access tool (RAT) family. Its aliases include Gh0st rat and ghost rat, and it has variants like Nood RAT for Linux. It is attributed to multiple groups including Lazarus Group, APT41, Kimsuky, Axiom, Leviathan, and Emissary Panda. Key technical behaviors involve data exfiltration over its command and control (C2) channel, using infrastructure like cdn.g8z.net and mail.adswt.com. Its primary target platforms are Windows and Linux.

1269.name: SharpZulip
1269.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SharpZulip is a malware that performs keylogging (T1056.001) to capture user credentials and exfiltrates stolen data over its command and control channel (T1041), as part of the Collection tactic (TA0009). Its known command and control infrastructure includes domains such as auth.bitdefenderupdate.com, payroll.mywire.org, mail.simpletra.com, spcg.lunaticfridge.com, and employee.mywire.org.

1270.name: TranslucentGh0st
1270.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TranslucentGh0st, also known as a variant of SilentGh0st, is a malware featuring dynamic plugin loading and a lighter footprint for evasive operation. It is associated with keylogging (T1056.001) and exfiltration over its C2 channel (T1041), targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Its command and control infrastructure includes domains such as fc.adswt.com, cdn.g8z.net, mail.adswt.com, word.emldn.com, and payroll.mywire.org.

1271.name: EtherealGh0st
1271.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]EtherealGh0st is a malware variant, part of a family including TranslucentGh0st and FluffyGh0st, and is an evolution of SilentGh0st. It features dynamic plugin loading and a lighter footprint for evasive operation. Its technical behaviors include Keylogging to capture credentials and Exfiltration Over C2 Channel to steal data. It uses infrastructure indicators such as dns.g8z.net, mail.theworkguyoo.com, mail.bomloginset.com, message.ooguy.com, and bitdefenderupdate.org.

1272.name: Gh0st Army
1272.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Gh0st Army is a malware entity distinct from the public Gh0st RAT family. Its key behaviors include keylogging for credential access and exfiltrating stolen data over its command and control (C2) channel. It has been associated with infrastructure domains such as upupdate.ooguy.com, sopho.kozow.com, auth.bitdefenderupdate.com, newy.hifiliving.com, and mail.simpletra.com. The malware operates within the broader MITRE ATT&CK tactics of Initial Access (TA0001) and Collection (TA0009).

1274.name: SerialPktdoor
1274.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SerialPktdoor, also known as PortDoor, is a backdoor malware that executes in memory via MSBuild to avoid disk artifacts, providing attackers with remote control. It is attributed to the TA428 threat group. Its key behaviors include Keylogging for credential access and Exfiltration Over C2 Channel for data theft. Associated infrastructure includes domains such as mail.adswt.com, mail.simpletra.com, upupdate.ooguy.com, message.ooguy.com, and manags.twilightparadox.com.

1275.name: SharpJSHandler
1275.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SharpJSHandler is a web shell that listens for HTTP requests and executes encoded JavaScript code. It is used in attacks attributed to the silentgh0st group. Key technical behaviors include keylogging to capture credentials and exfiltrating stolen data over its command and control (C2) channel. It targets Windows platforms and has been associated with infrastructure domains such as bit.kozow.com, mail.adswt.com, cdn.g8z.net, provider.giize.com, and fc.adswt.com.

1276.name: Unfading Sea Haze
1276.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Unfading Sea Haze is a Chinese state-sponsored threat actor, also known as Unfading Sea Haze, which demonstrates operational and toolset overlaps with APT41. Its key custom malware includes SilentGh0st (and its variants like FluffyGh0st) and SharpZulip, which perform keylogging and exfiltration over C2 channels. The group's TTPs involve spear-phishing with malicious LNK files, abusing MSBuild for fileless execution, and using custom tools like the 'xkeylog' keylogger and info-stealers for browsers. It is attributed to China and primarily targets data for collection and exfiltration.

1335.name: TA0001
1335.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity "TA0001" is an MITRE ATT&CK Tactic, specifically "Initial Access". This tactic represents the initial vector adversaries use to gain their first foothold within a network. The retrieved information, while describing various techniques, does not provide specific technical mechanics for the tactic itself, as TA0001 is a high-level category. Supplementary context from related entities indicates that compromised network devices can be leveraged to support initial access operations, and that groups like APT28, Volt Typhoon, and Leviathan are associated with techniques that fall under this tactical objective.

1336.name: TA0009
1336.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA0009 is the MITRE ATT&CK ID for the Collection tactic, which involves adversaries gathering target information prior to exfiltration. This tactic is platform-agnostic. A specific technique under Collection is T1213.003, Data from Information Repositories: Code Repositories, where adversaries target private or internally hosted code repositories to steal source code, API keys, or credentials. This is distinct from public repository reconnaissance (T1593.003). The tactic also encompasses techniques for securing data for exfiltration, such as T1001.001, Data Obfuscation: Junk Data, where random characters are added to C2 traffic to hinder analysis.

1337.name: T1056.001
1337.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique Input Capture: Keylogging, identified as T1056.001 under the Collection and Credential Access tactics for Windows, Linux, macOS, and Network Devices. It works by logging user keystrokes to intercept credentials, often employing methods like hooking API callbacks for keystroke processing, reading raw data from the hardware buffer, making Windows Registry modifications, using custom drivers, or modifying system images on network devices. It is notably used by numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and Kimsuky.

1339.name: Volatile Cedar
1339.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Volatile Cedar, also known as Lebanese Cedar and DeftTorero, is a Lebanese threat group that has been operating since at least 2012. Its custom malware includes Shroudedsnooper. The group's TTPs include reconnaissance to determine third-party infrastructure services and acquire OSINT data sets, as well as developing custom remote access tools and using fallback channels for command and control. It is politically and ideologically motivated and has targeted individuals, companies, and institutions worldwide.

1397.name: Remote access tool development
1397.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Remote Access Tool Development is a technique where adversaries create custom remote access software or malware components to establish command and control channels. This involves developing payloads, droppers, backdoors, and C2 protocols to maintain control of compromised systems, evade defenses, and execute post-compromise actions. The development process can include contracting specialized skills and obtaining infrastructure, such as web services, to support the malware's functionality. Actors may intentionally incorporate false indicators to mislead attribution.

1398.name: T1008
1398.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1008, known as Fallback Channels, is a command-and-control technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries establishing and using backup communication methods to maintain reliable command and control when the primary channel is compromised or becomes inaccessible. This technique is employed by groups like FIN7, APT41, Lazarus Group, OilRig, and UNC3886. It can be used in conjunction with other techniques like Dynamic Resolution (T1568) to reestablish lost connections.

1399.name: T1213.001
1399.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1213.001, also known as Confluence, is a Data from Information Repositories technique under the Collection tactic on the SaaS platform. Adversaries target Confluence repositories, often used for development documentation alongside JIRA, to mine valuable information. This can include internal policies, network diagrams, system architecture documentation, source code snippets, unsecured credentials, project schedules, and links to internal network shares and resources, as leveraged by groups like LAPSUS$.

1400.name: Determine 3rd party infrastructure services
1400.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity "Determine 3rd party infrastructure services" is a reconnaissance technique. Based on retrieved information, it involves adversaries identifying and gathering information about third-party services, such as cloud servers, domains, and web services, that are used by a target organization. This discovery can be performed through methods like scanning, API queries, or open-source intelligence to understand the external services a victim relies on, which aids in planning subsequent attacks like phishing or infrastructure compromise.

1401.name: Acquire OSINT data sets and information
1401.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Acquire OSINT Data Sets and Information is a reconnaissance technique where adversaries gather publicly available information about a target. This involves collecting data such as network domain properties (like registrar and contact details), assigned IP address blocks, and broader network topology from online sources, technical databases, or via phishing. The acquired intelligence, which can include organizational size and infrastructure hosting details, is used to inform subsequent targeting actions like active scanning, infrastructure acquisition, or initial access operations.

1405.name: PUBLOAD
1405.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PUBLOAD is a malware family attributed to the Mustang Panda threat group, which has been observed in phishing campaigns targeting entities in Europe and Russia. It is delivered via loaders that inject the PUBLOAD payload, and it connects to command-and-control (C2) servers such as 188.208.141[.]196. The malware employs defense-evasion techniques including Masquerading (T1036) and Subvert Trust Controls (T1553), and it establishes persistence through Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547). Its infrastructure uses domains like www.download.wndowsupdate.com and openservername.com.[/profile]

1406.name: PlugX
1406.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PlugX is a malware family also known as BackDoor.PlugX and BackDoor.Mikroceen. It is associated with numerous groups including APT22, APT26, APT31, APT41, Mustang Panda, and others. Its key TTPs involve defense evasion through System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) and Subvert Trust Controls (T1553), persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547), execution via Shared Modules (T1129), and data collection from removable media (T1025). It targets Windows platforms, uses encrypted payloads with XOR headers or THOR magic bytes, and operates through infrastructure involving domains like jcswcd.com and newsmailnet.com, dropping files to paths such as %PUBLIC%\SecurityScan.[/profile]

1408.name: Mustang Panda
1408.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Mustang Panda, also known as Honeymyte, Fireant, Polaris, Twill Typhoon, LuminousMoth, Stately Taurus, Camaro Dragon, TA416, Bronze President, BASIN, UNC6384, RedDelta, Red Lich, Earth Preta, and Tantalum, is a China-based cyber espionage group active since at least 2012. Its key malware includes PlugX, TONESHELL, and PUBLOAD, and it employs TTPs such as Shared Modules (T1129) for execution and Data from Removable Media (T1025) for collection. The group primarily targets government, diplomatic, and non-governmental organizations, including think tanks and religious institutions, across the United States, Europe, and Asia, with notable focus on Vietnam, Myanmar, Mongolia, Pakistan, and Russia, for intelligence gathering.[/profile]

1441.name: T1553
1441.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1553, Subvert Trust Controls, is a defense-evasion technique targeting macOS, Linux, and Windows. It involves undermining OS and security product trust mechanisms, such as code signing certificates or file attribute warnings, to allow untrusted execution. Adversaries may modify file permissions or registry settings, or steal/create fraudulent certificates to bypass these controls.

1444.name: Subvert Trust Controls
1444.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Subvert Trust Controls, identified as T1553, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves undermining OS and security product mechanisms that warn about or block untrusted activity, such as code signing or internet download warnings. Specific methods include modifying file/directory permissions or registry keys to disable these controls, and creating or stealing code signing certificates to falsely establish trust for malicious files.

1503.name: T1490
1503.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Inhibit System Recovery, designated T1490 under the Impact tactic, targets platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and network devices. Adversaries execute this technique by deleting or disabling built-in recovery mechanisms to prevent system restoration, often to augment data destruction or encryption attacks. Specific technical mechanics involve using native utilities like `vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet` or `wmic shadowcopy delete` to remove Volume Shadow Copies, `wbadmin.exe delete catalog -quiet` to delete the Windows Backup Catalog, and `bcdedit.exe` to disable automatic recovery features. On ESXi servers, adversaries may delete VM snapshots using commands like `vim-cmd vmsvc/snapshot.removeall`, and on network devices, they may wipe backup firmware images.

1504.name: T1530
1504.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1530, Data from Cloud Storage, is a collection technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to IaaS, Office Suite, and SaaS platforms. It involves adversaries accessing sensitive data from cloud storage objects like Amazon S3 buckets, Azure Storage, or Google Drive. Access is often achieved by exploiting common misconfigurations, such as overly permissive public access settings, or by using leaked credentials obtained from other sources. This data can include financial information, PII, or medical records, which adversaries may then exfiltrate.

1505.name: T1505
1505.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1505 (Server Software Component) is a persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries abusing legitimate extensible development features of enterprise server applications to install malicious components, such as scripts or software modules, thereby extending and abusing the server's functionality to maintain persistent access.

1506.name: T1550
1506.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1550, Use Alternate Authentication Material, is a Defense Evasion and Lateral Movement technique applicable to Linux, Windows, and cloud platforms. It involves using stolen legitimate authentication material like password hashes, Kerberos tickets, or application access tokens to authenticate to systems and bypass access controls without needing plaintext credentials, enabling lateral movement and persistence.

1618.name: Inter-Process Communication
1618.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Inter-Process Communication is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1559 under the Execution tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries abusing native OS mechanisms like Windows Component Object Model (COM) or Dynamic Data Exchange (DDE), and Linux sockets or pipes, to execute arbitrary code or commands locally between processes. This method can facilitate privilege escalation and evade detection, and is also leveraged by more sophisticated techniques like Process Injection for module communication via named pipes or other IPC channels.[/profile]

1620.name: T1129
1620.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1129, known as Shared Modules, is an execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries loading and executing malicious payloads via shared modules like DLLs, .so, or .dylib files to modularize malware functionality. This is achieved using platform-specific loaders such as `LoadLibrary` on Windows or `dlopen`/`dlsym` on Unix-like systems, allowing execution from arbitrary local or network paths. The technique is distinct from reflective loading, which executes code directly in memory without a file-backed module.

1621.name: Shared Modules
1621.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Shared Modules is a MITRE ATT&CK technique with ID T1129 under the Execution tactic for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries executing malicious payloads by loading shared modules like DLLs or shared objects. The technique leverages OS-specific loaders: on Linux/macOS, functions like `dlopen` from `dlfcn.h` load `.so` or `.dylib` files from arbitrary local paths, while on Windows, APIs like `LoadLibrary` via `NTDLL.dll` load DLLs from local or UNC network paths. This allows modular malware to run custom functions or invoke native APIs for tasks like command and control.

This method can be invoked via system calls or through higher-level frameworks like .NET, and is often used to subvert API-hooking defenses. Groups like Lazarus and Mustang Panda have employed this technique, and it is associated with vulnerabilities including CVE-2022-41049.[/profile]

1623.name: System Owner/User Discovery

This is achieved by querying system utilities like `whoami`, `w`, or `who`, examining environment variables such as `%USERNAME%` or `$USER`, and on network devices using CLI commands like `show users` or `show ssh`. Information can also be gathered from file ownership, process details, and system logs.[/profile]

1772.name: T1011

This allows adversaries to place and load a malicious DLL instead of the legitimate one, enabling arbitrary code execution under the guise of a trusted process, such as the LSA Subsystem Service (lsass.exe).

1775.name: Exfiltration Over Other Network Medium

Associated infrastructure includes domains like verify-person-entry.top, email-daemon.biz, drive-access.site, and bq-ledmagic.online, as well as the URL https://bitly.org.il/.[/profile]

2103.name: T1598

2110.name: T1078.002

Compromise is often achieved through means like OS Credential Dumping or password reuse, granting access to privileged domain resources and enabling lateral movement.

2112.name: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
2112.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.001 under the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows. It works by adding entries to specific Registry Run keys (e.g., HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run) or by placing executables in user or system-wide Startup folders (e.g., C:\Users\[Username]\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup), causing the referenced program to execute automatically upon user logon. A specific example is using the RunOnceEx key's Depend value to load a DLL at logon with a command like `reg add HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnceEx\0001\Depend /v 1 /d "C:\temp\evil.dll"`. This technique is widely used by numerous threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, and FIN7.[/profile]

This is achieved by embedding code within .NET COM assemblies using the [ComRegisterFunction] or [ComUnregisterFunction] attributes, which execute automatically when the utility runs, even if the registration process itself fails due to insufficient privileges.

2134.name: T1059.005

2135.name: T1218.009

2149.name: T1204.002

2211.name: T1562

This can involve blocking user logouts, preventing system shutdowns, disabling update processes, or targeting event aggregation and analysis. The technique is used by groups like BlackByte and Magic Hound and can be a follow-on action after cloud service discovery to evade identified defenses.[/profile]

2214.name: TA0003

It represents the adversary's goal to maintain their foothold on a system. The provided context shows it is referenced by specific techniques like modifying macOS plist files for automatic application reopening and abusing the cron utility for scheduled task execution, which are methods to achieve this persistence objective.

2215.name: T1192

2216.name: Impair Defenses

2217.name: Spearphishing Link

The technique relies on user interaction, such as clicking a link, which leads to a compromised website for browser exploitation, malware download, or credential harvesting via cloned login pages. Adversaries often obfuscate URLs using homograph attacks, URL schema abuse, or link shortening services, and may leverage the technique for OAuth token theft through malicious consent phishing applications.

2228.name: TA0037

Adversaries often employ IP address spoofing to obscure the attack source and increase difficulty for network defense filtering, with motivations ranging from political hacktivism to extortion and distraction for other malicious activities.

It is primarily attributed to Pakistan and targets diplomatic, defense, and research sectors, with a strong focus on India, Afghanistan, and Pakistan, motivated by cyberespionage.[/profile]

2400.name: ElizaRAT
2400.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ElizaRAT is a sophisticated Windows Remote Access Trojan (RAT) attributed to the APT36 group and associated with Operation C-Major. It employs defense evasion techniques like System Binary Proxy Execution and Boot or Logon Autostart Execution for persistence. For data theft, it uses Automated Collection and exfiltrates stolen information over web services. Its command-and-control infrastructure has utilized domains like adminsec.in and admindept.in, with targets including entities in India, Pakistan, and the British Indian Ocean Territory.[profile]

2402.name: ApoloStealer
2402.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ApoloStealer is a stealer malware deployed by the threat actors behind the ElizaRAT malware, associated with Operation C-Major. Its key technical behaviors include security software discovery (T1518.001), command and control via application layer protocols like HTTP(S) (T1071), and system network configuration discovery (T1016). It also leverages valid accounts (T1078) and abuses the Windows Task Scheduler for persistence (T1053.005). Its primary target platform is Windows, with infrastructure or targeting noted in the British Indian Ocean Territory and India.[profile]

2437.name: T1016
2437.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Network Configuration Discovery, identified as T1016, is a Discovery tactic technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries using native OS utilities like arp, ipconfig/ifconfig, nbtstat, and route to discover network details such as IP and MAC addresses. On network devices, commands like `show ip route` and `show ip interface` are used via a CLI, while on ESXi hosts, commands such as `esxcli network nic list` and `esxcli network ip interface ipv4 get` are leveraged. This gathered information is used to map the network and plan subsequent actions.

2438.name: Security Software Discovery
2438.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Security Software Discovery, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1063, is a Discovery tactic used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and IaaS platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating installed security tools like antivirus, firewalls, and monitoring agents to inform follow-on actions. Technical mechanics include using commands such as `netsh`, `reg query`, `dir`, and `Tasklist` on Windows, while macOS malware often specifically checks for LittleSnitch and KnockKnock software. This reconnaissance helps shape subsequent attack behaviors and evasion strategies.

2439.name: Malicious File
2439.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Malicious File, designated T1204.002, is an Execution technique targeting macOS, Linux, and Windows. It involves adversaries relying on a user to open a malicious file to gain execution, often following spearphishing. Common file types include .doc, .pdf, .xls, .exe, .lnk, and .iso. To increase success, adversaries employ masquerading, using familiar naming conventions, and obfuscation, such as password-protecting files. This activity can also occur post-initial access, like placing a file in a shared directory.

2440.name: System Network Configuration Discovery
2440.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]System Network Configuration Discovery, known as T1016, is a Discovery tactic technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries using native OS utilities like arp, ipconfig/ifconfig, nbtstat, and route to gather network details such as IP and MAC addresses. On network devices, they may use CLI commands like `show ip route`, and on ESXi servers, commands like `esxcli network nic list` to retrieve configuration data for follow-on actions.

2443.name: Mythic Poseidon
2443.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Mythic Poseidon, also known as Poseidon, is a Golang-based agent that compiles into Linux and macOS x64 executables and is designed to support the Mythic 3.0.0 command and control framework. Its key techniques include System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) for defense evasion and Exfiltration Over Web Service (T1567) for data theft. Associated infrastructure includes domains like admindesk.in, adminbr.in, and admincell.in, and it has been delivered via malicious PDF files such as 'https://admin-dept.in/approved_copy.pdf'. Its targeting has been observed against entities in India and Pakistan.[/profile]

2481.name: Access Token Manipulation
2481.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Access Token Manipulation is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1134 under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows. It involves modifying Windows access tokens to assume a different security context and bypass controls. Adversaries use built-in Windows API functions to copy tokens from processes, known as token stealing, to impersonate or spawn processes with elevated privileges, such as escalating from administrator to SYSTEM. Standard users can also create impersonation tokens using the `runas` command.

2482.name: T1134
2482.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Access Token Manipulation (T1134) is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows. It involves using Windows API functions like DuplicateToken or DuplicateTokenEx to copy access tokens from existing processes. An adversary, often already in an administrator context, can then apply this stolen token to an existing process via ImpersonateLoggedOnUser (Token Impersonation/Theft, T1134.001) or use it to spawn a new process with CreateProcessWithTokenW, thereby assuming the security context (e.g., SYSTEM level) and permissions of the token's owner to bypass access controls. Groups like FIN6 and APT28 have employed this method.

2484.name: CapraRAT
2484.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]CapraRAT is an Android Remote Access Trojan (RAT) used by the APT36 (also known as Earth Karkaddan or Transparent Tribe) cyberespionage group. It is deployed via trojanized applications and shares design similarities with the group's Crimson RAT for Windows. Its key behaviors include gathering victim host information (software and client configurations), capturing audio from the device's microphone, and exfiltrating data via web services. It specifically targets Android devices to steal SMS messages, call recordings, audio, screenshots, photos, file lists, device location, running apps, and notification text. Associated infrastructure includes domains like www.youuutube.com and ptzbubble.shop, with victimology focused on India and Pakistan.[/profile]

2486.name: CapraTube
2486.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]CapraTube is a malware targeting users in Pakistan and India, using phishing (T1566) for initial access. It establishes persistence by creating or modifying system processes (T1543) and employs Audio Capture (T1123) to record audio via system microphones. For command and control, it leverages Web Services (T1102), communicating with domains such as newsbizshow.net, shareboxs.net, and ptzbubble.shop.[/profile]

2495.name: Audio Capture
2495.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Audio Capture is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1123 under the Collection tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves using malware or scripts to interact with a system's microphones or voice/video call applications via operating system or application APIs to record audio. The captured audio files are typically written to disk for later exfiltration, as seen in activities by groups like APT37.

2496.name: Create or Modify System Process
2496.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Create or Modify System Process is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1543, falling under the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics. It is applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and Container platforms. This technique involves adversaries installing new or modifying existing system-level processes—such as Windows services, Linux daemons, or macOS launch agents—to execute malicious payloads at system startup or on a scheduled interval. This establishes persistence and can be leveraged for privilege escalation, as these processes often run with elevated SYSTEM or root privileges. A related vulnerability is CVE-2021-1675.[/profile]

2497.name: T1123
2497.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1123, also known as Audio Capture, is a collection technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. It involves adversaries using malware or scripts to interact with a system's audio input devices or applications through their APIs to capture audio recordings, such as sensitive conversations. These captured audio files are typically written to disk for later exfiltration.

2499.name: Mythic
2499.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Mythic is a cross-platform command and control (C2) framework used to install and manage agents, such as Nimplant and Apollo, which are built from its installation root. It supports agent features like peer-to-peer (P2P) communication and credential tracking. The framework is linked to infrastructure including the IP address http://157.245.139.146/trs-clip and has been observed targeting locations like the British Indian Ocean Territory and India. Associated adversary techniques include Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol, Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547), Hidden Files and Directories (T1564.001), Unix Shell execution, and Phishing (T1566).[/profile]

2500.name: Poseidon
2500.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Poseidon is a malware entity also known as Poseidon Stealer and is associated with the Odyssey Stealer family. It is a Golang-based agent that compiles into Linux and macOS x64 executables and supports the Mythic 3.0.0 command and control framework. Its key behaviors include abusing the Unix shell for execution, using cron for persistence on Unix-like systems, exfiltrating data over alternative protocols like HTTP, and discovering browser information. It employs binary padding for evasion. It has targeted users in Switzerland via malspam campaigns and infrastructure indicators include domains like publicinfo.in and winp247.cloud.[/profile]

2506.name: T1070.004
2506.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.004: Indicator Removal: File Deletion, used for Defense Evasion on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries deleting files like malware or tools to erase forensic evidence of their activity. This is commonly performed using native OS commands such as `del` on Windows, `rm` or `unlink` on Linux/macOS, and `rm` on ESXi. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT29, Lazarus Group, and Volt Typhoon, and has been linked to vulnerabilities like CVE-2024-0012.[/profile]

2507.name: T1048
2507.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1048, Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol, is an exfiltration tactic used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. It involves stealing data by sending it over a network protocol different from the main command and control channel, such as FTP, SMTP, HTTP/S, DNS, or SMB, often using native utilities like Net, SMB, or curl. This technique can be employed in automated exfiltration schemes and is associated with groups like TeamTNT and PLAY.[/profile]

2508.name: File Deletion
2508.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]File Deletion is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1070.004 under the Defense Evasion tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries deleting files left behind by intrusion activities, such as malware or tools, to remove forensic traces and minimize their footprint. This is commonly performed using native OS commands like `del` on Windows, `rm` or `unlink` on Linux and macOS, and `rm` on ESXi, or with utilities like SDelete.[/profile]

2509.name: Unix Shell
2509.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Unix Shell, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1059.004, is an execution technique within the Execution tactic targeting macOS, Linux, Network Devices, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries abusing native Unix shell interfaces (e.g., sh, bash, zsh) and scripts to execute arbitrary commands or payloads. This can occur through interactive shells accessed via command and control channels or during lateral movement, or through the deployment of shell scripts for sequential command execution, persistence, or task automation on compromised systems.

2510.name: Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol
2510.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol (T1048) is an Exfiltration tactic used on Windows, Linux, macOS, Network, IaaS, SaaS, and ESXi platforms. It involves stealing data by sending it over a network protocol different from the main command and control channel, such as FTP, SMTP, HTTP/S, DNS, or SMB, potentially to an alternate location. Execution can leverage native OS utilities like Net/SMB, FTP, or curl, and adversaries may further encrypt or obfuscate the data in transit. The technique is associated with groups like TeamTNT and Play.[/profile]

2511.name: T1059.004
2511.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1059.004, also known as Unix Shell, is a technique within the Execution tactic targeting macOS, Linux, Network Devices, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries abusing Unix shell commands and scripts, such as sh, bash, or zsh, to execute arbitrary commands or payloads. This can occur interactively via command and control channels like SSH or through the deployment of shell scripts for tasks like payload delivery or persistence. The technique is commonly associated with groups including UNC3886, Volt Typhoon, and APT41.

2513.name: pyshellfox
2513.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Pyshellfox is a malware targeting India, with indicators including domains like coordsec2.in and awesindia.online. It employs TTPs such as Binary Padding (T1027.001) for evasion, Cron (T1053.003) for persistence, and Python (T1059.006) and Unix Shell (T1059.004) for execution, along with Browser Information Discovery (T1217) for data gathering.

2515.name: globshell
2515.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The malware known as globshell is a Python-based threat targeting Linux systems. It establishes persistence by creating cron jobs and uses binary padding to evade detection. The malware gathers system information, including browser data, and communicates with command and control infrastructure hosted on domains such as warfarestudies.in, infosec2.in, clawsindia.in, coordsec2.in, and admincoord.in, which are associated with India.

2693.name: T1566.002
2693.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Spearphishing Link (T1566.002) is an Initial Access technique targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, and SaaS platforms. It involves sending targeted emails containing malicious links to download malware or exploit the browser, avoiding email attachment defenses. Execution requires user interaction, such as clicking the link, which may lead to browser compromise, malicious file downloads, or OAuth consent phishing to steal application access tokens. Adversaries often obfuscate URLs using special characters or URL schema quirks and employ social engineering to pose as a trusted source.

2699.name: T1059.006
2699.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1059.006, known as Python within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, is an execution technique (Tactic: Execution) targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries abuse the Python interpreter (python.exe) or .py scripts to perform malicious functions, leveraging built-in packages for system interaction, file operations, and device I/O to download and execute commands or other scripts. This technique is commonly associated with threat groups including APT37, MuddyWater, and Turla.

2700.name: T1217
2700.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1217, Browser Information Discovery, is a Discovery technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries enumerating browser data such as bookmarks, cached credentials, and browsing history from local files and databases (e.g., `%APPDATA%/Google/Chrome`) to gather personal user information and discover internal network resources. This technique can be paired with user activity monitoring to enable more effective credential phishing prompts.

2701.name: T1027.001
2701.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1027.001, known as Binary Padding, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries append junk data to malware binaries to alter their on-disk checksum and increase file size, which can bypass hash-based blocklists, evade static antivirus signatures, and exceed the scanning capabilities of some security tools or services. This padding does not affect the binary's core functionality. Groups like APT29 and Kimsuky have been observed using this method.

2702.name: Cron
2702.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Cron, designated as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1053.003, is a Scheduled Task/Job sub-technique within the Execution, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation tactics. It operates on macOS, Linux, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries abuse this time-based job scheduler by creating or modifying crontab files (e.g., `/etc/crontab`, `/var/spool/cron/crontabs/root`) to schedule the initial or recurring execution of malicious code at system startup or specific intervals. This provides a persistent mechanism for code execution without user interaction, as leveraged by groups like APT38, Rocke, and APT5.

2703.name: Python
2703.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity "Python" is mapped to MITRE ATT&CK technique T1059.006 (Command and Scripting Interpreter: Python) under the Execution tactic, targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries abusing the Python interpreter (`python.exe`) or `.py` scripts to execute commands interactively or via distributed scripts, which can also be compiled into binary executables. Python's built-in libraries enable file operations, device I/O, and downloading/executing further scripts or commands. This technique is used by groups such as APT37, MuddyWater, and APT29.

2704.name: Browser Information Discovery
2704.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Browser Information Discovery, identified as T1217, is a Discovery tactic used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. Adversaries enumerate browser data like bookmarks, accounts, and browsing history stored in local files and databases, such as `%APPDATA%/Google/Chrome`, to gather personal information and details about internal network resources. This information can also reveal cached credentials for follow-on targeting. Groups like APT38, Scattered Spider, and Volt Typhoon have been associated with this technique.

2705.name: Binary Padding
2705.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Binary Padding is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1027.001, a Defense Evasion tactic used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adding junk data to a malware binary's end or sections, which alters its on-disk checksum and file size without affecting functionality. This technique aims to evade hash-based blocklists, static antivirus signatures, and bypass security tool file size limitations, potentially hindering analysis by services like VirusTotal.

2706.name: T1053.003
2706.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1053.003 Cron, which falls under the Execution, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation tactics and targets macOS, Linux, and ESXi platforms. It involves abusing the cron utility, a time-based job scheduler on Unix-like systems, to schedule the execution of malicious code for persistence, often by creating or modifying crontab files such as `/var/spool/cron/crontabs/root` on ESXi.

2723.name: T1409
2723.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1409, also known as Stored Application Data, is a mobile attack technique within the Collection tactic targeting Android and iOS platforms. It involves adversaries accessing and exfiltrating sensitive data stored within application-specific directories, such as databases, configuration files, or cached information, to gather intelligence from compromised mobile devices.

2724.name: T1546
2724.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1546, also known as Event Triggered Execution, is a technique within the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics of the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, Office Suite, and SaaS platforms. It involves adversaries abusing system or cloud mechanisms that execute code in response to specific events like logons or application runs to maintain access. By creating or modifying event triggers to point to malicious content, execution can be proxied through higher-privileged accounts such as SYSTEM to escalate privileges.

2725.name: T1430
2725.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1430, also known as Location Tracking, is a mobile attack technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, falling under the Collection and Discovery tactics and targeting Android and iOS platforms. It involves adversaries accessing and collecting the geographical location data of a compromised mobile device, which can be used for tracking purposes or to inform further malicious actions.

2726.name: T1115
2726.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1115, known as Clipboard Data, is a collection technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows, macOS, and Linux platforms. Adversaries collect data stored in the clipboard from users copying information within or between applications. On Windows, this can be achieved using commands like `clip.exe` or `Get-Clipboard`, while macOS and Linux systems can be targeted with commands such as `pbpaste`. This technique has been associated with groups like APT38, APT39, and OilRig.

2732.name: Firmware
2732.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity "Firmware" is a reconnaissance technique, identified as T1592.003 under the Reconnaissance tactic, and operates on the PRE platform. It involves gathering information about a victim's host firmware, such as type and versions, which can be used to infer host details like configuration, purpose, and patch level. This information may be collected via phishing or from accessible data sets like job postings or network maps, revealing opportunities for further reconnaissance, capability development, or initial access.

2736.name: T1592.003
2736.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1592.003, also known as Gather Victim Host Information: Firmware, is a reconnaissance technique (Tactic: Reconnaissance, Platform: PRE) where adversaries collect details about a target's host firmware. This information, which can include firmware type and versions, is gathered through methods like phishing or from public data sets such as job postings or network maps. Acquiring this data can reveal host configuration and patch levels, potentially enabling follow-on actions like supply chain compromise or exploitation of public-facing applications.

2737.name: T1592.004
2737.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1592.004, known as Gather Victim Host Information: Client Configurations, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, operating on the PRE platform. It involves adversaries collecting specific client configuration details such as operating system version, architecture, language, and time zone. This information is gathered through methods like active scanning, phishing, or by compromising websites to deploy information-collecting scripts, and it can be sourced from public data like job postings or network maps. The collected data aids in further reconnaissance, capability development, or planning initial access vectors.

2738.name: Gather Victim Host Information
2738.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Gather Victim Host Information, identified as T1592, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to the PRE platform. It involves collecting details about a victim's hosts, such as administrative data, IP addresses, and configuration specifics like operating system and language. This information can be gathered through methods like Active Scanning, Phishing for Information, or by compromising websites to deploy malicious content that harvests data from visitors, including via User-Agent HTTP headers to identify software and OS versions for targeted follow-on actions.

2739.name: Client Configurations
2739.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Client Configurations, identified as T1592.004, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting the PRE platform. It involves gathering specific victim client details such as operating system version, architecture, language, and time zone. This information is collected through methods like active scanning of server banners and user agent strings, phishing for information, or by compromising websites to deploy malicious content that harvests host data from visitors. The gathered data aids in planning subsequent attacks like supply chain compromise or exploitation of external remote services.

2741.name: Megazord
2741.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Megazord, also known as Akira, is a Rust-based ransomware family attributed to the Akira group and active since at least August 2023. Its key technical behaviors include credential access via Kerberoasting and NTDS dumping, lateral movement using SMB/Windows Admin Shares, and inhibiting system recovery by deleting Volume Shadow Copies. It primarily targets Windows environments, exploiting vulnerabilities such as CVE-2020-3259, CVE-2024-0012, CVE-2024-9474, and CVE-2023-20269, with observed victim locations including Australia, Canada, and the United States.[/profile]

2743.name: Akira - S1129
2743.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Akira - S1129, also known as Akira ransomware, is a C++-based ransomware associated with the ransomware-as-a-service group Akira (G1024). It employs hybrid encryption and threading for efficient encryption, uses runtime arguments for tailored attacks, and has targeted sectors including manufacturing, education, and IT services across North America, Europe, and Australia. Key TTPs include Kerberoasting for credential access, NTDS dumping, lateral movement via SMB/Windows Admin Shares, and inhibiting system recovery via service stops and shadow copy deletion. It exploits vulnerabilities like CVE-2020-3259 and CVE-2024-9474, and notable variants target Windows and VMware ESXi platforms.[/profile]

2744.name: Akira
2744.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Akira, also known as Akira ransomware group or G1024, is a ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation. Its key malware is the Akira ransomware (S1129), which uses hybrid encryption and has targeted VMware ESXi. Key TTPs include Kerberoasting for credential access, lateral movement via SMB/Windows Admin Shares, and inhibiting system recovery through service stops (T1489) and shadow copy deletion (T1490). The group is attributed to financially motivated cybercriminals and has primarily targeted organizations in sectors like manufacturing, education, and IT services across North America, Europe, and Australia, including the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, and Australia.[/profile]

2805.name: T1558.003
2805.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1558.003 Kerberoasting is a Credential Access technique on Windows. It involves abusing a valid Kerberos ticket-granting ticket (TGT) to request Kerberos ticket-granting service (TGS) tickets for service principal names (SPNs). Portions of these tickets, often encrypted with the RC4 algorithm, contain the service account's hash, which is vulnerable to offline brute-force attacks to recover plaintext credentials. This enables persistence, privilege escalation, and lateral movement. The technique is associated with groups like Indrik Spider, FIN7, and Wizard Spider.[/profile]

2807.name: Inhibit System Recovery
2807.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Inhibit System Recovery is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1490 under the Impact tactic, targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and network devices. Its technical mechanics involve deleting or disabling system recovery features to prevent restoration, such as using commands like `vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet` to remove Volume Shadow Copies, `wbadmin.exe delete catalog -quiet` to delete the Windows Backup Catalog, and `bcdedit.exe` to disable automatic recovery. On ESXi servers, adversaries may delete VM snapshots via `vim-cmd vmsvc/snapshot.removeall`, and on network devices, they may wipe backup firmware. This technique is often used by groups like Wizard Spider and Sandworm Team to augment data destruction or encryption attacks.[/profile]

2808.name: Kerberoasting
2808.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Kerberoasting is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1558.003 under the Credential Access tactic for Windows. It involves an adversary with a valid Kerberos Ticket-Granting Ticket (TGT) requesting Ticket-Granting Service (TGS) tickets for Service Principal Names (SPNs) from a domain controller. The Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 hash (RC4-encrypted) within these tickets is vulnerable to offline brute-force attacks to recover the service account's plaintext password, enabling further access. This attack can also be performed using service tickets captured from network traffic.

2810.name: T1003.003
2810.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1003.003, also known as NTDS, is a Credential Access technique for Windows. It involves stealing the Active Directory domain database (NTDS.dit file), typically located at %SystemRoot%\NTDS\Ntds.dit on a domain controller, to harvest credential hashes and domain information. Adversaries may access the live file or search for backup copies using tools like Volume Shadow Copy, secretsdump.py, ntdsutil.exe, or Invoke-NinjaCopy. This technique is associated with groups including APT28, APT41, and Sandworm Team.[/profile]

2812.name: NTDS
2812.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]NTDS, also known as NTDS.dit, is formally identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1003.003 (OS Credential Dumping: NTDS). It falls under the Credential Access tactic on Windows platforms. The technique involves stealing the Active Directory domain database file, typically located at %SystemRoot%\NTDS\Ntds.dit on a domain controller, to harvest credential hashes and domain member information. Adversaries achieve this by creating copies using tools like Volume Shadow Copy, ntdsutil.exe, secretsdump.py, or Invoke-NinjaCopy, and may also target backup files containing the database. It has been associated with threat groups including APT28, APT41, and Scattered Spider.

2813.name: T1018
2813.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is MITRE ATT&CK Technique T1018, known as Remote System Discovery, which falls under the Discovery tactic and operates on platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. This technique involves adversaries enumerating other systems on a network using utilities like ping, `net view`, or `esxcli network diag ping`, and analyzing local data such as host files or ARP cache entries. It is also used to discover network infrastructure via CLI commands like `show cdp neighbors` on network devices. The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT41, Volt Typhoon, and Sandworm Team, and has been linked to vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-46604.[/profile]

2814.name: T1021.001
2814.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1021.001, also known as Remote Desktop Protocol, is a Lateral Movement technique within the MITRE ATTACK framework for Windows. It involves adversaries using valid accounts to log into remote systems via RDP to gain interactive graphical access, often following credential theft. This method is commonly exploited by groups like FIN7, APT41, and Volt Typhoon, and can be associated with vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-27997.

2815.name: Remote Desktop Protocol
2815.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Remote Desktop Protocol is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1021.001 (sub-technique of T1021 Remote Services) under the Lateral Movement tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries using valid accounts to log into remote systems via RDP (or Microsoft's Remote Desktop Services) to perform actions as the logged-on user, expanding access when the service is enabled. Adversaries often acquire credentials through Credential Access techniques and may use RDP in conjunction with techniques like Accessibility Features for persistence. The technique is distinct from VNC as it is resource-sharing software, and adversaries can also perform RDP session hijacking using tools like tscon.exe to steal active sessions without user prompts.

2816.name: Remote System Discovery

2926.name: Run Virtual Instance

2935.name: T1572

These jobs are self-contained in a database, often bypass firewalls, and can be configured for long-term execution or to trigger programs after reboots, enabling persistent background activity. 2939.name: T1098

2940.name: T1087

2941.name: T1069

2942.name: T1526

2945.name: Resource Hijacking

2946.name: T1525

2947.name: T1578

2948.name: Cloud Service Discovery

2950.name: System Services

3041.name: T1055.001

3111.name: T1027.005

3116.name: APT37

3851.name: T1068

3853.name: ROKRAT

3872.name: T1555
