5336.name: MERCURY
5336.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MERCURY is a malware entity. It is linked to the Iranian threat actor DEV-1084, which may be an independent partner or a destructive sub-team of MERCURY. Evidence for this connection includes shared infrastructure, such as the IP address 146.70.106[.]89 used for threatening emails, and the common use of MULLVAD VPN. Its technical behaviors include establishing persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547), collecting data through Email Collection (T1114), and leveraging Command and Scripting Interpreter (T1059) for execution. It exploits vulnerabilities CVE-2021-44228 and CVE-2021-45046, and has been associated with the indicator http://sygateway.com.[/profile]

5361.name: KerberCache
5361.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]KerberCache is a tool used to extract cached Kerberos tickets from a host's Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) memory, facilitating offline cracking via Kerberoasting (T1558.003). It is employed by groups like Cuba. Associated attack patterns include Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497), System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218), Non-Application Layer Protocol (T1095), Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486), and Native API (T1106). It leverages vulnerabilities such as CVE-2020-1472 and has been linked to indicators including the domains combinedresidency.org and optasko.com, and the email address poncho@combinedresidency.org.[/profile]

5362.name: SCREENSHOOTER
5362.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SCREENSHOOTER is a malware entity that performs screen capture activities, as indicated by its name and related content from entities like stealler and ispy keylogger. It employs techniques such as Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497) for defense evasion, System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) to proxy malicious commands via trusted binaries, and Native API (T1106) for low-level execution. It uses Non-Application Layer Protocol (T1095) for covert command and control and Data Encrypted for Impact (T1486) for destructive encryption. Associated infrastructure includes domains like combinedresidency.org and optasko.com, and it is linked to the vulnerability CVE-2020-1472.[/profile]

5363.name: ZeroLogon
5363.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ZeroLogon is a malware exploiting the CVE-2020-1472 vulnerability to perform Netlogon privilege escalation, specifically using phases like NetrServerReqChallenge, NetrServerAuthenticate2, and NetrServerPasswordSet2 with a zeroed client challenge. It is associated with groups such as APT29, APT32, APT41, Mustang Panda, UNC2452, and Vanilla Tempest, and has been used in conjunction with other malware like Cobalt Strike, IcedID, and Mount Locker. Its key TTPs include System Binary Proxy Execution and Native API for defense evasion and execution, primarily targeting Windows platforms, with infrastructure linked to domains like combinedresidency.org and optasko.com.[/profile]

5365.name: RomCom
5365.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RomCom is a remote access trojan (RAT) associated with the threat actor Gold Prelude. Its technical behaviors include lateral movement via SMB/Windows Admin Shares (T1021.002) and Remote Desktop Protocol (T1021.001), defense evasion through Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497) and System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218), and data collection via staging (T1074). It primarily targets Windows platforms and has used infrastructure domains such as publicshare.link, drvmcprotect.com, adobe.cloudcreative.digital, dns-msn.com, and fastshare.click.[/profile]

5366.name: Cuba
5366.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Cuba is a ransomware family that appends the ".cuba" file extension to encrypted files. It is associated with email addresses like admin@cuba-supp[.]com and admin@encryption-support[.]com, and a Jabber address for communication. Its technical behaviors include OS Credential Dumping via LSASS Memory (T1003.001), Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion (T1497), System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218), and command and control using Non-Application Layer Protocols (T1095). It exploits vulnerabilities such as CVE-2020-1472 and uses indicators like the domain combinedresidency.org.[/profile]

5367.name: Tropical Scorpius
5367.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Tropical Scorpius, also known as Gold Rebellion, White Dev 115, Dark Scorpius, and Wandering Spider, is a cyberespionage group attributed to Russia. It employs malware such as the Cuba ransomware, RomCom RAT, SCREENSHOOTER, and tools like KerberCache and ZeroLogon (CVE-2020-1472). Key TTPs include Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, System Binary Proxy Execution, Non-Application Layer Protocol for C2, and Data Encrypted for Impact. The group targets Ukraine and its allies, particularly following the 2022 invasion, and is motivated by supporting Russian geopolitical interests, though its exact government links are unconfirmed.[/profile]

5405.name: T1095
5405.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1095, also known as Non-Application Layer Protocol, is a command-and-control technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves adversaries using OSI layers below the application layer, such as ICMP, UDP, or VMCI in ESXi environments, for C2 communication to evade standard network monitoring tools. This technique is associated with groups like APT3, FIN6, and UNC3886, and has been exploited in conjunction with vulnerabilities including CVE-2021-21551 and CVE-2020-1472.[/profile]

5406.name: Non-Application Layer Protocol
5406.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Non-Application Layer Protocol, identified as T1095, is a command and control tactic used across Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries using OSI non-application layer protocols like ICMP, UDP, SOCKS, or Serial over LAN for covert communication, as these are less monitored than standard TCP/UDP. In ESXi environments, they specifically leverage the Virtual Machine Communication Interface (VMCI) for host-guest VM traffic that remains invisible to external network monitoring tools.

5407.name: Event Triggered Execution
5407.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Event Triggered Execution, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1546, is a technique used for Persistence and Privilege Escalation across Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. It involves abusing system or cloud service mechanisms that monitor for specific events—such as logons, application execution, or cloud API calls—to trigger the execution of malicious code. Adversaries create or modify these event subscriptions to repeatedly run their payloads, often proxying execution through higher-privileged accounts like SYSTEM to escalate privileges.

5409.name: ShadowPad
5409.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ShadowPad is a modular remote access toolkit (RAT) and malware family attributed to groups including APT41, APT17, Dagger Panda, Earth Lusca, Tonto Team, and Wet Panda. It employs loaders and payloads, and has been associated with infrastructure domains like tfirstdaily.store, update.microsoft-setting.com, and cdn-dev.helpkaspersky.top. It has been observed targeting locations such as the United States, South Africa, and Central African Republic, and exploits vulnerabilities including CVE-2022-21587 and CVE-2023-32315.

5410.name: ShadowPad - S0596
5410.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ShadowPad - S0596, also known as Shadowpad, is a modular remote access toolkit (RAT) actively developed and maintained. It is associated with multiple threat groups including APT23, APT41, APT17, Dagger Panda, Earth Lusca, Tonto Team, and Wet Panda. Its key technical behaviors involve using a loader component to deploy payloads and employing techniques like Dynamic-link Library Injection (T1055.001) for defense evasion and privilege escalation. It targets various platforms, as indicated by its exploitation of vulnerabilities such as CVE-2022-21587, CVE-2021-22555, CVE-2023-32315, CVE-2024-21412, and CVE-2016-5195. Its infrastructure includes domains like amelicen.com, support.helpkaspersky.top, update.microsoft-setting.com, update.centos-yum.com, and update.windows.server-microsoft.com.[/profile]

5411.name: PlugX - S0013
5411.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PlugX - S0013, also known as PlugX, is a modular remote access tool (RAT) used by multiple threat groups including APT22, APT26, APT31, APT41, Mustang Panda, Stone Panda, DragonOK, Winnti Group, and Gallium. It employs a plugin-based architecture for remote access and has been associated with indicators like support.helpkaspersky.top and update.centos-yum.com. It primarily targets Windows platforms and has exploited vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-32315 and CVE-2021-22555.

5412.name: XDealer
5412.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]XDealer is a cross-platform backdoor malware. Its aliases include WinDealer and SpyDealer. It is attributed to the LuoYu threat group. Key technical behaviors involve acting as a dropper for other malware families like ReverseWindow and ShadowPad, and it has been observed targeting the private Chinese banking sector. Its target platforms include Linux and Windows. Associated infrastructure domains include update.centos-yum.com, support.helpkaspersky.top, cdn-dev.helpkaspersky.top, softupdate.xyz, and tfirstdaily.store.

5413.name: CORESHELL
5413.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]CORESHELL, also known as SOURFACE, is a downloader malware attributed to APT28. It exploits vulnerabilities such as CVE-2022-21587, CVE-2016-5195, CVE-2023-32315, CVE-2024-21412, and CVE-2021-22555. Its infrastructure includes domains like update.centos-yum.com, cdn-dev.helpkaspersky.top, data-dev.helpkaspersky.top, update.microsoft-setting.com, and update.windows.server-microsoft.com, with targeting observed in locations including the United States of America, South Africa, Central African Republic, and American Samoa.[/profile]

5414.name: CORESHELL - S0137
5414.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]CORESHELL - S0137, also known as SOURFACE, is a downloader malware attributed to APT28. It is delivered as a .dll file attached to documents and includes unused code to mimic legitimate instructions, potentially for evasion. It exploits vulnerabilities including CVE-2021-22555, CVE-2016-5195, CVE-2022-21587, CVE-2023-32315, and CVE-2024-21412. Associated infrastructure includes domains like tfirstdaily.store, softupdate.xyz, and gtldgtld.store, with targeting observed in locations such as the United States, South Africa, and Central African Republic.[/profile]

5416.name: Earth Krahang
5416.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Earth Krahang is a distinct intrusion set, previously linked to but now considered separate from the China-linked Earth Lusca group. It is known to use malware families including CORESHELL (a downloader), XDealer (a cross-platform backdoor), and ShadowPad (a modular RAT), and exploits vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-32315 and CVE-2022-21587. Its operations involve hosting malicious payloads, conducting proxy attacks, and sending spear-phishing emails from compromised government accounts, with reconnaissance phases that involve harvesting large numbers of email addresses. Targeting has been observed against government entities in regions including the United States, South Africa, the Central African Republic, and American Samoa, indicating a broad espionage-focused campaign.[/profile]

5654.name: EnvyScout
5654.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]EnvyScout is a backdoor malware family used by APT29, which targeted Italian diplomatic organizations in a spear phishing campaign in June 2021. Its associated MITRE ATT&CK techniques include User Execution (T1204) and Phishing (T1566) for initial access, Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) for persistence, and Subvert Trust Controls (T1553) for defense evasion. Indicators of compromise include the domains techspaceinfo.com and crossfity.com.[/profile]

5655.name: APT29
5655.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]APT29, also known as Cozy Bear, Nobelium, Midnight Blizzard, The Dukes, and UNC2452, is a sophisticated intrusion set attributed to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). Its key malware and tools include Cobalt Strike and custom backdoors like SEADUKE, employing TTPs such as spearphishing with malicious attachments, using stolen tokens for authentication, deploying web shells on Exchange servers, and employing data obfuscation and standard application layer protocols for command and control. The group primarily targets government, diplomatic, and technology sectors in regions including Europe (e.g., Czechia) and Asia (e.g., Japan), with motivations centered on espionage and intelligence gathering, as evidenced by campaigns like the SolarWinds compromise.[/profile]

5690.name: Data from Cloud Storage
5690.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Data from Cloud Storage, identified as T1530, is a Collection technique targeting IaaS, SaaS, and Office Suite platforms. Adversaries access data from cloud storage solutions like Amazon S3, Azure Storage, Google Cloud Storage, OneDrive, and Google Drive, often by directly using Cloud APIs or exploiting common misconfigurations such as improperly set public access permissions. This technique is used to collect sensitive information, including financial and personal data, and has been associated with groups like Hafnium and Scattered Spider.

5796.name: TA0011
5796.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA0011, known as Command and Control, is a tactic within the MITRE ATTACK framework. It encompasses adversary efforts to communicate with and maintain control over compromised systems. Related techniques include using custom command and control protocols (T1094) to avoid standard application layer protocols and adding junk data (T1001.001) to these communications to hinder detection. Adversaries may also leverage data collected from databases to support their command and control infrastructure.

5797.name: TA0005
5797.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA0005, also known as Defense Evasion, is a core tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It encompasses techniques adversaries use to avoid detection throughout a compromise. This includes methods like adding junk data to command and control traffic (T1001.001) to obfuscate communications, abusing trusted system utilities (T1202) to execute commands without invoking standard interpreters, and employing custom command and control protocols (T1094) to blend in or bypass security controls. Groups such as APT28, Lazarus Group, and RedCurl have been observed using these evasion techniques.

5798.name: TA0042
5798.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA0042, also known as Resource Development, is a tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. This tactic encompasses adversary activities to establish and prepare resources needed for targeting and operations, such as acquiring infrastructure, compromising accounts, and developing capabilities. It supports subsequent phases like Command and Control (C2) by enabling adversaries to hide their infrastructure through methods like using proxies or VPNs to disguise IP addresses and blend with normal traffic, and by filtering network traffic to evade defensive tools and automated scanning.

5799.name: TA0002
5799.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA0002 is the MITRE ATT&CK ID for the Execution tactic, which encompasses adversary techniques for running malicious code on a local or remote system. This tactic is platform-agnostic. Technical mechanics involve using system features like Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) to execute commands and payloads, for example, using `wmic.exe` to delete shadow copies. The `at` utility can also be abused for task scheduling to perform execution.

5859.name: T1571
5859.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1571 (Non-Standard Port) is a command-and-control technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries communicating using a protocol and port pairing that are not typically associated, such as HTTPS over port 8088 or 587 instead of the standard port 443, to bypass filtering or obscure network analysis. Adversaries may also modify victim system settings, like Registry keys, to enable these non-standard port configurations. This technique has been used by groups including Gamaredon Group, FIN7, and Lazarus Group.[/profile]

5860.name: T1030
5860.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1030, known as Data Transfer Size Limits, is an exfiltration technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries breaking data into fixed-size chunks or limiting packet sizes during transfer to avoid triggering network monitoring thresholds that detect large data transfers. This method is used by groups such as APT28, APT41, and LuminousMoth to stealthily move stolen information.

6076.name: Connection Proxy
6076.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Connection Proxy, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK T1090 under the Command and Control tactic, is a technique for obfuscating network traffic. It involves using an intermediary system to relay communications between a compromised host and an adversary's infrastructure, avoiding direct connections. This is often implemented with tools like HTRAN, ZXProxy, or ZXPortMap for traffic redirection. The method masks the true command and control destination, reduces simultaneous outbound connections, and can leverage trusted internal paths or external resources like cloud servers for resilience and stealth.

6079.name: Standard Application Layer Protocol
6079.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Standard Application Layer Protocol is a technique used in the Command and Control tactic, aligning with MITRE ATT&CK ID T1071. It operates across multiple platforms, including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries use standard OSI application layer protocols like HTTP/S, DNS, SMB, SSH, or RDP to blend commands and data within normal network traffic, thereby avoiding detection and network filtering. This method is distinct from using custom or non-application layer protocols for communication.

6080.name: Exfiltration Over Command and Control Channel
6080.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exfiltration Over Command and Control Channel, identified as T1041, is an Exfiltration tactic technique applicable across multiple platforms. It involves adversaries stealing data by encoding and transmitting it over the same, existing command and control (C2) communication channel and protocol already established for remote access, blending stolen data with normal C2 traffic to avoid detection. This technique is commonly employed by groups such as Lazarus Group, APT39, and Wizard Spider, and stolen data is often encrypted prior to exfiltration using utilities like RAR or zip.

6081.name: Execution through Module Load
6081.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Execution through Module Load is a technique where adversaries execute malicious payloads by loading shared modules, which are executable files providing reusable code or OS API access. This can be done on Windows, Linux, and macOS systems using functions like LoadLibrary, dlopen, or dlsym to load modules from local or network paths. It enables modular malware design, allowing separation of C2 communications and other functions into distinct shared objects or DLLs for execution within a process.

6082.name: Execution through API
6082.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Execution through API, designated as T1106 Native API, falls under the Execution tactic and targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries directly or indirectly invoking native operating system APIs to execute behaviors, such as using functions like Windows API CreateProcess() or GNU fork() to start processes. It can be used to subvert defensive sensors by invoking syscalls directly from assembly, and higher-level frameworks like .NET or Cocoa provide language wrappers for these APIs.

6083.name: Windows Admin Shares
6083.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Windows Admin Shares is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1077 under the Lateral Movement tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries using administrator-level valid accounts to remotely access hidden network shares like C$, ADMIN$, and IPC$ over Server Message Block (SMB). This access enables remote file transfer, interaction via Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs), and remote execution of binaries through techniques like Scheduled Task or Service Execution, often initiated using the `net use` command. Access can also be achieved via Pass the Hash using NTLM hashes under specific system configurations.

6084.name: T1039
6084.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1039, Data from Network Shared Drive, is a collection technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows. Adversaries search accessible network shares and shared drives on compromised systems to find and gather sensitive files of interest prior to exfiltration, often using command shells like cmd. The technique has been associated with groups including Gamaredon Group, APT28, and Fox Kitten. A related vulnerability is CVE-2022-1388.[/profile]

6085.name: Rundll32
6085.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Rundll32 is a defense evasion technique (MITRE ATT&CK T1218.011) for Windows that abuses the legitimate rundll32.exe utility to proxy execution of malicious code, evading security tools that may whitelist the process. It can execute DLL payloads (e.g., `rundll32.exe DLLname,DLLfunction`), Control Panel Item files (.cpl), and scripts like JavaScript using syntax such as `rundll32.exe javascript:"\\..\\mshtml,RunHTMLApplication"`. Adversaries further obscure execution by abusing DLL function name loading order (checking for 'W' or 'A' suffixes first) or using signed system DLLs like zipfldr.dll.

6086.name: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription
6086.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription, also known as MITRE ATT&CK T1546.003 (Event Triggered Execution), is a persistence and privilege escalation technique within the Execution tactic, targeting the Windows platform. It works by creating WMI event subscriptions—comprising filters, consumers, and bindings—to execute arbitrary code when a specific system event occurs, such as a time trigger or user login. Execution is proxied through the WmiPrvSe.exe process, often with SYSTEM privileges. Adversaries may compile scripts into .mof files using mofcomp.exe to evade detection.

6090.name: NOOPDOOR
6090.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]NOOPDOOR is a malware that exploits vulnerabilities including CVE-2023-28461, CVE-2022-1388, CVE-2023-45727, CVE-2013-3900, and CVE-2023-3466. Its key Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) involve credential access via Unsecured Credentials and Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets, defense evasion via Create Process with Token, data collection from network shared drives, and command and control using Domain Generation Algorithms. It has targeted systems in Japan, British Indian Ocean Territory, Taiwan, and India, and has been associated with infrastructure domains such as blog.itochuci.co.jp, earth.hopto.org, ns1.tlsart.com, and tw8sl.com.[/profile]

6092.name: MirrorStealer
6092.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MirrorStealer is a credential stealer malware. It is deployed as a second-stage payload by the Lazarus Group, as seen in a 2022 compromise of a Hong Kong gambling company. Its key behavior is credential theft, specifically targeting and stealing victims' credentials, which aligns with the MITRE ATT&CK technique OS Credential Dumping (T1003). Associated infrastructure includes domains like tw8sl.com, earth.hopto.org, srmbr.com, and ns1.tlsart.com.[/profile]

6093.name: LODEINFO
6093.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]LODEINFO, also known as lodeinfo, is a malware attributed to the MirrorFace group. It operates by downloading and executing an HTA script via a malicious LNK file, then injects its payload into a svchost.exe process to run as a thread. The malware communicates with specific command and control hosts and operates based on received commands, with observed versions including v0.3.6 and v0.4.8. Its associated techniques include Create Process with Token, Unsecured Credentials, Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets, Domain Generation Algorithms, and Data from Network Shared Drive, and it has been linked to targets in Japan, Taiwan, India, and the British Indian Ocean Territory.[/profile]

6094.name: Earth Kasha
6094.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Earth Kasha, also known as MirrorFace, is an intrusion set attributed to the MirrorFace group. Its key malware includes LODEINFO and NOOPDOOR, and it has been observed using tools like Cobalt Strike. Its Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) involve credential access via Unsecured Credentials and Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets, defense evasion via Create Process with Token, data collection from network shared drives, and command and control using Domain Generation Algorithms. The group is believed to be of Chinese origin and has targeted entities in Japan, Taiwan, India, the British Indian Ocean Territory, and a diplomatic organization in the EU, with motivations likely aligned with espionage.

6114.name: Account Discovery
6114.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Account Discovery is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1087 under the Discovery tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating valid accounts, usernames, or email addresses to identify targets for follow-on actions like brute-forcing or spear-phishing. Specific technical mechanics include using built-in commands such as `net user /domain` on Windows, `dscl . list /Users` on macOS, `ldapsearch` on Linux, and cloud provider APIs like AWS ListUsers. This activity is often a precursor to techniques like Valid Accounts (T1078) and Brute Force (T1110).

6115.name: T1552
6115.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1552, Unsecured Credentials, is a Credential Access technique applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. It involves adversaries searching compromised systems for insecurely stored credentials, which can be located in plaintext files like shell history, OS/application repositories such as the Windows Registry, or specialized artifacts including private keys. The group Volt Typhoon has been associated with this technique.

6116.name: Unsecured Credentials
6116.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Unsecured Credentials is the technique T1552 under the Credential Access tactic. It applies across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries search compromised systems for credentials stored insecurely in various locations. This includes plaintext files like shell history, OS or application-specific repositories such as the Windows Registry, and specialized artifacts like private keys. The technique is associated with groups like Volt Typhoon and is linked to several CVEs, including CVE-2023-3519.[/profile]

6117.name: T1558
6117.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1558, Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets, is a Credential Access technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It subverts Kerberos authentication by stealing or forging tickets, such as Ticket Granting Tickets (TGTs) or service tickets, to enable Pass the Ticket lateral movement. Specific sub-techniques include forging Golden Tickets using the KRBTGT account hash for domain-wide access and creating Silver Tickets using a service account hash to access specific resources without contacting the Key Distribution Center (KDC). The built-in `klist` utility can be used to analyze cached tickets. This technique is associated with groups like Akira and is linked to vulnerabilities such as CVE-2022-24521 and CVE-2023-28461.[profile]

6118.name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
6118.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets (T1558) is a Credential Access technique targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It subverts Kerberos authentication by stealing cached tickets or forging new ones, such as Golden Tickets using the KRBTGT account hash or Silver Tickets using service account hashes, to enable Pass the Ticket attacks. The built-in `klist` utility can be used to analyze cached tickets, and related vulnerabilities include CVE-2013-3900.

6138.name: T1127.001
6138.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1127.001 (Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: MSBuild) is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It abuses the signed Microsoft Build Engine (MSBuild.exe) to compile and execute malicious C# or Visual Basic code embedded within its XML project files, thereby bypassing application allowlists that trust the legitimate binary. This leverages the inline task feature introduced in .NET version 4.

6145.name: T1134.002
6145.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1134.002, known as Create Process with Token, is a Windows-specific technique for Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation. It involves creating a new process using the security token of another user, often via functions like CreateProcessWithTokenW or the runas command, to bypass access controls. This action typically requires obtaining the target token through methods like Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) or Make and Impersonate Token (T1134.003). The technique has been associated with groups including Lazarus Group and Turla.[/profile]

6146.name: T1070.001
6146.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1070.001, also known as Clear Windows Event Logs, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. Adversaries with administrator privileges use commands like `wevtutil cl security` or PowerShell's `Remove-EventLog` to erase the System, Application, and Security logs, or directly delete files in `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\logs\`. This action hides intrusion evidence and can disable future logging after a reboot.

6147.name: T1560.001
6147.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Archive via Utility (T1560.001) is a Collection technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows. It involves compressing or encrypting collected data using system or third-party utilities to facilitate exfiltration. Adversaries abuse tools like `tar` on Linux/macOS, `zip` or `diantz` on Windows, or software like 7-Zip to package files. The technique is used by groups including APT41, MuddyWater, and Volt Typhoon.[/profile]

6148.name: T1562.004
6148.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1562.004, Disable or Modify System Firewall, is a Defense Evasion technique for macOS, Linux, Windows, Network Devices, and ESXi. Adversaries bypass network controls by disabling the firewall entirely or modifying specific rules via command-line, registry edits, or control panels, such as using the `esxcli network firewall set` command on ESXi. This enables unauthorized C2, lateral movement, or data exfiltration, often by adding rules for protocols like RDP on non-standard ports. Groups including APT38, FIN7, and Lazarus Group have used this technique, which is also associated with CVE-2022-1388.[profile]

6149.name: T1070.006

This activity is often performed using interactive command shells and utilities like cmd.exe, and has been associated with threat groups including APT28, Gamaredon Group, and Fox Kitten.

6151.name: Create Process with Token
6151.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Create Process with Token (T1134.002) is a Windows-specific technique used for Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation. 6152.name: MSBuild

6153.name: Clear Windows Event Logs
6153.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Clear Windows Event Logs, identified as T1070.001, is a Defense Evasion technique targeting Windows platforms. They may also directly delete log files from `C:\Windows\System32\winevt\logs\`. This technique is associated with groups including APT28, APT41, and Volt Typhoon.

6154.name: Disable or Modify System Firewall
6154.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Disable or Modify System Firewall, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1562.004, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. Adversaries execute it to bypass network controls by disabling the firewall entirely or adding, deleting, or modifying specific rules. This can be achieved through various methods, including command-line interfaces (e.g., using `esxcli network firewall set` on ESXi), editing Windows Registry keys, or using system control panels. The modification often aims to enable command and control, lateral movement, or data exfiltration, such as by creating a firewall rule for a protocol like RDP on a non-standard port.

6155.name: Timestomp

6156.name: Archive via Utility

6162.name: FIN7

6192.name: T1608.005

6196.name: SSH

6723.name: SystemBC

Its reconnaissance capabilities include gathering victim host (T1592) and network information (T1590). 6913.name: DodgeBox

6916.name: Bidirectional Communication

This return traffic can manifest as posting comments, issuing pull requests, updating documents, or sending tweets, leveraging the service's SSL/TLS encryption and common traffic for cover. Groups like APT28, Lazarus, and FIN7 have employed this method.

6919.name: T1102.002
6919.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1102.002, known as Bidirectional Communication, is a command-and-control technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable across macOS, Linux, Windows, and ESXi platforms. 6921.name: Gather Victim Network Information

Specific sub-techniques include gathering Domain Properties (T1590.001) and Network Topology (T1590.004). Groups like Hafnium, Indrik Spider, and Volt Typhoon have been associated with this activity.

6922.name: T1573.001
6922.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1573.001, Symmetric Cryptography, is a command-and-control technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It conceals C2 traffic by using symmetric encryption algorithms like AES, DES, 3DES, Blowfish, or RC4, where the same key encrypts plaintext and decrypts ciphertext. This method is employed by groups including MuddyWater, APT28, Lazarus Group, and Volt Typhoon.

6923.name: T1090.004
6923.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1090.004, known as Domain Fronting, is a command and control technique used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It obfuscates HTTPS traffic by exploiting Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) that host multiple domains. Adversaries use different domain names in the TLS SNI field and the HTTP Host header; if both domains are on the same CDN, traffic is routed to the host specified in the HTTP header after TLS decryption. A "domainless" variation uses a blank SNI field to bypass validation checks. This method has been associated with groups like APT29.

6924.name: StealthVector

Its key technical behaviors involve Defense Evasion techniques such as abusing InstallUtil for execution, performing Process Hollowing, and renaming legitimate utilities (T1036.003). It also uses Domain Fronting for command and control. The malware uses file names like wbwkem.dll, wkbem.dll, wmiwk.dll, C_20344.nls, and C_20334.nls to masquerade as legitimate system files.

6925.name: InstallUtil

6926.name: T1562.006
6926.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1562.006, known as Indicator Blocking, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves blocking or tampering with event collection to prevent detection, such as disabling Windows Event Tracing (ETW) by modifying registry keys like `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\EventLog\Security` or using PowerShell's `Set-EtwTraceProvider`. On Linux and ESXi, adversaries may reconfigure syslog using commands like `esxcli system syslog config set`. The technique can also involve creating firewall rules to block traffic to security monitoring systems like SIEMs.

6927.name: Domain Fronting
6927.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Domain Fronting, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1172, is a Command and Control technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It exploits Content Delivery Network (CDN) routing by placing a benign domain in the TLS header's SNI field and the true malicious domain in the HTTP Host header; if both domains are hosted on the same CDN, traffic is routed to the hidden backend. A "domainless" variation uses a blank SNI field to bypass validation checks.

6928.name: Symmetric Cryptography
6928.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Symmetric Cryptography is a command and control technique, identified as T1573.001, used to conceal C2 traffic on platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. It employs a single shared key for both encryption and decryption, with common algorithms being AES, DES, 3DES, Blowfish, and RC4. This method is distinct from asymmetric cryptography and is used by threat groups such as APT28, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater.

6929.name: T1036.003
6929.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The attack pattern T1036.003, known as "Rename Legitimate Utilities," is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS.
