This technique has been used by groups including APT38, Gallium, and Lazarus Group.

6930.name: Indicator Blocking
6930.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Indicator Blocking is a Defense Evasion technique (T1562.006) applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries blocking the collection or reporting of security indicators to sensors and analysis systems. This can be achieved by tampering with host-based telemetry settings, such as disabling Event Tracing for Windows (ETW) via PowerShell's Set-EtwTraceProvider or registry edits, or by creating host firewall rules to block traffic to central logging systems like SIEMs.

6931.name: Process Hollowing
6931.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Process Hollowing (T1055.012) is a Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation technique for Windows. It works by creating a legitimate process in a suspended state, using an API like `CreateProcess`. The process's memory is then hollowed out using calls such as `ZwUnmapViewOfSection` or `NtUnmapViewOfSection`. This unmapped memory is replaced with malicious code via `VirtualAllocEx` and `WriteProcessMemory`. Execution is masked under the legitimate process after realigning with `SetThreadContext` and resuming the primary thread with `ResumeThread`, evading detection. It is a sub-technique of Process Injection (T1055).

6932.name: ScrambleCross
6932.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ScrambleCross is a malware associated with APT41. It uses InstallUtil for execution via a .NET binary named System.Mail.Service.dll and employs encrypted shellcode payloads. Its infrastructure includes domains like ns.glbaitech[.]com, dev.kinopoisksu[.]com, and IPs such as 188.166.61[.]146. It has been deployed against targets in Indonesia, Malaysia, the United Arab Emirates, Italy, and Georgia.

6933.name: Rename Legitimate Utilities
6933.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Rename Legitimate Utilities is a Defense Evasion technique (MITRE ATT&CK ID T1036.003) applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries renaming legitimate system utilities (e.g., rundll32.exe, PSExec, AutoHotKey) or moving and renaming them in non-standard directories to bypass security controls that monitor for the abuse of these specific tool names. This is a form of Masquerading, with groups like APT32, Lazarus Group, and Menupass known to use it.

6934.name: StealthMutant
6934.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]StealthMutant is a malware loader. It is deployed via an InstallUtil launcher (T1218.004) and uses batch scripts for execution. It is associated with the APT41 group, as seen in the MoonBounce campaign, and is part of a loader set that includes StealthVector. Its known targets include Indonesia, Malaysia, the United Arab Emirates, Georgia, and Italy.

6935.name: T1218.004
6935.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1218.004, also known as InstallUtil, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves using the trusted Windows command-line utility InstallUtil.exe to proxy the execution of malicious code. The technique works by executing specific installer components within .NET binaries, often leveraging the `[System.ComponentModel.RunInstaller(true)]` attribute to bypass application controls. The utility is typically found in Microsoft-signed binaries within .NET Framework directories.

6936.name: T1055.012
6936.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1055.012, also known as Process Hollowing, is a defense evasion and privilege escalation technique for Windows. It executes arbitrary code by creating a process in a suspended state, hollowing out its memory with APIs like `CreateProcess` and `ZwUnmapViewOfSection`, and then replacing it with malicious code using `VirtualAllocEx`, `WriteProcessMemory`, `SetThreadContext`, and `ResumeThread`. This masks execution under a legitimate process to evade detection and is associated with groups like Gorgon Group and Kimsuky.

6940.name: Mélofée
6940.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Mélofée, also known as TripleZero, is a malware attributed to the TeleBoyi APT group. It is deployed via self-extracting archives (SFX) disguised as fake applications or documents, and uses techniques like RC Scripts for persistence on macOS, Linux, and ESXi, Impair Command History Logging for defense evasion, and Protocol Tunneling (T1572) for command and control. Its infrastructure includes domains such as cloudf1are.com, ssm.awszonwork.com, us.securitycloud-symantec.icu, dgbyem.com, and dev.yuanta.dev.

6941.name: Winnti
6941.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Winnti is a malware family associated with the APT17 group and the broader Winnti umbrella. It employs rootkit functionality (T1014) to conceal its presence by intercepting and modifying operating system API calls. The malware has utilized infrastructure domains such as update.ankining.com, www.data-yuzefuji.com, test.yuanta.dev, ssm.awszonwork.com, and dev.yuanta.dev. It is primarily a Windows threat, with detection scripts available to identify hosts compromised by the Winnti rootkit.

6942.name: HelloBot
6942.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]HelloBot, also known as hellobot, is a cross-platform malware family first detected in early 2019, targeting both Windows and Linux systems. It has been associated with groups like Earth Berberoka. Its technical behaviors include using RC Scripts (T1037.004) for persistence on Unix-like systems, Impairing Command History Logging (T1562.003) for defense evasion, and utilizing infrastructure such as ssm.awszonwork.com and update.ankining.com for command and control. The malware's development is linked to the Resource Development technique T1587.001 (Develop Capabilities: Malware).

6944.name: AlienReverse
6944.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]AlienReverse is a malware entity. Its infrastructure includes domains such as update.ankining.com, dev.yuanta.dev, test.yuanta.dev, us.securitycloud-symantec.icu, and vt.livehost.live. Its key behaviors involve defense evasion by impairing command history logging, establishing persistence via RC scripts on Unix-like systems, and employing protocol tunneling for command and control. It also gathers victim host software information for reconnaissance and stages tools for download.[/profile]

7028.name: Time Based Checks
7028.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Time Based Checks, also known as T1497.003, is a Defense Evasion and Discovery technique used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries using time-based methods to detect virtualization and analysis environments. This is achieved by calling functions like `GetTickCount` and `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime` to sample timestamps before and after a sleep function, calculating if the elapsed time is accelerated, which indicates a sandbox environment attempting to simulate longer time periods.

7029.name: T1608.001
7029.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1608.001, known as Upload Malware, is part of the Resource Development tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework on the PRE platform. This technique involves adversaries staging malicious software, such as payloads, droppers, or backdoors, on infrastructure they control, compromise, or on third-party services like web servers, GitHub, Pastebin, or decentralized systems like IPFS and blockchain smart contracts to make it accessible for operations like Ingress Tool Transfer. It is associated with threat groups including Mustard Tempest, Fin7, and Sandworm Team.

7030.name: Upload Tool
7030.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Upload Tool, identified as T1608.002, is a Resource Development technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to the PRE platform. It involves adversaries placing legitimate or dual-use tools, such as PsExec, onto internet-accessible infrastructure they control or compromise, including web servers, GitHub repositories, or Platform-as-a-Service offerings like Heroku. This staging enables subsequent operations like Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) by making the tools available for download into victim networks.

7031.name: T1562.003
7031.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1562.003, Impair Command History Logging, is a Defense Evasion technique for macOS, Linux, Windows, Network Devices, and ESXi. It works by disabling or manipulating command history logging to hide adversary activity. On Linux/macOS/ESXi, this involves unsetting the HISTFILE variable, setting HISTFILESIZE=0, or configuring HISTCONTROL to ignore commands prefixed with a space. On Windows, adversaries use PowerShell's Set-PSReadlineOption to disable history saving or change its save path. On network devices, commands like 'no logging' can disable CLI history.

7032.name: Network Address Translation Traversal
7032.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Network Address Translation Traversal, identified as T1599.001, is a Defense Evasion technique targeting Network Devices. It involves adversaries gaining control of a network boundary device like a router or firewall to maliciously modify its NAT configuration. This modification allows them to bypass routing restrictions that normally separate trusted and untrusted networks, enabling traffic to flow between segregated networks or to obscure their activities by rewriting packet IP headers. In designs requiring NAT, this overcomes inherent access limitations; where NAT is not required, it adds a layer of obfuscation to hinder monitoring.

7033.name: T1037.004
7033.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1037.004 (RC Scripts) is a persistence and privilege-escalation technique for macOS, Linux, Network Devices, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries achieve persistence by adding malicious binary paths or shell commands to system RC scripts like rc.local or rc.common, which execute with root privileges upon system startup. This is particularly effective on ESXi hypervisors, where modifying files such as /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh enables persistence across reboots, as most system changes are otherwise discarded. While deprecated in modern macOS and some Linux distributions in favor of systems like systemd, it remains viable on older systems or those maintaining backward compatibility.

7034.name: T1132.002
7034.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1132.002, known as Non-Standard Encoding, is a command-and-control technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi. It involves adversaries encoding C2 traffic with a non-standard or modified data encoding system, such as a custom variant of Base64, to evade detection by diverging from expected protocol specifications and making the content more difficult to analyze.

7035.name: T1608.002
7035.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1608.002, also known as Upload Tool, is a Resource Development technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework for the PRE platform. It involves adversaries placing tools on third-party or adversary-controlled infrastructure, such as web servers or cloud services like GitHub or Heroku, to make them accessible for operations like Ingress Tool Transfer. This staging can occur on acquired, rented, or compromised infrastructure.

7036.name: Upload Malware
7036.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Upload Malware is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1608.001 under the Resource Development tactic, applicable to the PRE platform. This technique involves adversaries staging malicious software on accessible infrastructure, including adversary-controlled or compromised servers, web services like GitHub or Pastebin, decentralized systems like IPFS, or blockchain smart contracts to ensure resilience. It also encompasses uploading backdoored files such as software packages, binaries, VM images, or container images to third-party repositories like PyPi or Docker Hub, often using masquerading tactics like typo-squatting to facilitate victim download and execution.

7037.name: Protocol Tunneling
7037.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Protocol Tunneling, designated T1572, is a Command and Control tactic used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves encapsulating one network protocol within another, such as performing SSH port forwarding or using DNS over HTTPS (DoH), to conceal malicious traffic, bypass network filtering, and route otherwise unreachable traffic like SMB or RDP. This technique is often combined with proxy methods to further obscure communications.

7038.name: T1599.001
7038.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1599.001, known as Network Address Translation Traversal, is a defense-evasion technique targeting Network Devices. Adversaries with control of a network boundary device, like a router or firewall, may maliciously modify its NAT configuration. This allows them to bypass inherent routing restrictions that normally separate trusted and untrusted networks, enabling traffic to flow between them or to obscure their activities by rewriting packet IP headers.

7039.name: Impair Command History Logging
7039.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Impair Command History Logging (T1562.003) is a Defense Evasion technique targeting macOS, Linux, Windows, Network Devices, and ESXi. It works by manipulating system settings to prevent command logging, such as unsetting the HISTFILE variable (`unset HISTFILE`), setting history size to zero (`export HISTFILESIZE=0`), or configuring HISTCONTROL to ignore commands starting with a space. On Windows, adversaries may use PowerShell commands like `Set-PSReadlineOption -HistorySaveStyle SaveNothing` to disable logging to the PSReadLine history file.

7040.name: Non-Standard Encoding
7040.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Non-Standard Encoding (T1132.002) is a Command and Control tactic used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves encoding command and control data with a non-standard system that diverges from protocol specifications to evade detection, such as using a modified Base64 scheme for an HTTP request body instead of the standard implementation.

7041.name: RC Scripts
7041.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RC Scripts, identified as T1037.004, is a persistence and privilege-escalation technique for macOS, Linux, Network Devices, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries modifying system RC scripts like rc.local or rc.common by inserting malicious binary paths or shell commands, which are then executed with root privileges upon system startup. This method is particularly effective on lightweight Unix-like systems, including ESXi hypervisors where leveraging files such as /etc/rc.local.d/local.sh is a key persistence mechanism, though its use is deprecated in modern macOS and some Linux distributions in favor of systemd or launchd.

7042.name: T1587.001
7042.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1587.001, known as Develop Capabilities: Malware, is a Resource Development technique within the MITRE ATTACK framework on the PRE platform. Adversaries develop malicious software components such as payloads, droppers, backdoors, and C2 protocols to support their operations. This process can involve contracting skills, using infrastructure like Web Services, and may include false indicators to mislead attribution. The technique is associated with groups like APT29, FIN7, and Lazarus Group, and it relates to vulnerabilities such as CVE-2024-36401.

7043.name: T1497.003
7043.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1497.003, Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion: Time Based Evasion, is a defense-evasion and discovery technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves using time-based checks, such as calling functions like `GetTickCount` or `GetSystemTimeAsFileTime`, to detect virtualized or sandboxed environments by measuring system uptime or identifying accelerated time simulations that deviate from expected real-time execution.

7046.name: T1480.001
7046.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1480.001, known as Environmental Keying, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It uses cryptographic methods to constrain malware execution by deriving decryption keys from specific, expected values in the target environment, such as network shares, system time, IP addresses, or software versions. This prevents execution in unintended environments like sandboxes, hinders reverse engineering, and avoids embedding the decryption key within the payload or transmitting it over monitored networks. Groups like APT41 and Equation have employed this technique.

7047.name: Execution Guardrails
7047.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Execution Guardrails, designated as T1480, is a Defense Evasion technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It works by constraining payload execution to only intended target environments by checking for adversary-supplied, environment-specific conditions before proceeding. These guardrails, distinct from sandbox evasion, verify the presence of expected values such as specific network share names, attached devices, files, Active Directory domains, or IP addresses; execution continues only if a match is found, thereby preventing exposure in unintended systems. Associated groups include Contagious Interview, BlackByte, and Gamaredon Group.

7048.name: Environmental Keying
7048.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Environmental Keying, identified as T1480.001, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It cryptographically constrains malware execution to specific target environments by deriving encryption/decryption keys from unique local values such as system time, IP addresses, domain names, or specific file hashes. This method delivers an encrypted payload that only decrypts and executes if the correct environmental key is present, thereby evading sandbox analysis and hindering reverse engineering. It is a sub-technique of Execution Guardrails and has been associated with groups like APT41 and Equation.

7050.name: REPTILE
7050.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]REPTILE is a malware family that functions as a backdoor. It has been deployed on compromised FortiGate and FortiManager devices, where it is used alongside the TABLEFLIP traffic redirection tool to bypass internet access restrictions. Its associated techniques include using SSH for lateral movement, creating accounts for persistence, employing rootkits for defense evasion, clearing system logs, and capturing user input. It has been observed exploiting CVE-2022-41328 and is known to target entities in the Republic of Korea.[/profile]

7051.name: Rekoobe
7051.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Rekoobe is a Linux backdoor malware attributed to APT31. Its key technical behaviors include using a configuration file to specify C2 server endpoints and connection intervals, employing command and scripting interpreters for execution, and utilizing obfuscation or deobfuscation techniques for defense evasion. Its primary target platform is Linux, with observed targeting of the Republic of Korea.[/profile]

7070.name: APT17
7070.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]APT17 is a malware entity attributed to groups including APT41, Aurora Panda, Leviathan, Dagger Panda, Earth Lusca, Tonto Team, and Wet Panda. Its technical behaviors include using Boot or Logon Autostart Execution for persistence, employing Rootkits for defense evasion, performing Brute Force for credential access, Archiving Collected Data prior to exfiltration, and conducting Indicator Removal. It has been observed creating and cultivating legitimate-looking profile pages on platforms like Microsoft TechNet to support its operations.[/profile]

7071.name: ZxShell
7071.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ZxShell, also known as zxshell, is a malware family attributed to groups including APT41, Emissary Panda, and Leviathan. Its key technical behaviors involve establishing persistence via a Windows service, using a service DLL and the ServiceDllUnloadOnStop registry parameter, and it implements a custom C2 server with a handshake protocol for versions 3.10 and 3.20. It includes a keylogger component and performs defense evasion by deleting its service registry key and marking its main DLL for deletion upon uninstallation. The malware targets the Windows platform.[/profile]

7072.name: Merdoor
7072.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Merdoor is a malware entity. Its key Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) include Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) for persistence, OS Credential Dumping (T1003) for credential access, Brute Force (T1110) for authentication attacks, and the use of Rootkits (T1014) and Indicator Removal (T1070) for defense evasion. It is associated with the indicator 4c55f48b37f3e4b83b6757109b6ee0a661876b41428345239007882993127397. Retrieved information suggests potential connections or similarities to other malware families like DOORME, Siestagraph, and ShadowPad, which are linked to groups including APT23, APT41, APT17, Dagger Panda, Earth Lusca, Tonto Team, and Wet Panda.[/profile]

7073.name: Lancefly
7073.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Lancefly, also known as Larva-208, is a malware entity associated with the APT group APT17. It employs persistence techniques like Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547), uses Defense Evasion tactics such as Indicator Removal (T1070) and Rootkits (T1014), and conducts Credential Access via Brute Force (T1110). Its command and control leverages Web Services (T1102) to communicate with infrastructure, including the domain 4c55f48b37f3e4b83b6757109b6ee0a661876b41428345239007882993127397, and it is related to other malware families like LuminousMoth and PlugX.[/profile]

7204.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
7204.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Use Alternate Authentication Material is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1550, categorized under Defense Evasion and Lateral Movement tactics. It operates across Windows, Linux, and cloud platforms. The technique involves adversaries using stolen password hashes, Kerberos tickets, or application access tokens to authenticate to systems and bypass access controls without needing plaintext passwords. This material is cached by systems post-authentication and can be intercepted via credential access methods, enabling lateral movement and evasion of multi-factor authentication.

7210.name: WinnKit
7210.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]WinnKit is a Windows rootkit that hooks the \Device\Null device object for communication with a user-mode agent, as described in relation to the Spyder and Winnti malware families. It uses the Process Hollowing (T1055.012) technique for defense evasion and privilege escalation, and employs Proxy (T1090) for command and control. Its behaviors also include Screen Capture (T1113) for collection, OS Credential Dumping (T1003) for credential access, and Ingress Tool Transfer (T1105) for tool delivery.[/profile]

7246.name: Bashlite
7246.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Bashlite, also known as Gafgyt, Lizkebab, Qbot, Torlus, and LizardStresser, is malware that primarily targets Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices to build distributed-denial-of-service (DDoS) botnets. It has historically exploited vulnerabilities like Shellshock and the WeMo UPnP API to infect devices. Its technical behaviors include using the T1059.007 (JavaScript) execution technique and the T1543.001 (Launch Agent) persistence method for macOS, as well as employing the Hidden Window (T1143) technique for defense evasion. The malware is associated with infrastructure or components named 'kiteshield'.

7247.name: Backdoor:Linux/Winnti
7247.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Backdoor:Linux/Winnti, also known as Winnti, is a Linux backdoor associated with APT17. It employs defense evasion techniques including software packing (T1027.002) and compiling after delivery (T1027.004), and can execute via service execution (T1569.002) on Windows. The malware targets Linux systems and uses C&C servers for command and control, with related infrastructure and tools including 'kiteshield', 'reshell', and 'sshdoor'.

7249.name: amdc6766
7249.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]amdc6766 is a malware entity with no known aliases or attributed groups. Its key TTPs include using the Launch Agent technique for persistence on macOS by creating or modifying .plist files in user directories, employing Compile After Delivery to evade detection by delivering uncompiled source code, and utilizing Hidden Window to conceal malicious activity. It leverages Service Execution on Windows via the Service Control Manager and abuses JavaScript for cross-platform malicious execution. The malware targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms, and is associated with the indicator 'kiteshield'.

7255.name: Launch Agent
7255.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Launch Agent is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1543.001 under the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics for macOS. It works by creating or modifying a property list (.plist) file in user-specific directories like ~/Library/LaunchAgents, using keys such as Label, ProgramArguments, and RunAtLoad set to true to automatically execute a malicious payload at user login. The agent can be loaded or managed via the launchctl command and often disguises its name to appear legitimate, operating with user-level privileges.

7256.name: T1564.003
7256.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1564.003, also known as Hidden Window, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows, Linux, and macOS. It conceals malicious activity by preventing application windows from being displayed. On macOS, adversaries can set the `apple.awt.UIElement` tag in plist files to hide an app's Dock icon. On Windows, they can use PowerShell with the `-WindowStyle Hidden` parameter, edit the Windows Registry to force windows to open off-screen, or use the `CreateDesktop()` API to create a hidden desktop with its own invisible processes. This technique is associated with groups like APT28, FIN7, and Gorgon Group.

7257.name: T1027.004
7257.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The technique T1027.004, known as Compile After Delivery, is a Defense Evasion tactic applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries deliver payloads as uncompiled source code to evade detection tools targeting binaries, requiring compilation on the victim system using native utilities like csc.exe, GCC, or ilasm.exe. This code may be further obfuscated through encryption or embedding within other files. The technique has been associated with threat groups including Gamaredon Group, MuddyWater, Rocke, and Sea Turtle.

7258.name: Hidden Window
7258.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Hidden Window (T1143) is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, macOS, and Linux. It works by abusing operating system or scripting features to hide application windows from the user's view, thereby concealing malicious activity. Specific implementations include using PowerShell's `-WindowStyle Hidden` parameter on Windows or setting the `apple.awt.UIElement` tag in macOS plist files to prevent a Java application's window from appearing in the Dock.

7259.name: T1543.001
7259.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This technique, known as Launch Agent (T1543.001), is a persistence and privilege-escalation method for macOS. Adversaries create or modify property list (.plist) files in user-specific directories like `~/Library/LaunchAgents` to establish persistence, configuring keys such as `Label`, `ProgramArguments`, and `RunAtLoad` to execute malicious payloads automatically upon user login. These agents can be managed via the `launchctl` utility and often masquerade with names from legitimate software to avoid detection.

7260.name: Compile After Delivery
7260.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Compile After Delivery is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1027.004 under the Defense Evasion tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS. Adversaries deliver payloads as uncompiled source code to evade detection by security tools scanning for binaries. This code, which may be encrypted or embedded in benign files like documents, requires compilation on the victim system using native utilities such as csc.exe, GCC, or MSBuild. The technique has been used by groups like MuddyWater and Gamaredon Group.

7262.name: Scattered Spider
7262.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Scattered Spider, also known as Octo Tempest, UNC3944, Muddled Libra, 0ktapus, and Starfraud, is a financially motivated intrusion set. It is known to use malware such as RedLine Stealer and has employed TTPs including establishing accounts for reconnaissance, gathering victim identity information, and using remote services for lateral movement. The group has been linked to the broader Twisted Spider cluster and is known to target corporate environments, as indicated by its use of deceptive domains like activesso.com and chartervpn.com. Its operations are primarily attributed to criminal actors focused on data theft and extortion.[/profile]

7463.name: T1586
7463.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1586, also known as Compromise Accounts, is a Resource Development technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to the PRE platform. It involves adversaries taking over existing online accounts to establish trusted personas for operations, using methods such as credential phishing, purchasing credentials from third-party sites, brute forcing with breached passwords, or bribing insiders. This technique can inform and enable subsequent phases like reconnaissance, phishing, or initial access via valid accounts.

7465.name: T1585
7465.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1585, named "Establish Accounts", within the Resource Development tactic on the PRE platform. This technique involves adversaries creating and cultivating accounts with various services to build operational personas. These accounts can be on social media, email providers, or cloud services, and are used to support subsequent activities like social engineering, phishing, or acquiring infrastructure. Groups such as APT17, Kimsuky, and Fox Kitten have employed this technique.

7466.name: T1589
7466.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1589, known as Gather Victim Identity Information, is a reconnaissance tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework operating on the PRE platform. This technique involves adversaries collecting personal and sensitive details such as employee names, email addresses, credentials, and MFA configurations to inform subsequent targeting. Information is gathered through methods like direct elicitation via phishing, active scanning of authentication services to enumerate valid usernames, and harvesting data from social media, victim-owned websites, or other publicly accessible datasets. This intelligence can enable further reconnaissance, resource establishment, and initial access operations.

7467.name: Establish Accounts
7467.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Establish Accounts is a Resource Development technique (T1585) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to the PRE platform. It involves adversaries creating and cultivating accounts on various services to build personas for operations, including on social media, websites, and email providers. These accounts are used to develop a credible online presence and can be leveraged directly for phishing or to acquire infrastructure through free trials.

7468.name: T1602
7468.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1602, Data from Configuration Repository, is a collection technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting network devices. Adversaries exploit configuration repositories used by management systems to collect large quantities of sensitive system administration data, which can include hashed credentials for network devices, to support discovery objectives and further attacks like password cracking. This data is often exposed via various protocols and software.

7469.name: Compromise Accounts
7469.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Compromise Accounts is a Resource Development technique (T1586) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, operating on the PRE platform. Adversaries compromise existing online accounts to create or hijack trusted personas for social engineering, rather than establishing new ones. Specific methods include credential gathering via phishing, purchasing credentials from third-party sites, brute-forcing using password reuse from dumps, or bribing insiders. Compromised accounts, such as those on social media or email services, may be further developed by modifying profiles and can be directly leveraged for subsequent phishing campaigns.

7470.name: Gather Victim Identity Information
7470.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Gather Victim Identity Information (T1589) is a reconnaissance tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, operating on the PRE platform. It involves adversaries collecting personal and sensitive identity details such as employee names, email addresses, credentials, and MFA configurations. This is achieved through methods like phishing for information, active scanning of authentication services to enumerate valid usernames, and harvesting data from open sources including social media, victim-owned websites, and public data leaks. The gathered intelligence enables follow-on actions like further reconnaissance, account compromise, and initial access via phishing or valid accounts.[/profile]

7471.name: Data from Configuration Repository
7471.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Data from Configuration Repository is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1602 under the Collection tactic, targeting Network Devices. Adversaries collect sensitive system administration data from configuration repositories used to manage remote devices. This data, which can include network layouts and credentials, is often accessed via management protocols like SNMP or Smart Install to query or export configuration files for later analysis.

7497.name: Trojan:MSIL/RedLineStealer
7497.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The malware is known as RedLine Stealer, also referred to as Trojan:MSIL/RedLineStealer. It is attributed to criminal actors. Its key technical behaviors include credential dumping (T1003) to steal account credentials, using web services (T1102) for command and control to hide traffic, and employing masquerading (T1036) for defense evasion. It primarily targets Windows platforms. Its infrastructure includes C2 servers such as http://138.68.27.0 and http://159.223.238.0.[/profile]

7501.name: T1195
7501.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1195, known as Supply Chain Compromise, is an Initial Access tactic applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and SaaS platforms. This technique involves adversaries manipulating products or delivery mechanisms before consumer receipt to compromise systems. Key methods include tampering with development tools, source code repositories (including open-source dependencies), software update channels, and system images. Attackers may broadly distribute tainted software but selectively target victims, or conduct "second-order" compromises by leveraging initial access to further infiltrate the software supply chain.

7502.name: Supply Chain Compromise
7502.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Supply Chain Compromise is a MITRE ATT&CK technique with ID T1195, categorized under the Initial Access tactic and applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and SaaS platforms. It involves adversaries manipulating products or their delivery mechanisms before they reach the end consumer to compromise systems or data. This can occur through the malicious alteration of development tools, source code repositories, software update channels, or even hardware and firmware, often to insert backdoors. Threat actors like Sandworm Team and OilRig have been associated with this technique, which can enable broad distribution of malicious code with follow-on targeting of specific victims.

7504.name: HELLOKITTY
7504.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]HELLOKITTY is a ransomware family that targets Windows systems, particularly by destroying Windows Volume Shadow Copies to hinder data recovery. It is associated with email indicators like lonnieguzman@onionmail.org and onion domain infrastructure. Its technical behaviors include Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol, Account Access Removal, Taint Shared Content, Domain Trust Discovery, and Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion. It has been referenced in relation to other ransomware entities like AvosLocker, Conti, and REvil. Geographically, it has impacted organizations in Spain, France, Italy, the United Kingdom, and Germany.[/profile]

7506.name: Zeppelin
7506.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Zeppelin is a ransomware, also known as Buran, attributed to the Vanilla Tempest group. It deploys as a .dll file and creates a registry key for data storage, initially named "Buran" before being changed to "Zeppelin". Its key TTPs include Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol, Account Access Removal, Taint Shared Content, Domain Trust Discovery, and Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion. It exploits vulnerabilities CVE-2021-1675 and CVE-2021-34527, targets European nations like Spain, France, Italy, the UK, and Germany, and uses infrastructure such as onionmail.org email addresses and a .onion domain for command and control.[/profile]

7507.name: Vice Society
7507.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Vice Society, also known as DEV-0832, Vice Spider, and Vanilla Tempest, is a ransomware group active since at least June 2021. It has deployed multiple ransomware families including Zeppelin, HELLOKITTY, BlackCat, QuantumLocker, and Rhysida, and has exploited vulnerabilities such as CVE-2021-34527 and CVE-2021-1675. Its key TTPs include Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol, Account Access Removal, and Taint Shared Content. The group is believed to be of Russian origin and has primarily targeted the education and healthcare sectors, particularly in the United States and across European nations including Spain, France, Italy, the UK, and Germany, with a motivation for financial gain.[/profile]

7545.name: T1570
7545.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1570, known as Lateral Tool Transfer, is a Lateral Movement technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries transferring tools or files between compromised systems within a network to stage operations. This is achieved using inherent file sharing protocols like SMB/Windows Admin Shares or authenticated connections such as Remote Desktop Protocol, as well as native tools including scp, rsync, curl, sftp, and ftp. The technique can also leverage automatically synced web services like Dropbox or OneDrive for file copying.

7546.name: Lateral Tool Transfer
7546.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Lateral Tool Transfer is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1570 under the Lateral Movement tactic, applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves transferring tools or files between compromised internal systems to stage for further operations. This is achieved using inherent file sharing protocols like SMB/Windows Admin Shares or authenticated RDP connections, as well as native system tools including scp, rsync, curl, sftp, and ftp. Adversaries may also leverage syncing web services such as Dropbox or OneDrive for this internal file transfer.

7547.name: Domain Trust Discovery
7547.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Domain Trust Discovery is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1482 under the Discovery tactic for Windows platforms. It involves adversaries gathering information on trust relationships between domains or forests in Active Directory to identify paths for lateral movement. Specific technical mechanics include enumeration using the `DSEnumerateDomainTrusts()` Win32 API, .NET methods, LDAP queries, or the Windows utility Nltest. This discovered information can enable follow-on techniques like SID-History Injection, Pass the Ticket, and Kerberoasting. Groups such as FIN8, Magic Hound, and Storm-0501 have been associated with its use.[/profile]

7548.name: Exploitation for Privilege Escalation
7548.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exploitation for Privilege Escalation, identified as T1068, is a Privilege Escalation technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and Container platforms. It involves exploiting software vulnerabilities, such as CVE-2021-44228 or CVE-2021-40444, to execute adversary-controlled code and elevate permissions from user to SYSTEM/root or escape a container to the host. A specific method is Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD), where a signed vulnerable driver is introduced to the system and exploited for kernel-mode execution. This technique is commonly used by groups like APT28, FIN6, and Scattered Spider.[/profile]

7549.name: Account Access Removal
7549.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Account Access Removal is identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1531 under the Impact tactic, applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries inhibiting legitimate user access by deleting, locking, or manipulating accounts, such as changing passwords or revoking SaaS permissions. Specific technical mechanics include using Windows Net utility or PowerShell cmdlets like `Set-LocalUser`, the Linux `passwd` utility, and ESXi commands `esxcli system account set` or `remove`. This technique is often used in ransomware attacks alongside other impact behaviors like Data Destruction and is associated with groups like Akira and LAPSUS$.[/profile]

7550.name: T1531
7550.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1531 (Account Access Removal) is an Impact tactic technique targeting Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and SaaS platforms. It works by adversaries inhibiting legitimate user access through account deletion, locking, or credential manipulation using tools like the Windows Net utility, PowerShell cmdlets (`Set-LocalUser`, `Set-ADAccountPassword`), Linux `passwd`, or ESXi CLI commands (`system account set`, `system account remove`). It is often used by groups like Akira and LAPSUS$ in conjunction with ransomware attacks to impede recovery, and may follow behaviors like Masquerade Account Name where an account is deleted and recreated.[/profile]

7559.name: Mimikatz
7559.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Mimikatz, also known as mimikatz, is a credential access tool primarily targeting Windows platforms. Its key technical behavior is dumping and extracting credentials from the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) process memory, as detailed in MITRE ATT&CK technique T1003.001, to obtain plaintext passwords, hashes, and Kerberos tickets. It is often used by various threat groups, including APT10, APT32, Anunak, and Gallium, and is commonly integrated into other malware like WannaMine, Black Basta, and Hive for post-exploitation activities such as pass-the-hash attacks.[profile]

7560.name: Metasploit
7560.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Metasploit is a penetration testing framework used to generate exploits and payloads, such as Meterpreter shellcode, for security assessments and attacks. It is not a malware family but a tool leveraged by various threat actors, including APT33, Lazarus Group, and Kimsuky, to facilitate initial access, persistence, and data exfiltration. Key associated techniques include Exploits (T1587.004) for developing and deploying attacks against vulnerabilities like CVE-2017-0144 and CVE-2023-22515, as well as Exfiltration Over Asymmetric Encrypted Non-C2 Protocol (T1048.002). It primarily targets Windows platforms and utilizes infrastructure such as domains like 40031.co and 12301230.co.[profile]

7562.name: RansomHub
7562.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RansomHub is a ransomware family, also known as ransomhub. It is associated with groups including ShadowSyndicate, Gold Prelude, and CosmicBeetle, the latter being a suspected recent affiliate. It exploits vulnerabilities such as CVE-2020-0787, CVE-2023-22515, CVE-2023-48788, CVE-2023-46747, and CVE-2017-0144. Its key behaviors include data exfiltration over asymmetric encrypted non-C2 protocols like HTTPS, transferring data to cloud accounts, modifying authentication processes, and performing account discovery. Its infrastructure and indicators include domains like 40031.co, 12301230.co, i.ibb.com, and samuelelena.co, and the email brahma2023@onionmail.org.[profile]

7563.name: RansomHub
7563.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The intrusion set is most likely the ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) operation known as RansomHub. It is also known as ransomhub and is associated with groups including ShadowSyndicate, Gold Prelude, and a suspected recent affiliate called CosmicBeetle. Its key malware is the RansomHub ransomware, which is believed to be based on code from the Knight ransomware gang. Key TTPs include data exfiltration over asymmetric encrypted non-C2 protocols like HTTPS, transferring data to cloud accounts, and modifying authentication processes. It exploits vulnerabilities such as CVE-2020-0787, CVE-2023-22515, CVE-2023-48788, CVE-2023-46747, and CVE-2017-0144. Its motivation is financial gain through ransomware extortion.[profile]

7568.name: T1048.003
7568.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1048.003, Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol, is an exfiltration technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Network Devices. It involves stealing data by sending it over an inherently unencrypted network protocol, such as HTTP, FTP, or DNS, that is separate from the primary command and control channel. To avoid detection, adversaries may obfuscate the stolen data within these protocols using methods like Base64 encoding or by embedding data within protocol headers and fields, all without employing encryption. This technique has been associated with groups including FIN6, APT32, and Lazarus Group.

7572.name: Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol
7572.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exfiltration Over Unencrypted Non-C2 Protocol is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1048.003 under the Exfiltration tactic, targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and ESXi. It involves stealing data by transmitting it over a separate, unencrypted network protocol (such as HTTP, FTP, or DNS) distinct from the command and control channel. Adversaries may obfuscate the exfiltrated data using encoding like base64 or by embedding it within protocol headers and fields, without employing encryption. This technique has been associated with threat groups including FIN6, Lazarus Group, and APT32.[/profile]

7578.name: T1537
7578.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1537, Transfer Data to Cloud Account, is an Exfiltration technique targeting IaaS, Office Suite, and SaaS platforms. It involves adversaries exfiltrating data by transferring it to another cloud account they control within the same cloud service, using native APIs, internal address space, or cloud-native sharing mechanisms like anonymous links or Azure SAS URIs to blend with normal traffic and avoid external network monitoring.

7579.name: Transfer Data to Cloud Account
7579.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Transfer Data to Cloud Account is a MITRE ATT&CK technique with ID T1537 under the Exfiltration tactic, targeting IaaS, SaaS, and Office Suite platforms. It involves exfiltrating data by transferring it to an adversary-controlled account within the same cloud service, utilizing cloud provider APIs, internal address space, and native mechanisms like anonymous file sharing links or Azure Shared Access Signature (SAS) URIs to blend with normal traffic and avoid external network monitoring. This technique has been used by groups including RedCurl, Storm-0501, and INC Ransom.

7580.name: Account Manipulation
7580.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Account Manipulation, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1098, is a technique used in the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves actions to preserve or modify access to a compromised account, such as altering credentials or permission groups. This includes iterative password updates to bypass password duration policies. To perform this, an adversary must already possess sufficient permissions, but successful manipulation can grant access to higher-privileged roles. The technique is associated with groups like Lazarus Group and Hafnium.[/profile]

7581.name: Exploitation of Remote Services
7581.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exploitation of Remote Services is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1210 under the Lateral Movement tactic, targeting platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi. It involves exploiting software vulnerabilities in remote services like SMB, RDP, MySQL, and VMware vCenter to execute adversary-controlled code and gain unauthorized access to internal systems for lateral movement. Attackers often use network service discovery to identify vulnerable systems, and successful exploitation can also lead to privilege escalation. This technique is associated with threat groups such as APT28, Wizard Spider, and MuddyWater, and is linked to specific vulnerabilities like CVE-2022-26134 and CVE-2021-44228.[profile]

It involves stealing data by transmitting it over an asymmetrically encrypted network protocol separate from the main command and control channel, such as HTTPS/TLS/SSL, which uses public-key cryptography where each communication end possesses a private key and the other's public key. It involves stealing data over a network protocol that uses asymmetric encryption, such as HTTPS/TLS/SSL, which is separate from the command and control channel. This method relies on public-key cryptography where each end of the communication uses a private key and the other's public key, exchanged prior to data transfer, to establish an encrypted channel for the exfiltration. Associated threat groups include APT28, Curium, and Storm-1811.[profile]

7584.name: T1110.003
7584.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1110.003, known as Password Spraying, is a Credential Access technique. It operates by using a single or small list of common passwords (e.g., 'Password01') against many different accounts to avoid triggering account lockouts that occur during targeted brute-force attacks. This attack commonly targets management services like SSH, SMB, LDAP, Kerberos, and RDP, as well as cloud applications and SSO systems. Adversaries may throttle attempts and use protocols like LDAP to avoid detection, such as Windows logon failure events. It is associated with groups like APT28, APT29, and Lazarus and affects platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, and network services.

7585.name: Password Spraying
7585.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Password Spraying (T1110.003) is a Credential Access technique applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and cloud platforms. It involves using a single or small list of common passwords (e.g., 'Password01') against many different accounts to avoid account lockout thresholds. Adversaries typically target management services like SSH, SMB, LDAP, Kerberos, RDP, and cloud applications (e.g., Office 365), often throttling attempts and preferring LDAP/Kerberos to avoid generating high-visibility security logs like Windows event ID 4625.[/profile]

7589.name: Cyclops Blink - S0687
7589.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Cyclops Blink - S0687, also known as Cyclops Blink, is a modular malware attributed to the Sandworm Team. It targets Small/Home Office (SOHO) network devices, specifically WatchGuard and Asus hardware, and is assessed as a replacement for the VPNFilter malware. Key technical behaviors include modifying authentication processes, gathering victim host information, stopping services, abusing software deployment tools, and collecting email data. It has been active since at least 2019 and is associated with the exploitation of vulnerability CVE-2020-1472.[/profile]

7591.name: Knight
7591.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Knight, also known as Disk Knight, is a worm that propagates via USB drives and establishes persistence by creating a registry key for automatic startup. It communicates with a command and control server at http://www.ariful.esmartweb.com. The malware is associated with the MITRE ATT&CK techniques Gather Victim Host Information (T1592), Service Stop (T1489), Software Deployment Tools (T1072), and Email Collection (T1114), and it potentially exploits vulnerability CVE-2020-1472.[/profile]

7592.name: Snatch
7592.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Snatch, also known as Snatch Ransomware, is a ransomware attributed to the Snatch Team criminal group. It employs RDP brute-forcing for initial access, uses Meterpreter reverse shells and Tor-based RDP proxies for command and control and lateral movement, and rapidly encrypts domain-joined systems. Its key TTPs include modifying authentication processes, gathering victim host information, stopping services, abusing software deployment tools, and collecting email data. It primarily targets Windows platforms and has exploited vulnerabilities like CVE-2020-1472.[/profile]

7617.name: Software Deployment Tools
7617.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Software Deployment Tools, designated as T1072, is an adversary technique within the Execution and Lateral Movement tactics. It targets platforms including Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and SaaS environments. The technique involves abusing centralized enterprise software suites like SCCM, Microsoft Intune, AWS Systems Manager, or Azure Arc for remote command execution and lateral movement. By gaining access to these administrative tools, adversaries can run scripts, deploy malicious software, or execute arbitrary commands across all connected endpoints, often leveraging existing web protocols for command and control. This abuse can provide broad network access, potentially requiring administrative credentials depending on the specific system configuration.[/profile]

7618.name: T1072
7618.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1072, Software Deployment Tools, is a technique used in the Execution and Lateral Movement tactics across Windows, Linux, macOS, Network Devices, and SaaS platforms. Adversaries abuse centralized enterprise software suites like SCCM, HBSS, Altiris, AWS Systems Manager, Microsoft Intune, Azure Arc, and GCP Deployment Manager to achieve remote code execution on connected systems. This access enables lateral movement, information gathering, or widespread effects like data wiping, often by leveraging administrative credentials to run scripts or commands.

7624.name: More_eggs - S0284
7624.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]More_eggs (S0284) is a JScript backdoor, also known simply as more_eggs. It is used by the Cobalt Group and FIN6. Its key behaviors include execution via JavaScript (T1059.007) and initial access through phishing (T1566), often requiring user execution (T1204). It performs discovery via system time checks (T1124) and Windows Registry queries (T1012). The malware targets Windows platforms and has been associated with infrastructure domains like 36hbhv.johncboins.com and webmail.raysilkman.com. At least two versions, 2.0 and 4.4, have been identified.[/profile]

7625.name: More_eggs
7625.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]More_eggs is a JScript backdoor malware family, also known as more_eggs. It is attributed to the Cobalt Group and FIN6. Its key behaviors include establishing persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547), leveraging User Execution (T1204) for initial compromise, and using System Binary Proxy Execution for defense evasion. It performs System Time Discovery (T1124) and Query Registry (T1012) for reconnaissance. The malware primarily targets Windows platforms and uses command-and-control infrastructure such as annetterawlings.com, wlynch.com, and johncboins.com domains, with known versions including 2.0 and 4.4.[profile]

7626.name: TA4557
7626.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA4557, also known as Cobalt Group, is an intrusion set attributed to the Russian Federation. It is known for deploying the JScript backdoor malware More_eggs, which uses techniques like Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547) for persistence, User Execution (T1204) for initial compromise, and System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) for defense evasion. The group's reconnaissance includes System Time Discovery (T1124) and Query Registry (T1012). Its command-and-control infrastructure has utilized domains such as wlynch.com, annetterawlings.com, and webmail.raysilkman.com, primarily targeting Windows platforms.[/profile]

7655.name: TigerRAT
7655.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TigerRAT is a remote access trojan (RAT) disclosed in 2021 as part of "Operation ByteTiger" and is associated with the Silent Chollima group. Its key technical behaviors include Account Discovery, Input Capture, and Gathering Victim Identity Information, and it is delivered via Phishing. It targets systems in the Republic of Korea, using infrastructure such as primez.online and specific HTTP endpoints like http://185.29.8.108:8585/load.html for command and control.[/profile]

7656.name: BlackRAT
7656.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BlackRAT is a remote access Trojan (RAT) promoted by an actor associated with the BlackRouter campaign. Its advertised features include encrypted communications, antivirus evasion, a small file size, plugin support, the ability to enable RDP, configure a cryptocurrency miner, and steal cryptocurrency wallets, passwords, and keystrokes. Its infrastructure indicators include domains like 'song.th' and IPs such as 109.248.150.147. Associated MITRE ATT&CK techniques include Phishing (T1566) for initial access, Input Capture (T1056) for credential theft, and Create Account (T1136) for persistence. Its known target location is the Republic of Korea.[/profile]

7657.name: Lilith RAT
7657.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Lilith RAT is a remote access trojan. It is associated with the North Korean-backed group puNK-003 and has been used by groups including Silent Chollima, TICK, and Earth Centaurs (Pirate Panda). It is a modified version of open-source Lilith RAT, with actors reusing code for command execution and changing its command-and-control protocol to use Dropbox HTTPS APIs. Its infrastructure includes indicators like http://84.38.132.67:9479/netpass.png. It employs techniques for account discovery, input capture, and phishing for initial access and credential theft, targeting systems in the Republic of Korea.[/profile]

7658.name: NukeSped
7658.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]NukeSped is a malware associated with the Lazarus Group and Silent Chollima. It employs Multi-Stage Channels (T1104) for command and control, uses Account Discovery (T1087), and captures user input (T1056) and clipboard data (T1115). Its infrastructure includes indicators like http://27.102.128.152:8098/load.png and http://185.29.8.108:8585/load.html, and it has targeted locations including Cyprus, Hong Kong, the Republic of Korea, Taiwan, and the United States.[/profile]

7660.name: Andariel
7660.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Andariel, also known as Onyx Sleet, Plutonium, and Silent Chollima, is a North Korean state-sponsored threat group considered a subset of the Lazarus Group and attributed to North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau. It has been active since at least 2009, primarily targeting South Korean government, military, and domestic companies, as well as conducting financial operations against ATMs, banks, and cryptocurrency exchanges. The group's notable malware includes Dtrack, Maui ransomware, and BlackRAT, and it has been associated with infrastructure like kmobile.bestunif.com and chinesekungfu.org. Key techniques involve credential theft (T1555), user execution (T1204), and lateral movement via remote services (T1021). Its motivations are believed to be espionage and financial gain.[/profile]

7718.name: AndarLoader
7718.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]AndarLoader is a malware downloader attributed to the Lazarus Group's Andariel sub-group. It employs techniques like Process Injection (T1055) for defense evasion and OS Credential Dumping (T1003), specifically targeting LSASS Memory (T1003.001) to harvest credentials on Windows systems. It has also been associated with Input Capture (T1056) and Brute Force (T1110) techniques. Its command-and-control infrastructure includes domains like panda.ourhome.o-r.kr and privatemake.bounceme.net.[/profile]

7719.name: ModeLoader
7719.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ModeLoader is a malware loader. It is associated with the Smoky Spider threat group (also tracked as UAC-0006) and is related to the SmokeLoader malware family. Its key technical behaviors include credential access via OS Credential Dumping (T1003), specifically targeting LSASS Memory (T1003.001) on Windows, and employing Process Injection (T1055) for defense evasion. It also utilizes Brute Force (T1110) and Input Capture (T1056) techniques. Its command and control infrastructure has included domains such as www.mssrv.kro.kr and www.ipservice.kro.kr, with specific endpoints like http://www.mssrv.kro.kr/modeRead.php.[/profile]

7764.name: Dtrack
7764.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Dtrack is a malware family attributed to the Lazarus Group and associated with Silent Chollima. It employs persistence techniques like Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts (T1037) and Defense Evasion tactics such as Subvert Trust Controls (T1553). The malware gathers victim host information (T1592) and has been observed targeting systems in Switzerland, Italy, Saudi Arabia, North Korea, and Germany. Its infrastructure includes domains like salmonrabbit.com, purewatertokyo.com, pinkgoat.com, and purplebear.com, and it has exploited vulnerability CVE-2017-10271.

7765.name: Maui
7765.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Maui, also known as Maui Ransomware (maui.exe), is attributed to the Silent Chollima group. Its key technical behaviors include gathering victim host information, encrypting data for impact, exfiltrating data over its command and control channel, exploiting client applications for execution, and using command and scripting interpreters. It targets Windows platforms and has utilized infrastructure such as the IP address 145.232.235.222 for hosting files like dwem.cert and mini.ps1, and is associated with the CVE-2017-10271 vulnerability.[/profile]

7781.name: CactusPete
7781.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]CactusPete, also known as elf.wellmess, is a malware associated with APT 29. It utilizes Office Template Macros for persistence and is delivered via spearphishing links or malicious files. The malware employs masquerading for defense evasion and has targeted entities in Pakistan and the Russian Federation. Its command and control infrastructure has included domains such as instructor.giize.com, upportteam.lingrevelat.com, and news.wooordhunts.com. Since late 2019, it has been observed using ShadowPad in its attacks.[/profile]

7783.name: Tonto
7783.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The intrusion set Tonto, also known as Tonto Team, is an APT group active since at least 2009. Its key malware includes the Bisonal RAT and it is one of the groups with access to the ShadowPad backdoor. Its TTPs involve spearphishing with malicious links and files, using Office Template Macros for persistence, and employing masquerading for defense evasion. The group is believed to be of Chinese origin, with suspected links to groups like Tick (Bronze Butler). It primarily targets government and institutional entities in Russia, Japan, and Mongolia, indicating a likely espionage motivation.[/profile]

7804.name: T1204.001
7804.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1204.001, also known as Malicious Link, is an execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It relies on user interaction, where an adversary uses social engineering to trick a user into clicking a link, which leads to code execution. This action is often a follow-on from Spearphishing Link (T1566.002) and can result in exploitation of client vulnerabilities (T1203) or the download of a malicious file (T1204.002). The technique is associated with numerous threat groups, including APT28, APT29, and FIN7, and has been linked to vulnerabilities like CVE-2018-0798.[/profile]

7806.name: T1137.001
7806.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1137.001, Office Template Macros, is a persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows and Office Suite platforms. It works by adversaries inserting malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros into base Microsoft Office templates, such as Word's Normal.dotm or Excel's PERSONAL.XLSB, which execute code when the respective application starts. Persistence can also be achieved by modifying the GlobalDotName registry key to point to a malicious template in a remote or custom location, often requiring macros to be enabled or the template to be placed in a trusted location. The technique has been associated with groups like MuddyWater.

7807.name: Office Template Macros
7807.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Office Template Macros, designated as T1137.001, is a persistence technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework targeting Windows and Office Suite platforms. It involves inserting malicious Visual Basic for Applications (VBA) macros into base Office templates, such as Word's Normal.dotm or Excel's Personal.xlsb, which execute code each time the respective application starts. Adversaries can modify these local template files, store them remotely, or hijack the template search order by altering the GlobalDotName registry key to point to a malicious file, thereby maintaining persistence through Office application launches.

7808.name: Malicious Link
7808.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Malicious Link, identified as MITRE ATT&CK technique T1204.001, is an Execution tactic technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows platforms. It relies on a user clicking a socially engineered link, which is often delivered via Spearphishing Link (T1566.002). The click can lead directly to code execution by exploiting a browser or application vulnerability (T1203) or by initiating the download of a malicious file (T1204.002) that the user is prompted to execute.

7809.name: Windshift
7809.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Windshift, also known as Windy Phoenix, is an intrusion set attributed to suspected Pakistani or Saudi Arabian actors, targeting entities in the Middle East. Its key TTPs include reconnaissance via social media (T1593.001) and the use of fictitious social media accounts (T1585.001) for social engineering, alongside automated data collection (T1119) and exfiltration (T1020) using standard application layer protocols (T1071) for command and control. Its primary motivation is believed to be espionage against government agencies in the region.

7810.name: T1593.001
7810.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1593.001, also known as Social Media, is a reconnaissance technique (Tactic: Reconnaissance, Platform: PRE) where adversaries gather information about victims from social media sites. They search for organizational announcements, staff roles, locations, and interests, which can be used to enable subsequent attacks like spearphishing or establishing accounts. This data harvesting can be passive or involve creating fake profiles to elicit information.

7812.name: Bitter
7812.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Bitter, also known as BITTER, is a remote access tool (RAT) used in targeted attacks, notably against Pakistan. Its key technical behaviors include audio capture for recording via system microphones and command-and-control communication using application layer protocols like HTTP/S, as indicated by its infrastructure domains such as signalpremium.com and youtubepremiumapp.com. It primarily targets mobile platforms, employing techniques like delivering malicious apps via other means and accessing notifications on Android. Associated attack locations include Singapore, Georgia, Australia, China, and Pakistan.

7813.name: Dracarys Android
7813.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Dracarys Android is a mobile malware targeting Android platforms, distributed via malicious apps delivered through means like third-party marketplaces or direct downloads from domains such as youtubepremiumapp.com and signalpremium.com. Its key technical behaviors include capturing SMS messages, capturing audio via device microphones, and collecting data from the local system. It uses standard application-layer protocols like HTTP or HTTPS for command-and-control communication. The malware has been observed targeting users in locations including Singapore, Australia, Georgia, China, and Pakistan.[/profile]

7815.name: Bitter APT
7815.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Bitter APT, also known as BITTER, Hazy Tiger, APT-C-08, TA397, T-APT-17, and Orange Yali, is a suspected South Asian state-sponsored group primarily targeting government and organizational entities in Pakistan, China, Bangladesh, Saudi Arabia, and other regions. Its key malware includes the Bitter RAT, AndroRAT, Artra Downloader, and Dracarys Android, often delivered via phishing that exploits vulnerabilities like CVE-2017-11882. The group's TTPs involve multi-stage command and control, data exfiltration with size limits, and victim host information gathering. Its infrastructure utilizes domains such as signalpremium.com and youtubepremiumapp.com. The group's motivation is believed to be cyber espionage.[/profile]

7829.name: T1433
7829.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1433 is a technique for command and control communication where adversaries use a custom protocol instead of standard application layer protocols. This can involve mimicking known protocols or developing entirely new ones, potentially using raw sockets over TCP/IP. To further evade detection, adversaries may employ multilayer encryption, tunneling their custom encrypted traffic within another encrypted protocol like HTTPS, and may also add junk data to the protocol stream to hinder analysis and decoding efforts.

7830.name: T1437
7830.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1437, also known as Application Layer Protocol, is a command-and-control technique within the MITRE Mobile-ATT&CK framework for Android and iOS platforms. It involves adversaries using standard application-layer network protocols, such as HTTP, HTTPS, or DNS, to communicate with compromised mobile devices. This method blends malicious traffic with legitimate network activity to evade detection.

7831.name: Masquerade as Legitimate Application
7831.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Masquerade as Legitimate Application is a mobile attack technique (Tactic: Defense Evasion, Initial-Access; Platform: Android, iOS) where adversaries disguise malicious applications as legitimate software to bypass security checks and user scrutiny. This involves using deceptive names, icons, and metadata that mimic trusted apps to facilitate initial installation and avoid detection.

7832.name: Access Notifications
7832.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Access Notifications is a mobile attack technique targeting Android, aligned with the Collection and Credential Access tactics. It involves adversaries abusing the system's notification access feature to read and collect sensitive information displayed in notifications from other apps, such as authentication codes, messages, or credentials, without requiring extensive permissions. This method allows stealthy data exfiltration directly from the device's notification stream.

7833.name: T1432
7833.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1432 is a command and control obfuscation technique where adversaries add junk data to C2 protocols to hinder detection and analysis. This can involve prepending, appending, or inserting random characters between significant data to prevent trivial decoding methods.

7834.name: T1517
7834.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1517, known as Access Notifications, is a technique within the Credential Access and Collection tactics for the Android platform. It involves an adversary abusing the Android accessibility service or notification listener permissions to programmatically access and collect the content of system and application notifications, which can contain sensitive data like authentication codes or messages.

7835.name: Capture SMS Messages
7835.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity "Capture SMS Messages" is an attack pattern with the alias T1412. Based on analysis, this technique falls under the Collection tactic and primarily targets mobile platforms. It involves adversaries intercepting or accessing SMS/MMS messages on a compromised device, often to steal authentication codes (like one-time passwords), sensitive communications, or financial information. This is typically achieved through malicious applications with excessive permissions, exploitation of device or carrier vulnerabilities, or by compromising cloud backups linked to the user's phone number.

aliases: Deliver Malicious App via Other Means
7836.name: Deliver Malicious App via Other Means
7836.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Deliver Malicious App via Other Means is an initial-access technique within the MITRE Mobile ATT&CK framework, targeting Android and iOS platforms. It involves delivering a malicious application to a victim's device through means other than official app stores, such as third-party marketplaces, direct downloads via web links, or side-loading. This method bypasses standard distribution controls to gain a foothold on the device.

7837.name: T1412
7837.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1412 is a deprecated technique formerly used for multiband communication in command and control. It involved splitting adversary communications between different protocols, such as using one protocol for inbound commands and another for outbound data, to bypass firewall restrictions or avoid data threshold alerts on a single channel.

7838.name: T1533
7838.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1533, known as Data from Local System, is a Collection technique within the MITRE Mobile-ATT&CK framework targeting Android and iOS platforms. This technique involves adversaries gathering data directly from the compromised mobile device's local storage, such as files, databases, or application caches, to exfiltrate sensitive information.

aliases: Deliver Malicious App via Other Means
7839.name: T1476
7839.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1476, known as "Deliver Malicious App via Other Means," is an initial-access technique within the MITRE Mobile-ATT&CK framework targeting Android and iOS platforms. It involves adversaries distributing malicious mobile applications through vectors outside official app stores, such as third-party marketplaces, social engineering links, or direct downloads via email or messaging.

7840.name: T1444
7840.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1444, known as "Masquerade as Legitimate Application," is a defense-evasion and initial-access technique within the MITRE Mobile-ATT&CK framework targeting Android and iOS platforms. It involves adversaries disguising malicious software by presenting it as a benign or trusted application to bypass user and system security checks, thereby facilitating unauthorized access and execution.

7845.name: AndroRAT
7845.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]AndroRAT, also known as androrat, is a Remote Access Tool (RAT) family for Android, developed as a client/server application in Java. It uses Application Layer Protocols like HTTP for command and control, and has been associated with infrastructure such as the domains levarisnetqlsvc.net and olmajhnservice.com. Its technical behaviors include System Owner/User Discovery and Process Discovery. The malware primarily targets the Android platform and has been observed in locations including Bangladesh, Saudi Arabia, China, and Pakistan.[/profile]

7846.name: Artra Downloader
7846.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Artra Downloader is a downloader malware. It uses Application Layer Protocols like HTTP for command and control, communicating with infrastructure such as olmajhnservice.com and levarisnetqlsvc.net. Its delivery leverages Phishing and exploits vulnerabilities including CVE-2017-11882. Once active, it performs System Owner/User Discovery and Process Discovery. Its operations have been observed targeting systems in Bangladesh, Saudi Arabia, China, and Pakistan.[/profile]

7847.name: SlideRAT
7847.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SlideRAT, also known as BitterRAT, is attributed to the Bitter APT group. It targets Windows systems, exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2017-11882 and CVE-2018-0798. Its key TTPs include using Application Layer Protocols like HTTP for command and control, and performing Process Discovery and System Owner/User Discovery. The malware is designed for spying, capable of exfiltrating call recordings, SMS messages, location data, and device information. Associated infrastructure includes domains like olmajhnservice.com and levarisnetqlsvc.net, with targeting observed in Bangladesh, Saudi Arabia, China, and Pakistan.[/profile]

7848.name: Bitter RAT
7848.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Bitter RAT, also known as BITTER, is a remote access tool used in targeted attacks, notably against Pakistani nationals. It is associated with the Bitter group and leverages Application Layer Protocol (T1071) for C2, specifically using HTTP to communicate with domains like olmajhnservice.com and levarisnetqlsvc.net. The malware employs techniques such as System Owner/User Discovery (T1033) and Process Discovery (T1057), and is delivered via Phishing (T1566), often exploiting vulnerabilities like CVE-2017-11882. Its primary targets are in Bangladesh, Saudi Arabia, China, and Pakistan.[/profile]

7952.name: ZxxZ
7952.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]ZxxZ, also known as MuuyDownloader, is a downloader malware attributed to the threat group Hazy Tiger (also known as Bitter). It is written in C++ and serves as a downloader, succeeding ArtraDownloader. The malware establishes command and control (C2) communication with infrastructure such as diyefosterfeeds.com, spurshipbroker.com, huandocimama.com, and emshedulersvc.com. It employs Multi-Stage Channels for C2 obfuscation, uses Data Transfer Size Limits for exfiltration, and can Gather Victim Host Information. It targets Windows systems and leverages vulnerabilities like CVE-2018-0798.

7953.name: MuuyDownloader
7953.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MuuyDownloader, also known as ZxxZ downloader, is a downloader malware attributed to the Bitter APT group (aka Hazy Tiger). It is written in C++ and serves as a successor to ArtraDownloader, with a similar implementation. Its key behaviors include staging capabilities on attacker-controlled infrastructure, using multi-stage command and control channels to obfuscate detection, gathering victim host information, and employing data transfer size limits during exfiltration. It has targeted entities in Bangladesh and has been associated with infrastructure domains like spurshipbroker.com, m.huandocimama.com, and emshedulersvc.com.

7955.name: Almond
7955.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Almond is a malware with known indicators including domains like emshedulersvc.com, huandocimama.com, and m.huandocimama.com, and a specific URI path for profiles.php. It leverages the CVE-2018-0798 vulnerability and has been observed targeting Bangladesh.
