9450.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]QakBot, also known as Qbot or QuackBot, is a malware family associated with groups like Gold Cabin, FIN6, TA2101, and Pinchy Spider. It employs techniques such as Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets for credential access, uses Software Deployment Tools for execution and lateral movement, and leverages External Remote Services for initial access. It targets Windows platforms and has been linked to infrastructure indicators including domains like depotejarat.ir and plax.duckdns.org, as well as cryptocurrency addresses. It has exploited vulnerabilities like CVE-2022-24521 and CVE-2020-1472.[/profile]

9451.name: Redline
9451.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Redline, also known as Redline Stealer, is an infostealer malware. It establishes persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution, such as by creating a Windows Registry key. It is delivered through User Execution, often via Phishing campaigns. The malware performs Network Share Discovery (T1135) and can exfiltrate data from cloud storage (T1530). Associated infrastructure includes domains like plax.duckdns.org, zaminkaran.ir, direct-trojan.com, codezian.com, and winery.nsupdate.info.[/profile]

9452.name: DOUBLEBACK
9452.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]DOUBLEBACK, also known as doubleback, is a third-stage backdoor malware. It has been observed beaconing to command and control servers such as hxxps://klikbets[.]net/admin/client.php and hxxps://lasartoria[.]net/admin/client.php. Its technical behaviors include using techniques like Right-to-Left Override and double file extensions to masquerade its executable files and evade detection, and it leverages persistence mechanisms like Boot or Logon Autostart Execution (T1547). Its initial access is often achieved through Phishing (T1566) and User Execution (T1204). Associated infrastructure includes domains like ghcc.duckdns.org, codezian.com, and winery.nsupdate.info.[/profile]

9454.name: XWorm
9454.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]XWorm is a Remote Access Trojan (RAT) malware, also known as xworm. It is associated with the threat group Hive0137 and has been used in phishing campaigns targeting Italian-speaking victims. Its key technical behaviors include establishing persistence via Boot or Logon Autostart Execution, using User Execution for initial access, and communicating with command-and-control (C2) servers using specific keys like "<123456789>" for version 5.6 and "<666666>" for version 6, with observed C2 domains including onenotegem.com, barricks.org, and mo1010.duckdns.org. It primarily targets Windows platforms and also performs Network Share Discovery for lateral movement.[/profile]

9455.name: TA577
9455.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA577, also known as Hive0118, is a prolific cybercrime threat actor tracked since mid-2020. It is known to deliver a wide range of payloads including Qbot, IcedID, SystemBC, SmokeLoader, Ursnif, Cobalt Strike, DOUBLEBACK, XWorm, AsyncRAT, NETWIRE, and Redline. Its key TTPs include using Phishing and User Execution for initial access, and employing techniques like Boot or Logon Autostart Execution for persistence, and Network Share Discovery and Data from Cloud Storage for discovery and collection. The group conducts broad targeting across various industries and geographies, with its primary motivation believed to be financial gain.[/profile]

9539.name: Network Share Discovery
9539.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Network Share Discovery, identified as T1135, is a Discovery tactic used on Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries enumerating shared folders and drives on remote or local systems to identify information sources for collection and lateral movement. Specific technical mechanics include using the `net view \\\\remotesystem` command to query remote Windows shares, `net share` for local shares, and the `sharing -l` command on macOS to list SMB service share points.

9541.name: Volt Typhoon
9541.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Volt Typhoon, also known as UNC3236, BRONZE SILHOUETTE, Vanguard Panda, Storm-0391, and Voltzite, is a People's Republic of China (PRC) state-sponsored actor active since at least 2021. It primarily targets critical infrastructure organizations in the United States and its territories, including Guam, with a pattern of behavior assessed as pre-positioning for potential disruptive attacks on operational technology. The group emphasizes stealth, using living-off-the-land (LOTL) binaries, web shells, stolen credentials, and hands-on-keyboard activities. Its known TTPs include vulnerability scanning (T1595.002) and exploitation of remote services (T1210) for lateral movement.[/profile]

9547.name: DONOT
9547.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The intrusion set known as DONOT, also referred to as APT-C-35, DoNot Team, Viceroy Tiger, Operation Hangover, Orange Kala, and Sectore02, is attributed to a group believed to operate from South Asia. It employs custom malware named Donot, which uses persistence techniques like Office Application Startup (T1137) and is delivered via spearphishing. The group's key TTPs include internal spearphishing (T1534), replication through removable media (T1091), and clipboard data collection (T1115). It primarily targets entities in South Asia, including Sri Lanka, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Nepal, and China, with motivations likely aligned with cyber espionage. Its infrastructure includes domains such as packetbite.live and info.printerupdates.online.[/profile]

9613.name: T1074.001
9613.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1074.001, known as Local Data Staging, is a Collection technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Adversaries use it to consolidate collected data into a central directory or file on the compromised local system before exfiltration, often employing command shells like cmd or bash for the copying process. Staging locations can include local folders, databases, or the Windows Registry, and data may be aggregated using methods like Archive Collected Data (T1560). This technique is commonly associated with threat groups including APT28, Lazarus Group, MuddyWater, and Volt Typhoon.

9614.name: T1534
9614.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The technique Internal Spearphishing, identified as T1534, is a Lateral Movement tactic used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and SaaS platforms. It involves adversaries leveraging a previously compromised legitimate internal account to conduct spearphishing campaigns against other users within the same organization. This increases the success rate of phishing attempts, often using methods like Spearphishing Attachment or Spearphishing Link to deliver payloads or credential capture sites, and can be propagated through internal chat applications like Microsoft Teams.

9615.name: T1036.005

9615.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location, identified as T1036.005, is a Defense Evasion technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, ESXi, and Containers. Adversaries evade detection by naming or placing malicious resources to closely resemble legitimate ones, such as placing an executable in a trusted directory like System32 or naming it after a trusted process like svchost.exe. In containerized environments, this involves creating resources in trusted namespaces or using naming conventions that match legitimate pods. This technique is used by numerous threat groups including APT29, Lazarus Group, and MuddyWater.

9664.name: T1091
9664.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1091, Replication Through Removable Media, is an attack pattern for Initial Access and Lateral Movement on Windows. It involves copying malware to removable media like USB drives to exploit Autorun features for automatic execution when the media is connected. The technique can also use modified executable files on the media or malware disguised as legitimate files to trick users. Mobile devices connected via USB can similarly infect systems if they contain compatible malware. Related groups include APT28, Gamaredon Group, and FIN7.

9667.name: Donot
9667.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Donot, also known as APT-C-35 and DoNot Team, is a malware attributed to the Viceroy Tiger group. It employs persistence techniques like Office Application Startup (T1137) and defense evasion via Indicator Removal (T1070) and Impair Defenses (T1562). It collects and archives data (T1560) for exfiltration, often delivered via spearphishing (T1566). Its infrastructure includes domains like blogs.firelive.pics and crushter.info, and it primarily targets entities in Sri Lanka, China, and Pakistan.[/profile]

9742.name: TrojanSpy
9742.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TrojanSpy is a malware entity. Its technical behaviors include defense evasion via T1036.006 (Space after Filename) on macOS/Linux and T1134.001 (Token Impersonation/Theft) on Windows, discovery via T1087 (Account Discovery) and T1482 (Domain Trust Discovery), and command and control via T1071.004 (DNS). Associated infrastructure indicators include ms101.cloudshappen.com, cdn-6dd0035.oxcdntech.com, nx2.microware-help.com, east.smartpisang.com, and cdn-7a3d.vultr-dns.com. It has been observed in locations including Malaysia, South Africa, the Philippines, Germany, and Taiwan.[/profile]

9743.name: Earth Estries
9743.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Earth Estries, also known as UNC4841 and SLIME57, is a cyberespionage intrusion set attributed to China, targeting government and technology sectors across multiple regions including Malaysia, South Africa, the Philippines, Germany, and Taiwan. Its key malware is TrojanSpy, which employs defense evasion techniques such as Space after Filename (T1036.006) on macOS/Linux and Token Impersonation/Theft (T1134.001) on Windows, and utilizes discovery techniques like Domain Trust Discovery (T1482). The group's command and control infrastructure includes domains like ms101.cloudshappen.com and east.smartpisang.com. Its primary motivation is intelligence gathering through prolonged campaigns.[/profile]

9815.name: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage
9815.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Exfiltration to Cloud Storage (T1567.002) is an Exfiltration tactic technique for macOS, Linux, Windows, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries exfiltrating data to a remote cloud storage service like Dropbox or Google Docs over the Internet, often using the service's standard APIs over HTTPS. This method can provide significant operational cover if the targeted network already has legitimate traffic to these common services, blending malicious data transfers with normal activity.

9816.name: T1053.006
9816.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This entity is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1053.006, named "Scheduled Task/Job: Systemd Timers", which falls under the Execution, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation tactics for Linux platforms. It involves abusing systemd timer unit files (with a .timer extension) to schedule malicious code execution either on a calendar event or after a relative time span. Each .timer file requires a corresponding .service file. Timers can be activated locally or remotely via the `systemctl` utility, with privileged timers installed in directories like `/etc/systemd/system/` for root-level persistence and user-level timers in `~/.config/systemd/user/`.

9817.name: AppleScript
9817.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]AppleScript, designated as T1059.002, is a macOS-specific execution technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework. It involves abusing the AppleScript language to send AppleEvent messages for inter-process communication, enabling adversaries to control applications, send keystrokes, and interact with open windows. Scripts are executed via the command line using `osascript /path/to/script` or `osascript -e "script here"`, or can be embedded within mach-O binaries using native APIs like `NSAppleScript`. This method can be used to interact with remote SSH sessions, present fake dialog boxes, and launch further payloads like Python reverse shells.

9818.name: T1134.001
9818.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1134.001, known as Token Impersonation/Theft, is a Windows-specific technique under the Defense Evasion and Privilege Escalation tactics. It involves duplicating an existing user's token using Windows API functions like `DuplicateToken` or `DuplicateTokenEx`. This duplicated token is then used to impersonate that user's security context, typically by attaching it to an existing thread via `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser` or `SetThreadToken`, allowing the adversary to bypass access controls and escalate privileges, particularly useful when targeting a user with a local, non-network logon session on the system.

9819.name: T1036.006
9819.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1036.006 (Space after Filename) is a Defense Evasion technique for macOS and Linux platforms. It works by appending a space character to the end of a malicious executable's filename (e.g., 'evil.txt '), which can cause the operating system to ignore the file extension and instead execute the file based on its true Mach-O binary format, thereby tricking users into launching it. This method is notably used by groups like APT38.

9820.name: Token Impersonation/Theft
9820.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Token Impersonation/Theft, identified as T1134.001, is a defense evasion and privilege escalation technique for Windows. It involves duplicating an existing user's access token using functions like `DuplicateToken` or `DuplicateTokenEx`. The stolen token is then applied to an existing thread using `ImpersonateLoggedOnUser` or `SetThreadToken` to impersonate that user's security context, allowing the adversary to bypass access controls. This is distinct from creating new tokens and is often used when targeting a user's specific non-network logon session.

9821.name: T1567.002
9821.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1567.002, Exfiltration to Cloud Storage, is an exfiltration technique for Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves adversaries transferring stolen data to internet-based cloud storage services like Dropbox or Google Docs. This method can evade detection by blending with legitimate network traffic to these common services, as noted in activity by groups like FIN7, Hafnium, and Wizard Spider.

9822.name: Systemd Timers
9822.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Systemd Timers is a MITRE ATT&CK technique with ID T1053.006 under the Execution, Persistence, and Privilege Escalation tactics for Linux platforms. It involves abusing systemd timer unit files with a .timer extension to schedule malicious code execution on calendar events or relative time spans, serving as an alternative to Cron. Each .timer file must have a corresponding .service file; privileged timers are written to /etc/systemd/system/ or /usr/lib/systemd/system for root persistence, while user-level timers are in ~/.config/systemd/user/. Timers can be activated remotely via the systemctl command over SSH.

9823.name: T1059.002
9823.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1059.002, also known as AppleScript, is a Command and Scripting Interpreter technique within the Execution tactic for macOS. It involves abusing the AppleScript language to control applications and the OS via AppleEvents. Scripts can be executed from the command line using `osascript`, through mechanisms like Mail rules or Automator, or programmatically via macOS Native APIs like `NSAppleScript`. This enables behaviors such as sending keystrokes, interacting with remote applications over SSH, presenting fake dialog boxes, and launching further payloads like Python reverse shells.

9824.name: Space after Filename
9824.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Space after Filename is a Defense Evasion technique (ID T1036.006) targeting macOS and Linux platforms. It involves appending a space character to the end of a filename, which can cause the operating system to ignore a deceptive file extension and instead correctly identify and execute the file's true binary format, such as a Mach-O executable. This tricks users into launching malicious files disguised as benign documents.

9826.name: GHOSTTOWN
9826.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GHOSTTOWN is a malware associated with the threat actor UNC3886. It exhibits behaviors aligned with MITRE ATT&CK techniques including Credentials from Password Stores (T1555) for credential access, and Clear Linux or Mac System Logs (T1070.002) and Rootkit (T1014) for defense evasion. It also leverages SSH (T1021.004) for lateral movement and can Create Accounts (T1136) for persistence, primarily targeting Linux and macOS platforms. It has been observed exploiting vulnerability CVE-2022-41328.[/profile]

9827.name: PITHOOK
9827.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PITHOOK is a malware deployed by threat group UNC5325, which is assessed with moderate confidence to be associated with UNC3886. It shares TTPs and malware code overlaps with LITTLELAMB.WOOLTEA and other UNC3886 malware. Its technical behaviors include leveraging SSH for lateral movement, using rootkits for defense evasion, creating accounts for persistence, clearing Linux or Mac system logs, and extracting credentials from password stores. It targets Linux and macOS platforms and exploits vulnerability CVE-2022-41328.[/profile]

9828.name: BUSYBOX
9828.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BUSYBOX is a legitimate multi-call binary that combines many common Unix utilities into a single executable, but it is frequently abused by malware for malicious purposes. It is used by threat actors like TeamTNT and Rocke to download and execute scripts via commands like `busybox wget` and `busybox tftp`. Associated TTPs include creating accounts for persistence, using SSH for lateral movement, deploying rootkits for defense evasion, and clearing Linux system logs (T1070.002) to hide evidence. It targets Linux and ESXi platforms, often exploiting vulnerabilities such as CVE-2022-41328.[/profile]

9829.name: SEAELF
9829.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SEAELF is a malware entity. It has been associated with the Andariel group, which is linked to the Silent Chollima cluster. Its key technical behaviors include clearing Linux or Mac system logs (T1070.002), creating accounts for persistence (T1136), using SSH for lateral movement (T1021.004), deploying rootkits for defense evasion (T1014), and harvesting credentials from password stores (T1555). It targets Linux and macOS platforms and has been observed exploiting the vulnerability CVE-2022-41328.[/profile]

9830.name: MEDUSA
9830.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MEDUSA is a malware family, also known as MedusaHTTP and MedusaIRC. It is associated with threat groups from Russia, such as Stevenkings. It targets Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms, and exploits vulnerabilities like CVE-2022-41328.[/profile]

9831.name: GOBRAT
9831.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GOBRAT is a Go-based Remote Access Trojan (RAT) targeting Linux routers, as observed in attacks in Japan around February 2023. Its key technical behaviors include using SSH for lateral movement, creating accounts for persistence, and clearing Linux system logs (T1070.002) for defense evasion. It also employs rootkit functionality to hide its components and attempts to harvest credentials from password stores. Its command and control (C2) communication utilizes the Go-specific gob serialization format. The malware is associated with exploiting the vulnerability CVE-2022-41328.[/profile]

9832.name: TINYSHELL
9832.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TINYSHELL is a backdoor malware. It is a custom variant used by the threat group UNC2891, which leverages an external encrypted configuration file. Some variants include functionality to communicate via an HTTP proxy with basic authentication. Associated techniques include using SSH for lateral movement, clearing Linux or Mac system logs for defense evasion, and potentially using rootkits. It targets Linux and macOS platforms, and has been observed in campaigns alongside malware like SLAPSTICK.[/profile]

9833.name: UNC3886
9833.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]UNC3886, also known as Lifting Zmiy, is a cyber espionage intrusion set attributed with low confidence to a China nexus. Its key malware includes MEDUSA, GOBRAT, PITHOOK, REPTILE, and TINYSHELL, which are deployed to target Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. Key TTPs involve using SSH for lateral movement, creating accounts for persistence, deploying rootkits and clearing Linux/Mac system logs for defense evasion, and extracting credentials from password stores. The group exploits vulnerabilities such as CVE-2022-41328 and its motivation is assessed to be highly targeted cyber espionage.[/profile]

Key targeted logs include /var/log/messages for system messages, /var/log/secure or /var/log/auth.log for authentication records, and /var/log/utmp or /var/log/wtmp for login histories. 9853.name: Famous Chollima

9870.name: Mimus
9870.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Mimus is a malware that exploits vulnerabilities including CVE-2022-26134, CVE-2022-29464, CVE-2021-44228, and CVE-2023-46604 for remote service exploitation and privilege escalation. It uses a proxy for command and control, with infrastructure indicators such as the domain windows.n1tro.cyou, the URL http://windows.n1tro.cyou:4544, and cryptocurrency address 15Jz1fmreZx9wG93DKjTXMhuLpPpCgvEQk.[/profile]

9871.name: Mimo

Its associated infrastructure includes domains like windows.n1tro.cyou and cryptocurrency addresses such as 15Jz1fmreZx9wG93DKjTXMhuLpPpCgvEQk. It is related to techniques like Exploitation of Remote Services and Proxy for command and control.[/profile]

9872.name: Batch
9872.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The malware named Batch is a malicious batch script. It employs the Impair Defenses technique to hinder security mechanisms, uses Exploitation of Remote Services and Exploitation for Privilege Escalation to gain unauthorized access and elevate permissions, and utilizes Proxy for command and control traffic redirection. It is associated with vulnerabilities including CVE-2022-26134, CVE-2022-29464, CVE-2021-44228, and CVE-2023-46604. 9874.name: CoinMiner

9875.name: mimo

It is also known as Lifting Zmiy. Its key malware includes the custom Mimo malware, along with tools like Batch scripts, Mimus, and the public coinminer XMRig. Its primary TTPs involve exploiting known vulnerabilities such as Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), CVE-2022-26134, CVE-2022-29464, and CVE-2023-46604 for initial access and privilege escalation, and using proxy techniques for command and control. The group's origin is not clearly attributed, but its operations show a focus on opportunistic exploitation for financial gain. Its target sectors and regions are not specifically defined, but its activity is consistent with broad, automated attacks against vulnerable internet-facing services. Its core motivation is financial profit through cryptojacking.[/profile]

9912.name: UNC1151
9912.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]UNC1151, also known as Ghostwriter, DEV-0257, UAC-0057, Pushcha, and TA445, is an intrusion set. Its key malware includes GrimPlant (Elephant), MICROBACKDOOR, and GraphSteel, which are used for credential theft and remote access, often delivered via spear-phishing with spoofed Ukrainian governmental emails. Key TTPs involve Local Email Collection of Outlook files, Credentials in Files, and the use of Asymmetric Cryptography for C2 communication. The group is attributed to Belarus and shows no observed overlaps with tracked Russian APT groups. It primarily targets sectors and regions in Ukraine and Belarus, with motivations linked to information operations and espionage.

9962.name: PicassoLoader
9962.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]PicassoLoader is a malware loader attributed to the threat actor UAC-0057 (also known as Ghostwriter). Its key technical behaviors include using Asymmetric Cryptography (T1573.002) for C2 traffic, establishing Bidirectional Communication (T1102.002) via legitimate web services, and employing defense evasion techniques such as Process Injection (T1055) and execution via Rundll32 (T1218.011). It targets Windows systems and has been observed using infrastructure like the domains everythingandthedog.shop, resident.ngo, and pigglywigglystores.shop for distribution and C2, with a noted focus on victims in Belarus and Ukraine.

9983.name: GrimPlant
9983.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GrimPlant, also known as Elephant, is a backdoor malware component that enables remote execution of PowerShell commands. It is delivered via spear phishing campaigns using spoofed Ukrainian governmental emails. The malware's C2 server address is provided by a Java-sdk.exe component using a command-line parameter and is encoded in base64(AES(<C&C>)) syntax. Its key behaviors include Local Email Collection (T1114.001) to exfiltrate Outlook files, Credentials from Web Browsers (T1555.003), Credentials in Files (T1552.001), and Query Registry (T1012) for discovery. It uses Asymmetric Cryptography (T1573.002) for C2 communication. Observed infrastructure includes domains like nirsoft.me and IPs like 194.31.98.124.

9984.name: MICROBACKDOOR
9984.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MICROBACKDOOR, also known as microbackdoor, is a malware associated with the APT group UNC1151 (linked to the Ghostwriter campaign). Its key behaviors include collecting local email data via T1114.001, archiving data for exfiltration using utilities (T1560.001), employing asymmetric cryptography (T1573.002) for C2 communication, and harvesting credentials from files (T1552.001) and web browsers (T1555.003). It targets Windows systems and has used infrastructure such as the domains nirsoft.me and IP 45.84.0.116, with delivery mechanisms including spearphishing ZIP archives, CHM droppers, and JS droppers.[/profile]

9985.name: GraphSteel
9985.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GraphSteel is a malware component, also associated with GrimPlant, used for credential theft and remote access, delivered via spear-phishing with spoofed Ukrainian governmental emails. Its key Tactics, Techniques, and Procedures (TTPs) include Local Email Collection (T1114.001) to steal Outlook data files, Credentials in Files (T1552.001) and Credentials from Web Browsers (T1555.003) for harvesting stored passwords, and it conceals command-and-control traffic using both Symmetric (T1573.001) and Asymmetric Cryptography (T1573.002). It targets Windows platforms and has utilized infrastructure including domains like xbeta.online and IP addresses such as 45.84.0.116.

10053.name: Credentials from Web Browsers
10053.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Credentials from Web Browsers (T1555.003) is a Credential Access technique for macOS, Linux, and Windows platforms. Adversaries acquire saved website credentials by reading and decrypting browser-specific files, such as the Chrome `Login Data` database queried via SQL, and using the Windows `CryptUnprotectData` API with the victim's logon key for decryption. Credentials can also be extracted by searching browser process memory for common patterns, and stolen credentials are often recycled for lateral movement and privilege escalation.

10054.name: Local Email Collection
10054.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Local Email Collection is technique T1114.001 under the Collection tactic, targeting Windows platforms. It involves adversaries acquiring sensitive data by exfiltrating local email storage files from a user's system. Specifically, this includes Outlook offline data files (.ost) and Outlook Data Files (.pst), which are typically stored in directories like `C:\Users\<username>\Documents\Outlook Files` or `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Outlook`. Groups such as APT1, Magic Hound, and Redcurl have been observed using this technique.

10055.name: T1552.001
10055.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1552.001, known as "Credentials In Files," is a credential-access technique within the MITRE ATTACK framework applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, Containers, and IaaS platforms. It involves adversaries searching local and remote file systems for insecurely stored credentials, which can include user-created files, shared credential stores, configuration files containing passwords, or source code with embedded secrets. In cloud environments, credentials are often found in local configuration files or as parameters within container logs, and these can be read or copied for authentication.

10056.name: T1114.001
10056.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1114.001, Local Email Collection, is a Collection technique for Windows. It targets sensitive email data from local system files like Outlook Data Files (.pst) or Offline Outlook Data Files (.ost), which are typically stored in directories such as `C:\Users\<username>\Documents\Outlook Files` or `C:\Users\<username>\AppData\Local\Microsoft\Outlook`. This method has been used by groups including APT1, Magic Hound, and Winter Vivern.

10058.name: SnipBot

It is delivered via WinRAR exploits, using malicious LNK files to execute a signed but invalidly coded EXE. The malware decrypts strings using the filename as a key to execute shellcode, which communicates with a dynamic HTTP C2 server and interacts with specific Windows Registry keys. Its associated TTPs include Data Staging (T1074), Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion, Software Discovery, and Query Registry (T1012). It primarily targets Windows systems and has used infrastructure domains like drvmcprotect.com, mcprotect.cloud, and adobe.cloudcreative.digital.[/profile]

10060.name: RomCom
10060.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The intrusion set is most likely the threat actor known as Gold Prelude, also known as RomCom, Storm-0978, and UAT-5647. It is attributed to this group and is associated with the custom RomCom remote access trojan (RAT) and the SnipBot malware variant. Key techniques include lateral movement via SMB/Windows Admin Shares and Remote Desktop Protocol, and defense evasion through Virtualization/Sandbox Evasion. The group has targeted sectors and organizations in Slovakia, Singapore, Spain, France, and South Korea, and has exploited vulnerabilities such as CVE-2021-40444 and CVE-2023-36884. Its primary motivation appears to be espionage and data theft, often using spearphishing and malicious documents for initial access.[/profile]

10123.name: TA0040
10123.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA0040 is the MITRE ATT&CK ID for the Impact tactic, which encompasses techniques adversaries use to manipulate, interrupt, or destroy systems and data. This tactic is platform-agnostic, applicable across enterprise networks. Specific techniques within this tactic, such as Data Encrypted (T1560) or Data Destruction (T1485), involve actions like exfiltrating and encrypting stolen data to hinder recovery or deleting critical files to disrupt operations.

10124.name: TA0010
10124.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]TA0010 is the MITRE ATT&CK ID for the Exfiltration tactic. It is a high-level tactic, not a specific technique, and therefore does not have a unique technical mechanism. It describes the adversary's objective of stealing data from a network. Related techniques, such as those for exfiltrating data from databases, demonstrate how stolen information can be used for this purpose.

10188.name: Hancitor
10188.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Hancitor is a malware family, also known as Chanitor or Tordal. It is attributed to the cybercriminal group Scully Spider and is known for its role as a downloader, often delivering secondary payloads like Danabot. Key technical behaviors include using HTTP POST for command and control (C2) communication, employing specific URLs for tasks, and utilizing Bitcoin addresses (e.g., bc1qhtwfcysclc7pck2y3vmjtpzkaezhcm6perc99x) for operations. It primarily targets Windows platforms and has been associated with exploiting vulnerabilities such as CVE-2020-1472 (Zerologon). Its infrastructure involves multiple C2 servers and task URLs, and it is frequently distributed via malicious email campaigns.[/profile]

10251.name: Remote Service Session Hijacking
10251.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Remote Service Session Hijacking is the MITRE ATT&CK technique T1563 under the Lateral Movement tactic, targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms. It involves adversaries taking control of existing, authenticated remote sessions (e.g., RDP, SSH, telnet) to execute actions without needing valid credentials. A specific method for RDP uses the native Windows command `tscon.exe` with system permissions to hijack sessions silently. This technique is distinct from creating new sessions and can be associated with vulnerabilities like CVE-2020-1472.[/profile]

10313.name: T1563
10313.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Remote Service Session Hijacking (T1563) is a Lateral Movement technique applicable to Windows, Linux, and macOS. It involves adversaries taking control of pre-existing, authenticated user sessions on remote services like RDP, SSH, or telnet to perform actions on remote systems, rather than creating new sessions with stolen credentials. This hijacking can be facilitated by exploiting vulnerabilities such as CVE-2022-24521.[/profile]

10315.name: Underground
10315.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Underground is a malware entity. It is associated with the Wizard Spider group via the Conti ransomware, and its infrastructure has been referenced by Taurus Stealer. Its technical behaviors include using Standard Encoding for C2 traffic obfuscation, staging collected data before exfiltration, clearing Windows event logs, inhibiting system recovery by deleting backups, and encrypting data for impact. It has targeted systems in Slovakia, Singapore, Spain, France, and South Korea, and has exploited vulnerability CVE-2023-36884.[/profile]

10322.name: T1132.001
10322.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1132.001, known as Data Encoding: Standard Encoding, is a command-and-control technique used across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves encoding C2 traffic using common, protocol-compliant schemes like ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, or MIME to obfuscate content and evade detection. Some implementations, such as gzip, may also compress the data. This technique has been associated with threat groups including Hafnium, MuddyWater, and Lazarus Group.[profile]

10323.name: Standard Encoding
10323.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Standard Encoding is a command and control technique (T1132.001) within the Command and Control tactic, applicable across Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It involves encoding C2 traffic using established, protocol-compliant schemes like ASCII, Unicode, hexadecimal, Base64, and MIME to obfuscate content and evade detection. This technique is associated with groups including Hafnium, MuddyWater, Lazarus Group, and Sandworm Team.

10327.name: MeshAgent
10327.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]MeshAgent is a malware entity used by threat groups like LilacSquid for command and control, employing non-standard ports (T1571) such as speed.ableoil[.]net:443. Its key techniques include User Execution (T1204) via phishing (T1566), masquerading tasks or services (T1036.004) to evade detection, and deleting files (T1070.004) to remove forensic evidence. It has been associated with infrastructure in the Russian Federation and domains like kwazindernuren.com.[/profile]

10329.name: Awaken Likho
10329.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Awaken Likho is a suspected Russian APT group, also known as Angry Likho and Sticky Werewolf, and is part of the broader "Likho" activity cluster. Its key malware is MeshAgent, used for command and control over non-standard ports. Its primary TTPs include phishing for initial access and user execution, along with masquerading tasks or services for defense evasion. The group is attributed to the Russian Federation and has targeted infrastructure using domains such as softsandtools.com, contileservices.net, and microsoftsupertech.com.[/profile]

10427.name: Raspberry Robin
10427.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Raspberry Robin is a malware family that has targeted entities in Mexico, Brazil, Pakistan, and the United States, and has been detected targeting insurance and financial institutes in Europe. Its infection chain involves multiple processes for initial compromise and has continued to evolve. The malware's infrastructure includes indicators such as the domains hiperfdhaus.com and tddshht.com, and C2 servers like http://jirostrogud.com/gate.php and http://88.214.27.100/gate.php. It is associated with the exploitation of vulnerability CVE-2022-31199 and employs techniques including Gather Victim Network Information (T1590), Gather Victim Host Information (T1592), System Binary Proxy Execution (T1218) for defense evasion, Remote Services (T1021) for lateral movement, and Data Destruction (T1485) for impact.[/profile]

10428.name: Truebot
10428.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Truebot is a malware attributed to the Silence Group and TA505. It performs reconnaissance by gathering victim host information, including OS version, processor architecture, and computer/domain names. It uses system binary proxy execution for defense evasion and exploits the CVE-2022-31199 vulnerability (Netwrix Auditor). Its infrastructure includes domains like nefosferta.com and tddshht.com, and it has targeted locations including the United States, Mexico, Brazil, and Pakistan.[profile]

10429.name: Clop
10429.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Clop is a ransomware family also known as CL0P, attributed to the TA505 threat group. It employs techniques like System Binary Proxy Execution for defense evasion and Remote Services for lateral movement, and it targets systems across multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS. Its infrastructure involves domains like tddshht.com and jirostrogud.com, and C2 servers such as http://nefosferta.com/gate.php. It has been used in attacks against organizations in locations including the United States, Brazil, Mexico, and Pakistan, and has exploited vulnerabilities like CVE-2022-31199. The malware is designed for data exfiltration and destruction, demanding ransom payments from victims.[/profile]

10430.name: Grace
10430.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Grace, also known as Flawed Grace, is a malware entity. It has been associated with groups like Silence Group and TA505. Its key technical behaviors include gathering victim network and host information (T1590, T1592), data destruction (T1485), and using system binary proxy execution (T1218) and remote services (T1021) for defense evasion and lateral movement. It targets Windows, Linux, and macOS platforms and has been observed using infrastructure like the domains hiperfdhaus.com and IP addresses 88.214.27.100/101 and 179.60.150.53, with connections to locations including Brazil, Mexico, Pakistan, and the United States.[/profile]

10432.name: Silence group
10432.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The Silence Group, also known as TA505, is a financially motivated cybercrime gang believed to be of Russian origin. It primarily targets financial organizations globally, with observed victim locations including Brazil, Mexico, Pakistan, and the United States. The group is associated with custom malware such as Silence (a RAT), Grace (Flawed Grace), and Truebot, and has also used tools like Clop ransomware, Raspberry Robin, and Cobalt Strike. Its key TTPs include exploiting the CVE-2022-31199 vulnerability (Netwrix Auditor), using System Binary Proxy Execution for defense evasion, and performing reconnaissance via Gather Victim Network/Host Information. Its infrastructure involves domains like jirostrogud.com and C2 servers such as http://88.214.27.100/gate.php.[/profile]

10487.name: SharpHound
10487.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SharpHound is a C# version of the BloodHound Ingestor tool used for Active Directory reconnaissance. It enumerates usernames, computer names, groups, domains, and OUs to map network relationships and identify potential attack paths to the AD server, operating at high speed and stability. Its activity is characterized by performing an excess of LDAP queries, such as searches for specific `samaccounttype` values, which can be detected in Windows event logs (e.g., Event ID 5145). It is associated with the BloodHound project and has been used by groups like Pinchy Spider (associated with REvil). Its infrastructure has included domains like mangayaro.com and centre-samekh.ch.[/profile]

10488.name: GootKit
10488.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]GootKit, also known as Gootkit, is a banking trojan that can deliver additional payloads, siphon data from victims, and stealthily persist in a compromised environment. It employs Defense Evasion techniques like Subvert Trust Controls (T1553) and Process Injection (T1055), and uses Multi-Stage Channels (T1104) for command and control. Initial access is gained via Phishing (T1566) or Drive-by Compromise (T1189). Its infrastructure includes domains like educabla.com, emitrablog.com, thedinkpickleball.com, and ntumatches.tw, and it has targeted Australia.[/profile]

10490.name: menuPass
10490.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]This intrusion set, most likely the APT group known as APT10 (also known as Stone Panda, Cloud Hopper, menuPass Team, Bronze Riverside, and Red Apollo), has been observed using tools like GootKit malware, LODEINFO, and SharpHound for reconnaissance. Its key TTPs include Subvert Trust Controls, Multi-Stage Channels for command and control, and initial access via Phishing and Drive-by Compromise. The group is attributed to China and has targeted sectors and regions including Australia and Japan, with motivations believed to be cyber espionage. It employs techniques such as base64 and XOR string obfuscation, modifies open-source tools like Impacket and Mimikatz, and uses tools like Csvde and PowerSploit for data collection and execution.[/profile]

10582.name: Turla Group
10582.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Turla, also known as Venomous Bear, Waterbug, Uroburos, Snake, and UNC4210, is a sophisticated cyber espionage group attributed to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). Its key malware includes the ComRAT backdoor (a descendant of Agent.btz), TinyTurla, Crutch, HyperStack, and QUIETCANARY. The group employs techniques like Component Object Model Hijacking for persistence and exfiltration over alternative protocols. It primarily targets government, military, diplomatic, and research sectors across more than 50 countries, with operations dating back to at least 2004, and is motivated by strategic intelligence collection.[/profile]

10631.name: Component Object Model Hijacking
10631.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Component Object Model Hijacking is a persistence technique (T1546.015) within the Defense Evasion and Persistence tactics, targeting the Windows platform. It involves modifying Windows Registry references to legitimate COM objects so that malicious code is executed instead when the hijacked component is invoked by the system. Adversaries typically target frequently used COM objects to maintain stealth, and variations include abusing Type Libraries to redirect functionality to remote scripts via the "script:" moniker. This method has been associated with groups like APT28.

10718.name: Kazuar - S0265
10718.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Kazuar - S0265, also known as Kazuar, is a backdoor malware attributed to the Turla group. It employs encrypted channels for command and control, uses process injection for defense evasion and privilege escalation, and obfuscates files or information to avoid detection. The malware also utilizes masquerading and deobfuscation techniques. Its infrastructure has used domains such as bibliotecaunicef.uy, altavista.rs, and m6front.sam-maintenance.com. It targets Windows systems and has been associated with activity linked to the Russian Federation.[/profile]

10720.name: Pelmeni
10720.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Pelmeni is a malware entity, not a family, with no known aliases from the provided data. It is linked to the Russian Federation. Its key technical behaviors include establishing an encrypted command and control (C2) channel, process injection for defense evasion and privilege escalation, and obfuscating or deobfuscating files and information. It also employs masquerading to appear legitimate. Its infrastructure uses specific HTTPS URLs for C2, such as altavista.rs, m6front.sam-maintenance.com, and bibliotecaunicef.uy. It is referenced in the context of other entities like Cutlet, Project Alice, and Ploutus ATM.[/profile]

It targets Windows platforms and has used infrastructure domains including hanagram.jp, jeepcarlease.com, cert.ngo, carleasingguru.com, and buy-new-car.com.[/profile]

10824.name: TurlaPower-NG

Associated infrastructure indicators include domains like hanagram.jp, carleasingguru.com, buy-new-car.com, thefinetreats.com, and jeepcarlease.com.[profile]

10953.name: T1035

It targets Linux platforms and has been deployed via JavaScript and MSIL droppers, such as "Scr.js" and "appidpolicyconverter.js", often using decoy documents like "Save the Date G20 Digital Economy Taskforce 23 24 October.pdf". 11056.name: T1543.002
11056.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1543.002: Systemd Service is a MITRE ATT&CK technique for Persistence and Privilege Escalation on Linux platforms. It involves creating or modifying systemd service unit files (.service) to execute malicious payloads. Adversaries manipulate directives like ExecStart within these files, which are stored in directories such as /systemd/system, to run commands at boot or service start. Modifying the User directive can enable privilege escalation, and symbolic links or systemd generators may be used to establish or maintain persistence.

11057.name: Systemd Service
11057.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Systemd Service is a Linux-specific MITRE ATT&CK technique (T1543.002) used for Persistence and Privilege Escalation. It involves creating or modifying systemd service unit files (with the .service extension) to execute malicious commands. These files, stored in directories like /etc/systemd/system/ for system-level or ~/.config/systemd/user/ for user-level persistence, contain directives such as ExecStart to run payloads at boot or on service events. Adversaries use tools like systemctl to manage these services, enabling recurring execution and potential privilege escalation by altering the User directive or using symbolic links.

11388.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Steganography is a Command and Control technique (Tactic: Command and Control, ID: T1001.002) used on Windows, Linux, macOS, and ESXi platforms. It hides data or C2 traffic within digital media like images, audio, video, or text files to evade detection. Specific examples include malware like Duqu hiding exfiltrated data in images and threat groups using tools like Invoke-PSImage to embed and execute PowerShell commands from image files (.png).

11483.name: Jackal
11483.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Jackal is a malware entity, not a family, linked to spear-phishing campaigns associated with the group COBALT SPIDER, as seen in EXTREME JACKAL Summer operations. Its technical behaviors include establishing persistence via Windows Scheduled Task creation (T1053.005), gathering system information (T1082), and using encrypted channels for command and control (T1573). It targets Windows platforms primarily through spearphishing attachments (T1566.001) as an initial access vector.[/profile]

11484.name: GoldenJackal
11484.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The intrusion set known as GoldenJackal, also referred to as Earth Longzhi and SnakeCharmer, is a distinct APT group. Its key malware is Jackal, a tool used in spear-phishing campaigns that establishes persistence via Windows Scheduled Tasks (T1053.005), performs System Information Discovery (T1082), and uses Encrypted Channels (T1573) for command and control (TA0011), with initial access often gained through Spearphishing Attachments (T1193). The group's origin and specific target sectors are not detailed in the provided information, though its operational focus and tooling suggest espionage motivations.[/profile]

11486.name: Lazarus Group
11486.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The Lazarus Group, also known as Hidden Cobra, APT38, and Guardians of Peace, is a state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) group attributed to North Korea (DPRK). It employs custom malware families including Lazarus, LPEClient, and BLINDINGCAN, and utilizes techniques such as Subverting Trust Controls (T1553), Indirect Command Execution (T1202), and Data Encoding (T1132). The group primarily targets defense, government, and financial sectors globally, with operations observed in Western Europe, the United States, and Asia. Its motivation is believed to be financial gain and espionage, supporting North Korean state interests.[profile]

11597.name: BLINDINGCAN
11597.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BLINDINGCAN, also known as blindingcan, is a remote access Trojan (RAT) malware family attributed to the Lazarus Group, a North Korean state-sponsored actor. It has been used in cyber operations since at least early 2020, primarily targeting defense, engineering, and government organizations in Western Europe, the United States, and locations including the Netherlands, Belgium, Cyprus, Hong Kong, and Taiwan. Key technical behaviors include data exfiltration via HTTP POST to specific C2 servers (e.g., stracarrara.org, turnscor.com), clipboard data theft (T1115), data encoding for C2 traffic (T1132), and subverting trust controls (T1553). Its infrastructure involves compromised websites for command and control.

11598.name: Trojan:Win64/NukeSped
11598.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Trojan:Win64/NukeSped, also known as Backdoor/Win.NukeSped, is a Windows backdoor. It has been associated with threat groups including APT33, Lazarus Group, Operation C-Major, and Silent Chollima. Its technical behaviors involve Subvert Trust Controls and Access Token Manipulation for defense evasion and privilege escalation, and it uses Data Encoding for command and control. It targets Windows systems and has been delivered via websites in the Netherlands and Belgium, exploiting vulnerability CVE-2021-21551 and using specific URLs for its infrastructure.[/profile]

11599.name: Trojan:Win32/Nukesped
11599.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Trojan:Win32/Nukesped, also known as Backdoor/Win.NukeSped, is a Windows-targeting backdoor. It has been associated with APT groups including APT33, Lazarus Group, and Silent Chollima, and has been observed in operations such as C-Major. Its technical behaviors involve subverting trust controls and impairing defenses to evade detection, and it utilizes data encoding for command and control. Associated infrastructure includes domains like thetalkingcanvas.com and stracarrara.org, and it has been delivered by exploiting vulnerabilities such as CVE-2021-21551, with primary targeting observed in locations like the Netherlands and Belgium.[/profile]

11609.name: T1587
11609.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1587, known as Develop Capabilities, is a Resource Development tactic within the MITRE ATT&CK framework for the PRE platform. This technique involves adversaries building their own in-house tools, such as malware, exploits, or self-signed certificates, to support operations throughout their lifecycle. This development can utilize internal skills or contracted expertise, with the adversary shaping requirements to maintain exclusive control over the capability. It is associated with groups like Contagious Interview, Moonstone Sleet, and Kimsuky, and can be informed by intelligence gathered from closed sources.[/profile]

11610.name: Develop Capabilities
11610.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Develop Capabilities is a Resource Development technique (T1587) within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to the PRE platform. It involves adversaries building their own tools in-house, such as malware, exploits, and self-signed certificates, by identifying development requirements and utilizing either internal skills or contracted developers to create exclusive capabilities for their operations.

11615.name: RustBucket
11615.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]RustBucket, also known as Rust-based Samples, is a macOS-targeting malware attributed to the BlueNoroff APT group, a sub-group of Lazarus. It employs persistence via launch mechanisms (T1547), uses phishing for initial access (T1566), masquerades to evade detection (T1036), and conducts file discovery (T1083). Its command-and-control infrastructure includes domains like cloud.dnx.capital and deck.31ventures.info, as well as IP addresses such as 104.200.137.32.[/profile]

11621.name: Lazarus
11621.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Lazarus, also known as Lazarus Group, is a state-sponsored advanced persistent threat (APT) group attributed to North Korea (DPRK). It employs techniques such as modifying authentication processes (T1556), developing its own capabilities (T1587), subverting trust controls (T1553), using boot or logon scripts for persistence (T1037), and staging data (T1074). The group targets various platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS, and has been linked to infrastructure like daehang.com, gongsilbox.com, and sinae.or.kr. Its activities, tracked back to at least 2007, include financial attacks, ransomware campaigns like WannaCryptor, and exploiting vulnerabilities in widely used software.[/profile]

11659.name: Wolfic
11659.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Wolfic is a malware that utilizes the T1132 (Data Encoding) technique for command and control, employing standard encoding systems like Base64 to obfuscate its traffic. Its operations are supported by reconnaissance techniques T1593 (Search Open Websites/Domains) and T1591 (Gather Victim Org Information) to collect target intelligence, and it relies on T1583 (Acquire Infrastructure) to obtain necessary servers or domains. Execution is achieved through T1204 (User Execution), tricking users into opening malicious documents or links. The malware's activities span multiple platforms including Windows, Linux, and macOS.[profile]

11665.name: T1593
11665.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Search Open Websites/Domains, also known as T1593, is a reconnaissance technique within the MITRE ATT&CK framework, applicable to the PRE platform. Adversaries gather victim intelligence from freely available online sources such as social media, news sites, and business operation pages. This information can enable subsequent activities like phishing, establishing accounts, or identifying initial access vectors. Groups including Kimsuky, Sandworm Team, and Volt Typhoon have been associated with this technique.

11666.name: Search Open Websites/Domains
11666.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Search Open Websites/Domains is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1593 under the Reconnaissance tactic, applicable to the PRE platform. It involves adversaries gathering victim intelligence from freely accessible online sources like social media, news sites, and business operation pages. This information can enable subsequent phases such as Phishing for Information, establishing accounts, or gaining initial access via methods like External Remote Services. The technique is associated with threat groups including Kimsuky, Sandworm Team, and Volt Typhoon.

11668.name: Agent Tesla
11668.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Agent Tesla is a malware family, also known as Agent Tesla RAT, and is attributed to the Sweed group. Its key TTPs include abusing elevation control mechanisms (T1548) and system binary proxy execution (T1218) for defense evasion, using boot or logon autostart execution (T1547) for persistence, and employing input capture (T1056) for credential theft. It utilizes multi-stage channels (T1104) for command and control. Target platforms are primarily Windows, as indicated by its associated techniques. Infrastructure includes domains like ftp.qurvegraphics.com and mail.thesharpening.com.au, and payload download locations such as hxxps://ahgwqrq[.]xyz and hxxp://193.239.147[.]103.[/profile]

11678.name: T1548
11678.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1548, known as Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism, is a defense evasion and privilege escalation technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, Office Suite, and Identity Provider platforms. It involves circumventing native system controls like User Account Control (UAC) or sudo mechanisms to gain higher-level permissions. For instance, adversaries can abuse tools like CMSTP.exe with malicious INF files to bypass UAC and execute arbitrary commands.

11679.name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
11679.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism, identified as MITRE ATT&CK T1548, is a defense evasion and privilege escalation technique applicable to Windows, Linux, macOS, IaaS, Office Suite, and Identity Provider platforms. It involves circumventing native system controls like Windows User Account Control (UAC) or Linux sudo mechanisms to gain higher-level permissions without proper authorization. Specific methods include abusing auto-elevating processes like `eventvwr.exe`, using tools like UACMe, or leveraging lateral movement with compromised admin credentials to bypass local security prompts.

11681.name: BlueNoroff
11681.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]BlueNoroff is a malware attributed to the Lazarus Group. It employs defense evasion techniques such as Process Injection via Portable Executable Injection (T1055.002), Mark-of-the-Web Bypass using container files (T1553.005), and proxy execution via Msiexec (T1218.007). It also performs System Checks for virtual environments (T1497.001) and uses Template Injection (T1221) in documents. Its infrastructure includes domains like smbcgroup.us, abf-cap.co, and bankofamerica.us.org.

11736.name: T1218.007
11736.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity T1218.007, known as Msiexec, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows that abuses the msiexec.exe command-line utility to proxy execution of malicious payloads. It can launch local or network MSI files and execute DLLs, leveraging its Microsoft signature to bypass application controls. Execution may be elevated to SYSTEM privileges if the AlwaysInstallElevated policy is enabled, and it has been used by groups including Rancor, APT38, and TA505.

11737.name: T1553.005
11737.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]T1553.005, known as Mark-of-the-Web Bypass, is a Defense Evasion technique for Windows. It involves abusing container file formats like disk images (.iso, .vhd) or archives (.arj, .gzip) to bypass security controls. When these containers are downloaded, they are tagged with the Mark-of-the-Web (MOTW) via an NTFS Alternate Data Stream. However, the files extracted or mounted from within these containers do not inherit this MOTW tag, allowing malicious payloads to execute without triggering protections like Protected View in Office or Windows Defender SmartScreen.

11738.name: T1547.008
11738.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]The entity is MITRE ATT&CK technique T1547.008, named LSASS Driver, which falls under the Persistence and Privilege Escalation tactics for Windows. This technique involves adversaries modifying or adding malicious drivers to the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS) to achieve persistence on a compromised system. By hijacking execution flow through these drivers, adversaries can continuously execute malicious payloads within the security subsystem's context.

11739.name: LSASS Driver
11739.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]LSASS Driver is a persistence and privilege escalation technique for Windows, corresponding to MITRE ATT&CK ID T1547.008 under the Persistence tactic. Adversaries achieve persistence by modifying or adding illegitimate drivers to the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS), enabling continuous execution of malicious payloads through LSA operations, often via driver hijacking methods like DLL side-loading.

11740.name: Template Injection
11740.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]Template Injection, identified as T1221, is a Defense Evasion technique primarily targeting Windows platforms. It involves modifying document templates, such as Office Open XML (.docx, .pptx, .xlsx) or RTF files, to insert references to remote URLs. When the document is opened, it fetches and executes a malicious payload from that external source, enabling initial code execution while evading static analysis since no overt malicious content like macros exists in the file initially. This method can also be used to force authentication attempts by referencing SMB or HTTPS URLs. It is associated with groups like Gamaredon Group and APT28.

11745.name: VMConnect
11745.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]VMConnect is a malware that uses the C2 domains www.git-hub.me and tableditermanaging.pro. It employs Multi-Stage Channels for command and control and uses Web Services for C2 relay. Its techniques include Boot or Logon Autostart Execution for persistence, Access Token Manipulation for defense evasion and privilege escalation, and Supply Chain Compromise for initial access. It is known to target processes including vmconnect, vmcompute, and vmms, indicating a focus on virtualization and backup software platforms.[/profile]

11747.name: SentinelSneak
11747.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]SentinelSneak, also known via indicators like tableditermanaging.pro and www.git-hub.me, is a malware that employs Access Token Manipulation and Boot or Logon Autostart Execution for persistence and privilege escalation. It uses Multi-Stage Channels and Web Service techniques for resilient command and control, potentially leveraging compromised supply chains for initial access, as indicated by its connection to the Supply Chain Compromise technique.[/profile]

11748.name: QRLog
11748.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]QRLog is a malware attributed to the Lazarus Group's Labyrinth Chollima sub-group. It employs Multi-Stage Channels for command and control, using initial infrastructure like 'www.git-hub.me' and 'tableditermanaging.pro' to relay to subsequent stages. Its technical behaviors include Access Token Manipulation for privilege escalation and Boot or Logon Autostart Execution for persistence. The malware targets Windows systems and was deployed via a supply chain compromise.[/profile]

11749.name: JokerSpy
11749.profile_without_enhance_5: [profile]JokerSpy is a malware used in a supply chain compromise (T1195) targeting a cryptocurrency exchange in Japan. It employs multi-stage command and control (T1104) and uses web services (T1102) like 'www.git-hub.me' for C2 communication. The malware leverages access token manipulation (T1134) for defense evasion and establishes persistence via boot or logon autostart execution (T1547). It is associated with the Lazarus Group.[/profile]
